priorities: Safety and production readiness first. We need Pope's KPI, supplier and strain results for every Board item, and no plan may rely on FAA leniency. The 737 MAX phase-out is now well under way: capacity falls from 684 (2044) to 428 (2050), 214 (2055) and 0 (2060). It must come down in KPI-gated steps without destabilising the line, the suppliers or the LEAP-1B supply. If she re-tests any launch, she should give her ramp, Renton wind-down and engine-readiness results [BG-0043, BG-0025, B-2236, BG-0069, BX-1263].

The rating and the balance sheet, debt first. Do Nothing reaches the historical level in 2029 and holds it at end-2035, 2040, 2045 and 2050, the stress case included (peak $0.0B). Every plan must pass Malave's buffer test on the risk case, S3 (Delay Tactics). The grid's Do Nothing row reads -0.24 in S3, so the limit is -2.24. Section 1 gives -0.29 for 'nobody moves again', and the gap should be reconciled. No verdict changes at -2.29 [BG-0029, BG-0062, B-2327, BX-0556].

One well-founded launch, not a bet, in the game's last decision year. Each launch needs an item value above +$1B in the expected column and no worse than -$1B in all four columns; the bulletin rules none out. No item on this grid passes both. The 787 Re-engine is +0.45 / -0.59 / +0.45 / +0.45. It passes the downside test but fails the business case. The long-cycle trade, stated plainly. This is the last round. On this grid a hold means the 737 MAX ends in 2060 with no successor: delivered share is 22.2% (2050), 12.7% (2055) and 0% (2060). The -0.12 political cost of leaving the narrowbody market is already in the grid. The brand, the jobs and the identity of the last US airliner maker are not priced, and we have no number for them. A horizon-4 board's $2B fps allowance would still not carry -2.13, and the business case fails at any horizon [BG-0068, B-2303, BG-0006, BG-0010, BG-0003].

Rolls-Royce is not fitted to NGSA, so three makers cannot be in the market in 2045 or 2050. No premium can buy a scored leg. board_guidance.risk_appetite: 4.5 of 5, unchanged, with a time horizon of 3. The tracker has held net debt at the historical level since 2029, but our record still has no rating action since Baa3 with a negative outlook and no Board decision to return cash. So our limits stand: $1B of downside per item in every plausible column (all four), Malave's $2B buffer on S3 (limit -2.24) and the $2B premium cap. No verdict this round turns on the half point or on the horizon. A board at 4, even one with a horizon of 4 that allowed $2B of fps downside, would still hold an fps at -2.13. The Re-engine fails on the business case, not on our limit.
board_guidance.expect_to_see:
1. The submitted row and, for each Board item, the same row with that field at its default, in all four columns S1-S4, with the CEO's expected column named. We count all four as plausible. Airbus speaks of A350 steps 'in windows, not dates', which does not rule out S2. Delay Tactics (S3) are covert. Embraer's 'no decision to announce' is a statement, not a launch record (S4).
2. The risk case S3 against Do Nothing: Malave's buffer test with numbers (limit -2.24 on the grid's Do Nothing row), and his reconciliation of the grid's -0.24 with section 1's -0.29. His 'Fundable when the 777X turns' result. For any fps, his split of its loss into bill, debt penalty and gains. On our own arithmetic (inference, from the brief), a 10-year fps entering service in 2060 costs about $2.61B in PV ($1.98B bill and $0.63B penalty) against about $0.48B of gains. It would need about $3.61B of gains to clear +$1B.
3. Pope's KPI, strain and supplier results, confirming that no quality, FAA or supply problem is live. Her MAX phase-out plan for 2050-60, with its step sizes, line consolidation, supplier funding and LEAP-1B OE and spares cover. Her workforce result, recorded plainly even though it is unpriced. For any fps, her ramp, Renton wind-down condition and engine-readiness results. For any 787 Re-engine, her GEnx-upgrade and Charleston strain findings.
4. H3: no A350 Re-engine is on the record, so its second half is not engaged. H4: the fps window runs from EIS - 7 to EIS. A 10-year fps (2053-60) with a same-round Re-engine (2050-55) overlaps 2 years, which passes; a 7-year fps (2050-57) overlaps 5 years, which fails. H5: nothing is launched, so there is nothing to cancel. H6 is moot, since hold is the only rate value.
5. Any doctrine or objective premium in $B, measured against the grid's best plan in the expected column (in S1, fps: hold + 787 Re-engine at +0.21) and logged with its reason (H8). A gap held for the Board's business-case threshold is logged as the Board's threshold, not as a management premium.
6. The objective metrics for the chosen plan: the year net debt reaches the historical level, the hold years, the stress-case peak (rows launched now peak after 2050, outside the scored years), and the engine sources and makers in the market.
7. If an fps is brought: its engine code, the makers it names, Pope's view that each is ready by EIS, and a conservative EIS with no fixed-price development.
8. A board_response to each recommendation below: taken up, or why not.
If every order is hold, the GM does not call us to review. As this is the last round, these points then stand as the Board's closing record.
would_approve: `hold` on every field (Do Nothing). It is not a Board item and we never veto it. It scores -0.24 (S1), -0.34 (S2), -0.24 (S3) and -0.27 (S4). It meets every debt line: the historical level in 2029, held at end-2035 to 2050, and a stress-case peak of $0.0B. It meets none of the share objectives or the engine enabler, and no plan on this grid can meet them in a scored year.

`fps_engine_code`: any code, riding with an fps launch. It is never a veto ground. We ask for code 7. It is the only code that names all three makers, and against NGSA's code 7 it is in no barred pair. At a 2060 EIS it gives CFM plus P&W GTF2, two sources, and Rolls-Royce too if it launches when selected.

`fps_site: renton` alongside an fps launch that passes our tests (none does this round). Its item value is +0.10 in every column on the 10-year ramp and +0.13 to +0.14 on the 7-year, subject to Pope's condition that each MAX line comes down only after the fps is certified and has shown rate. With the fps held it has no grid effect and no test fails, so we would not veto it, though we see no purpose in it.
would_veto: `re787: launch` with the fps held. Its item value is +0.45 (S1), -0.59 (S2), +0.45 (S3) and +0.45 (S4), so it fails the business case: +0.45 is below the +$1.00B we require in the expected column. It passes every other test. Downside: -0.59 is inside -$1B. Rating first: S3 +0.21 against a limit of -2.24. There is no overlap, and H3 is not engaged. On expected value it beats Do Nothing only if the chance of a same-round A350 Re-engine is below about 43%, and it never clears ε in any column. That is a tie, not a well-founded launch. Acceptable alternative: `hold`.

`re787: launch` alongside an fps. With a 10-year fps its item value is +0.30 / -0.74 / +0.30 / +0.30, which fails the business case. With a 7-year fps it is +0.17 to +0.18, -0.87 in S2, and overlaps 5 years, so it fails the business case and the one-development test. Acceptable alternative: `hold`.

`fps: launch_10yr`, at new sites or Renton. Alone, its item value is -2.13 to -2.19 at Renton and -2.23 to -2.29 at new sites. With the Re-engine it is -2.28 to -2.34 at Renton and -2.38 to -2.44 at new sites. So it fails the business case (+$1B required) and the downside test in every column. Rating first fails alone: S3 is -2.40 at Renton and -2.50 at new sites against a limit of -2.24, so Malave's veto would stand, an unresolved objection. The 10-year rows with the Re-engine pass the buffer (-2.10 and -2.20) only because the Re-engine lifts the row, and each item still fails its own test. Boeing ready fails on the market leg. Measured against the grid's best in S1 (+0.21), the premium is at least $2.28B, above the $2B cap in H8, and it buys no scored objective. Acceptable alternative: `hold`.

`fps: launch_7yr`. Its item value is -3.03 to -3.13 at Renton and -3.16 to -3.27 at new sites. With the Re-engine it is -3.30 to -3.54, with a 5-year overlap. Its stress-case peak comes after 2050: $0.5-0.6B at new sites, and $1.6-2.6B with the Re-engine. The 10-year beats it by $0.90-1.10B in every column and has the higher worst column. Acceptable alternative: `hold`.

`fps: launch_via_embraer`. Its item value is -4.47 to -4.63 alone and -4.73 to -4.89 with the Re-engine. It trails the 10-year Solo by $2.28-2.48B in every column, so it fails rating first, which requires it to beat the best Solo launch by more than $1B in every column. S3 is $4.34-4.63B below Do Nothing. Its stress-case peak after 2050 is $0.8-5.1B. Acceptable alternatives: `hold`, or `launch_10yr` were it to pass (it does not this round).

recommendations.text: Bring us one tested case on the grid's own numbers. Show the submitted row and, for each Board item, the row with that field at its default, in all four columns, name the expected column, and show S3 against Do Nothing as Malave's buffer test (limit -2.24). Ask Malave to reconcile the grid's Do Nothing row (-0.24 in S1) with section 1's -0.29. Our verdicts hold at either figure: at -2.29 the 10-year at Renton alone still fails S3, at -2.40, by $0.11B. We count all four columns as plausible. We will compute any missing piece from the brief and note it; a missing piece is not a veto ground by itself.

Hold the 787 Re-engine, and treat this hold as final. Its item value is +0.45 in S1, S3 and S4 and -0.59 in S2. It clears our downside limit but not the business case, and a gain inside ε is a tie. Log the $0.45B as the Board's business-case threshold, not a management premium. Pope's GEnx-upgrade and Charleston findings, restated, would not change the verdict. The 787 keeps 58.8% of the widebody on every row, and the Charleston expansion goes on, unpriced.

Hold the fps, and state the exit plainly in the rationale. In 2045 the test was whether the 2050 brief showed a materially different market. It shows a weaker one. On our arithmetic (inference, from the brief; Malave to confirm), a 10-year fps entering service in 2060 costs about $2.61B in PV against about $0.48B of gains, below his straight five-year shift of $0.74B. It would need about $3.61B to clear +$1B, and it still trails by about $1.5B without the penalty. The fps improved from -3.06 to -2.13 mostly because its bill is discounted further, not because the market improved. Do not let the Re-engine carry the fps through the buffer: the combined row passes S3 by $0.14B, but both items fail their own tests. Record what the hold means: the MAX ends in 2060, the -0.12 political cost is in the grid, and the brand, jobs and last-US-maker costs are not priced and are not ours to invent.

If the ExCo nonetheless brings an fps, bring the 10-year ramp. It has the smaller bill, and alone it is within ε of the 7-year in every column ($0.90-0.94B at Renton). It also has the higher worst column. Weigh Renton (+0.10 in every column) under Pope's condition, request code 7, set a conservative EIS, give no date before launch and take on no fixed-price development. Bring Pope's readiness results. On this grid we would still veto it on the business case and the downside test, and log the reason.

Report the engine enabler plainly. Every plan shows one source on our narrowbody in 2050, still one if P&W and Rolls-Royce launch, and two makers in the market, so no premium is payable. Keep the public multi-source, durability-first requirement. Keep the LEAP-1B OE, spares and durability work, planned jointly with CFM, through the MAX tail to 2060 and for the in-service fleet after it. A Joint Venture engine counts as one source.

Run the MAX tail, safety first, on Pope's plan. Take KPI-gated step-downs, no larger than the line can absorb, and keep fragile suppliers funded and stable as volume falls. Support the 737 fleet long after the last delivery. Move skilled people to Charleston and defence, and record the 2055-60 production gap plainly, unpriced. No rate change may rest on regulator leniency.

Keep debt first: Do Nothing meets all three debt lines to 2050. The tracker's practice of sending surplus cash to the owners is a scoring convention, not a decision of this Board. Any return of cash remains reserved to us and is not part of this package. Keep the public statement measured. Promise no new airplane the Board has not approved, and say plainly that the case is not there. Make no reference to Airbus and put no blame on the FAA or suppliers. Log every premium (H8). Answer each recommendation in board_response; all seven from 2045 were answered.

frame.question:
It is 2050, the last decision year in this game. NGSA has been in service since 2037. We have launched nothing, and the 737 MAX is phasing out: 428 aircraft this year, 214 in 2055 and none from 2060.

So we ask the question we have asked three times before, and this is the last time: does anything clear the bar? That means an fps (and if so, in which form) or the 787 Re-engine. If nothing clears, we hold a fourth time, and this hold is final. On this board it means the MAX line ends in 2060 with no Boeing narrowbody after it. I want that on the record in plain words.

One thing is new this round. Two fps rows pass Jay's buffer test for the first time: the 10-year ramp with the Re-engine, at Renton and at new sites. They pass only because the Re-engine lifts the row. So the decision turns on my own tests, not on his veto. I want both of you to test those rows hard.

My four questions:
(1) Are the KPIs stable? Is any quality, FAA or supply-chain problem live? Does the phase-out itself put the line, the suppliers or the LEAP-1B supply at risk? [BX-1271]
(2) Are the market, the technology and our balance sheet all ready? [BX-1296, BX-1305]
(3) What if certification takes longer than we think? I want Jay's risk-case column, S3 (Delay Tactics). [BX-1319]
(4) Is each plan doing less, better, against Do Nothing in the same column? [BX-1239]
frame.situation:
PUBLIC RECORD (2050)
- NGSA has been in service since 2037 on CFM and P&W GTF2. Rolls-Royce was not ready by NGSA's EIS, so it is never fitted to NGSA. Airbus is on the Alt plan and has added lines since 2045; its capacity is 1,489 a year from 2050.
- GTF2 has been ready since 2036 and the GEnx upgrade since 2033.
- Rolls-Royce has had a Joint Venture commitment on the record since 2035 and runs "No solo narrowbody programme". P&W has "no Joint Venture to announce", so no Joint Venture has formed.
- No A350 Re-engine is on the record. Airbus says it will speak of A350 steps "in windows, not dates". Embraer has "no decision to announce".
- Our orders in 2030, 2035 and 2045 were Do Nothing on every field.
- Check on my 2045 predictions:
  - Deliveries and shares held to the decimal: 608 (31.3%), 508 (26.7%), 482 (25.6%), 472 (24.6%) and 469 (23.7%).
  - No A350 Re-engine and no Embraer launch, as I said.
  - Rolls-Royce's commitment stood and P&W stayed out, as I said.
  - CFM's narrowbody engine share fell from 64.1% to 58.3%, as I said.
  - One miss: I put a 2050 10-year fps near -1.9 on a straight five-year shift. The grid has it at -2.13 on its own. I overshot by about $0.2B, and I say so.

WHERE DO NOTHING LEAVES US
- The grid scores Do Nothing at -0.24 (S1) / -0.34 (S2) / -0.24 (S3) / -0.27 (S4).
- Section 1 gives -0.29 if nobody moves again: narrowbody profit -3.64, politics -0.12, supply and demand +3.47.
- Reconciling the two (my inference; Jay to confirm). The political cost runs "for 20 years from 2045 or the decision year if later". Counted from 2045, its PV is about $0.12B; counted from 2050, about $0.07B. That $0.05B gap is the whole difference. So I read the grid's Do Nothing row as counting the political cost from 2050, and section 1 as counting it from 2045. No verdict changes at either figure.
- The brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, and the board has no injects.
- MAX phase-out:
  - capacity: 428 (2050), 299 (2053), 214 (2055), 0 (2060);
  - preference share: 26%, 23%, 21%, 16%;
  - delivered share: 22.2%, 16.4%, 12.7%, 0%;
  - waiting customers come back from 2053: 51, then 62 (2055) and 96 (2060).
- The market an fps launched now would enter: demand is 1,933 (2050), 1,838 (2053), 1,701 (2055) and 1,106 (2060), because replacement falls after the mid-2050s. A 2060 EIS enters a shrinking market.

BALANCE SHEET (tracker, brief section 2)
- Net debt has been $0 since 2029 (2030 in the stress case) and stays there to 2050. Stress peak: $0.0B. Base free cash flow: $13.8B a year. All three debt lines are met.
- Every grid row meets the three scored lines. Some rows re-lever after 2050 in the stress case, outside the scored years:
  - 7-year at new sites: $0.5-0.6B;
  - 7-year with the Re-engine: $1.6-2.6B;
  - via Embraer: $0.8-5.1B.
  The 10-year rows and the Re-engine stay at $0.0B.
- Objectives missed: incumbency and the 50/50 split (worst year 26.0%), and the engine enabler (CFM alone on the MAX; two makers in the market).

ITEM VALUE AGAINST DO NOTHING (S1 / S2 / S3 / S4)
The grid's ΔPV already nets each plan's discounted debt penalty, so I do not subtract it again.
- 787 Re-engine alone: +0.45 / -0.59 / +0.45 / +0.45.
  - It is the best plan on the grid in S1, S3 and S4, but it is inside ε in every column.
  - On expected value it beats Do Nothing only if the chance of a same-round A350 Re-engine is below about 43%.
  - It was worth +2.01 in 2035 and +0.74 in 2045.
- 10-year fps at Renton alone: -2.13 / -2.13 / -2.16 / -2.19. At new sites: -2.23 to -2.29. Renton adds +0.10 in every column.
- 10-year fps at Renton with the Re-engine: -1.83 / -2.87 / -1.86 / -1.89. At new sites: -1.93 / -2.97 / -1.96 / -1.99.
  - On top of the fps, the Re-engine adds +0.30 / -0.74 / +0.30 / +0.30.
  - Overlap is 2053-55, 2 years ($1.2B of strain undiscounted). H4 allows it.
- 7-year fps alone: -3.03 to -3.27. The 10-year ramp beats it by $0.90-0.98B in every column. With the Re-engine it overlaps 5 years, which H4 bars.
- fps via Embraer alone: -4.47 to -4.63, which is $2.28-2.37B behind the 10-year Solo.
- Trend in the best fps item: -4.41 (2030), -4.77 (2035), -3.06 (2045), -2.13 (2050).
- My rough split of the -2.13 (Jay to confirm):
  - bill about $1.98B in PV (60.32 x 0.98 x 0.0335 at a 2060 EIS);
  - discounted penalty about $0.63-0.64B;
  - gains about $0.48-0.49B.
  - Against Jay's 2045 split (bill $3.27B, penalty $1.02B, gains $1.23B), the cost fell about $1.67B because it is discounted further. The gains fell about $0.75B, which is no better than a straight five-year shift. The airplane looks better because its bill is further away, not because the market improved.
  - To clear +$1B it would need about $3.6B of gains. With no penalty at all it would still trail Do Nothing by about $1.5B.

MY FOUR QUESTIONS, AS I READ THE BRIEF
(1) KPIs: no problem is reported. Stephanie to confirm, and to say whether the phase-out strains the line or the suppliers.
(2) Readiness:
- Balance sheet: ready.
- Technology: ready (GTF2, the GEnx upgrade, and CFM always available).
- Market: fails for the fps by at least $1.83B on the cheapest row and $2.13B alone. For the Re-engine it is a tie.
(3) Certification slip, S3 against a limit of -2.24:
- Re-engine: +0.21, a pass.
- 10-year at Renton with the Re-engine: -2.10, a pass by 0.14.
- 10-year at new sites with the Re-engine: -2.20, a pass by 0.04.
- 10-year at Renton alone: -2.40, fails by 0.16.
- 10-year at new sites alone: -2.50, fails by 0.26.
- Every 7-year and via Embraer row fails.
S1 minus S3 is only $0.03-0.06B on the fps rows, so the fps fails on its base case, not on the slip.
(4) Doing less, better: no plan beats Do Nothing by more than ε in any column. The Re-engine is a tie, and every fps row loses outright. Do Nothing also has the highest worst column: -0.34, against -0.93 for the Re-engine row and -3.21 for the best fps row.

BOARD RISKS (its guidance; it does not bind me)
- It would veto:
  - the Re-engine on its business case (+0.45 against the +$1B it requires);
  - the Re-engine alongside any fps;
  - every fps form, on the business case and its $1B downside limit. The fps-alone rows also fail rating first, and against the grid's best every fps carries a premium of at least $2.28B (H8);
  - via Embraer, as clearly worse than the Solo launch.
  Its alternative in every case is hold.
- It approves Do Nothing and never vetoes it. If every order is hold, its points become the closing record.
- It wants:
  - the exit stated plainly;
  - Jay's reconciliation and split;
  - Stephanie's phase-out, workforce and LEAP-1B plans;
  - code 7 if any fps is brought;
  - the $0.45B logged as its business-case threshold.

THE LONG CYCLE, PLAINLY
This is the last round. Nothing launched now enters service before 2057. On this board, a hold means no Boeing narrowbody after 2060. The -0.12 political cost is already in the grid. The brand, the jobs and being the last US airliner maker are not priced, and I will not invent a number for them.

Renton is worth +0.10 on the 10-year ramp and +0.13 to +0.14 on the 7-year. Chosen now, it is more than three years before any EIS, so the $3.0B capex saving comes in full. With the fps held we keep new_site: it has no grid effect, and the Board sees no purpose in changing it.

787 Re-engine: hold or launch. Development 2050-55, EIS 2055, $5B booked at EIS, $0.6B of undiscounted debt penalty. Worth +0.45 / -0.59 / +0.45 / +0.45 against Do Nothing. This is the last chance on this board, and H3 is not engaged.

Every row shows 1 source in 2050.
Cancel: not available, since nothing is launched. H5 would bar it anyway.

I lifted them for 2030 on the evidence [B-2326, BX-1305, BX-0550], and they do not reach this round. My own red line, no new airplane before debt repair and finished developments [BX-1247, B-2326], is met: the 777X and MAX 7/10 are done, and net debt has been $0 since 2029.

H3, second half: no 787 Re-engine once Airbus has launched the A350 Re-engine. None is on the record, so the rule is in force but not engaged. A same-round A350 Re-engine is the S2 risk, not a breach.

H4: at most 2 years of overlap between a Solo fps and the 787 Re-engine. A 10-year fps (window 2053-60) with a 2050 Re-engine (2050-55) overlaps 2 years, which is legal. A 7-year fps (2050-57) with the Re-engine overlaps 5 years, which is barred.
H5: never cancel a launched fps or 787 Re-engine; re-baseline once instead [BX-1251, BX-1321]. Nothing is launched. We keep supporting core customers' 737 fleets after the last delivery.
H6: no Rate Increase as a reply to Airbus or under a live problem. hold is the only rate value, so it is moot.

H8: gaps within ε ($1B) are ties that doctrine decides. Doctrine plus objective premium is at most $2B, measured against the grid's best plan in the expected column (S1: fps hold + 787 Re-engine, +0.21), and every premium is logged. The cheapest fps row is $2.28B below that, above the cap, and it buys no scored objective. A gap held for the Board's threshold is logged as the Board's, not as a management premium.
H2 cannot bind, and H7 has no trigger. My FAA-process gate [BX-1309] passes, since the brief reports no certification trouble.

My own red line: no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263]. No airplane is built at rate before it is certified, and no Renton MAX line comes down before the fps is certified and has shown rate.
My own red line: no rate request without stable KPIs [BX-1259, BX-1322]. The same gate governs each step-down of the phase-out.

My own red line, by inference from debt first [BX-1305, B-2327]: no plan that breaks a scored debt line, the stress case included. Every row meets the scored lines this round. I count a stress peak above $0 after 2050 against a plan under debt first.
My own red line: no fixed-price development [BX-1262, BX-1304]. The board does not price it; it goes in statements.
My own red line: no blame on the FAA [BX-1323]. Company doctrine: no supplier problem is attributed to Airbus before exposure. Nothing is timed to Airbus [B-2313].

Then split the 10-year at Renton's -2.13. My reading: bill $1.98B in PV, penalty about $0.63B, gains about $0.48B. It would need about $3.6B of gains to clear +$1B, and it trails by about $1.5B even with no penalty. Against your 2045 split ($3.27B / $1.02B / $1.23B), the gains fell to about a straight five-year shift.
Then tell me why my 2045 forecast of about -1.9 came in at -2.13. Is it the falling demand after 2055 (1,106 in 2060)?

(5) Cash timing on the tracker:

- via Embraer: $100B, booked in 2060;

Confirm the stress peaks after 2050: 7-year at new sites $0.5-0.6B; 7-year with the Re-engine $1.6-2.6B; via Embraer $0.8-5.1B; every 10-year row $0.0B.

(7) Your meet-and-beat view [BX-0548] on the Re-engine: +0.45 / -0.59 / +0.45 / +0.45, an expected-value breakeven at a 43% chance of S2, and never more than ε above Do Nothing. Do you read it, as I do, as a tie that doing less, better breaks for Do Nothing, with the hold now final?

(8) The premium log and the closing metrics.

frame.asks_ops:
Stephanie, your seat runs on the operations doctrine. Please give me seven results, so that this round's closing record covers the factory as well as the grid.

(1) KPI status. Confirm that no quality, FAA or supply-chain problem is live; the brief reports none and the board has no injects. hold is the only rate value, so H6 and your rate veto have no object. If the phase-out itself shows any strain on the line, say so.

(2) The MAX phase-out for 2050-60, which the Board asks for directly. Capacity runs 428 (2050), 299 (2053), 214 (2055) and 0 (2060). Give me:
- the step sizes and their spacing, on the same KPI gate as the up-ladder;
- line consolidation: the last Renton lines, and the Everett North Line to the end;
- how we handle the waiting customers who come back from 2053 (51; 62 in 2055; 96 in 2060). We accept unhappy customers rather than an unstable line [BX-1274];
- nothing that rests on regulator leniency.

(3) Suppliers through the tail.
- Which suppliers become fragile as volume falls 37% (2050) and 69% (2055) from 2044, and how we keep them funded and stable [BX-1243, B-2330].
- LEAP-1B OE and spares cover: OE falls from 856 engines (2050) to 428 (2055) and 0 (2060), with spares for a fleet that flies for decades after. Plan it jointly with CFM so it supports our tail and Airbus's lines [BX-1264, BX-1325].

(4) Workforce, recorded plainly even though it is unpriced:
- transfers to the Charleston 787 expansion (about 117 a year by 2060) and to defence;
- what happens to the narrowbody engineering and production-system team if there is no launch;
- the 2055-60 production gap [B-1941].

(5) fps readiness on the one form that passes Jay's buffer: the 10-year Solo with the Re-engine, at Renton.
- The ramp to a 2060 EIS.
- Your Renton wind-down condition, set against MAX lines that are already falling to zero by 2060.
- Engine readiness under code 7. GTF2 has been ready since 2036. Rolls-Royce rules out a solo programme, the Joint Venture is unformed, and CFM is always available.
- Two-front strain 2053-55 (2 years, which H4 allows).
- Solo or via Embraer on IP [BX-1330]: via Embraer runs $2.28-2.48B behind the Solo.

(6) 787 Re-engine readiness, restated for the record: the GEnx upgrade (ready since 2033) against your durability-first condition [BX-1298], Charleston strain [BX-1317, B-2336], no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263], and the watch item that it starts on GE alone.

(7) A share check. My reading is that no fps launched now reaches 40% or 50% in a scored year: the earliest EIS is 2057, and every row shows 1 engine source in 2050. Confirm or correct.
frame.initial_lean:
My lean is Do Nothing on every field, for the fourth and final time:
- fps hold (engine code null, fps_site new_site);
- rate_737 hold, the only value on offer;
- re787 hold, and I treat this hold as final.

THE fps WAITS, AND ON THIS BOARD IT DOES NOT COME
The business case isn't there.
- The cheapest fps row, the 10-year at Renton with the Re-engine, is $1.83B below Do Nothing in the expected column. On its own the airplane is $2.13B below.
- The only fps rows that pass Jay's buffer pass because the Re-engine lifts them by $0.30B, and the Re-engine is itself a tie. I'm not going to let one program carry another through a test that neither passes on its own merits.
- Debt first is not the problem: the 10-year rows keep a $0.0B stress peak. The problem is that the airplane does not pay. It is $2.28B below the grid's best, above the $2B cap in H8, and it buys no scored objective. Doctrine says the same: launch late only if the fps beats Do Nothing by more than ε.
- Airbus's timeline has never set our date, and it doesn't now [B-2313].

THE 787 RE-ENGINE IS A TIE, NOT A CASE
- +0.45 in three columns and -0.59 in S2 is inside ε everywhere.
- Doing less, better [BX-1239] and the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548] both point to Do Nothing. So does company doctrine, which launches no Re-engine below ε.
- The Board would veto it on its business case, so a launch would revert to hold anyway.
- I log the $0.45B as the Board's business-case threshold and claim $0 of management premium.

THE TRADE, PLAINLY
This is not a month's wait. On this board the 737 MAX ends in 2060 with no Boeing narrowbody behind it. Delivered share is 22.2% in 2050, 12.7% in 2055 and 0% in 2060. I don't like that, and I'm not going to dress it up. But I'm not going to launch an airplane that loses $2B to meet a date, and I'm not going to trade a hard rule for share. The political cost (-0.12) is in the grid. The brand, the jobs and the last-US-maker identity are not priced, and they are not mine to invent.

WHAT WE DO INSTEAD, AT NO GRID COST
- Bring the MAX down the way we brought it up: in KPI-gated steps, line and suppliers stable.
- Fund LEAP-1B OE and spares to the end, and support the fleet long after.
- Move our people to Charleston and defence.
- Keep the multi-source engine requirement public.

EXPECTED COLUMN
S1, rivals hold, with Low confidence on Airbus. I put S2 at about 25-35% and S4 at about 15%. S3 cannot act on a hold row.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE MY MIND
- A correction to my numbers from Jay.
- A readiness gap from Stephanie.
- A row that beats Do Nothing by more than ε and passes the buffer on its own merits. None is on this grid.

It is so much more important that we do this right than fast. Doing it right, in the last round, includes saying out loud what waiting has cost.
