cfo.would_change_mind_if:
fps:
- My binding veto on the 10-year alone, the 7-year and via Embraer lifts only if the grid's S3 figures change, for example through a GM correction, so that a row sits no more than $2B below Do Nothing. At -2.29 instead of -2.24 nothing changes.
- On the 10-year with the Re-engine, I would move from advice to support only if three things held: the fps passed the buffer on its own, with headroom that survives a realistic overrun; it beat Do Nothing by more than ε, or came within H8's $2B cap of the grid's best with a scored objective to show for it; and every debt line held with a $0.0B stress peak. None of the three is on this grid.
787 Re-engine:
- I would move to launch only if the ExCo and the Board judged S2 implausible. My tie-break would then favour it: its worst column would be S4 at +0.18, against Do Nothing's -0.27. The Board's +$1B business case would still fail it.
- Never once an A350 Re-engine is on the record (H3).
Cash:
- I would revisit any plan if the tracker showed a debt line at risk on the chosen row, the stress case included.
- A live problem in the MAX phase-out, reported by Pope, would strengthen the hold, not change it.
cfo.memo:
Kelly, closing numbers, risk case as baseline.

Buffer test, S3 no lower than -2.24: Do Nothing passes at -0.24, the Re-engine row at +0.21. The 10-year with the Re-engine passes, by $0.14B at Renton and $0.04B at new sites. Everything else fails: the 10-year alone by $0.16-0.26B, the 7-year by $0.91-1.22B, via Embraer by $2.34-2.63B. My veto on those binds under the team rule. At -2.29 no verdict changes.

My test reads the row as written, and I won't stretch it. But that pass isn't protected. Delay Tactics don't touch the Re-engine, so it lifts S3 by $0.30B; in S2 it takes $0.74B away and the row sits $2.87B below Do Nothing. A $2.7B overrun on the fps bill at Renton, $0.8B at new sites, uses up the margin. That is not a baseline we can meet and beat, and at $2.28B below the grid's best it breaks H8's $2B cap.

Your reconciliation is right: the political cost is $0.07B from 2050, $0.12B from 2045. The split: bill $1.98B, penalty $0.62B, gains $0.47B. We both landed near -1.9; the miss is in operating gains, mostly a smaller 2060 market and a deeper lead deficit.

The Re-engine is a tie, and Do Nothing has the higher worst column. So hold on every field, $0 of management premium, $0.45B logged as the Board's threshold. Debt stays at the historical level, barring a launch that re-levers it. While disappointing, this is the higher-confidence plan: the MAX ends in 2060 with no successor.

tests.name: On-time, predictable delivery (record: BX-1331, applied to airplanes by inference; CEO ask 3)
tests.threshold: Can each plan's EIS be delivered as stated? Read the risk-case column S3 (Delay Tactics) against S1 and say how much of each plan's value depends on the nominal date. Where S3 does not test a plan's own date, read its worst column.
tests.numbers: S3 minus S1 by row: Do Nothing 0.00 (-0.24 in both); Re-engine row 0.00 (+0.21 in both); 10-year fps -0.03 in all four forms; 7-year -0.05 to -0.06; via Embraer -0.03. At most 1.9% of any fps row's value (0.06 of -3.09) rides on the fps date, so every fps fails on its bill, not on its date. The CEO's reading is confirmed. S3 does not test the Re-engine's own date. Its worst column is S2 (row -0.93, item -0.59), which is a rival-timing risk, not a delivery risk. The board does not price our own slip. Doctrine priors (profile.md, inference): clean sheet +3 years central (range +2 to +5); major derivative +2 (range +1 to +4). Applied: a 10-year fps EIS of 2060 becomes 2063, three years after the MAX's last delivery in 2059, and a 7-year EIS of 2057 becomes 2060. The Re-engine's 2055 becomes 2057. My sensitivity is about $0.04B of item value per year of Re-engine slip (0.45 x (1 - 1/1.105)): $0.08B at +2 years and $0.15B at +4 (inference). Do Nothing delivers exactly the capacity path: 428 (2050), 299 (2053), 214 (2055), 0 (2060). Basis: my record for the delivery-first rule, doctrine for the priors.

tests.name: KPI gate: the test behind my binding veto (doctrine; CEO ask 1)
tests.threshold: No Rate Increase while a quality, FAA or supply-chain problem is live. Steps of 5, at least 6 months apart, KPI-gated. Never a reply to Airbus (H6). No plan may rely on FAA leniency.
tests.numbers: Confirmed: the brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, and the board has no injects. rate_737 hold is the only value on offer, so my veto has no object and H6 is moot. The brief carries no measured KPI data, so this confirms that no problem is reported; it is not a six-KPI result [B-2283]. No plan relies on FAA leniency. The FAA holds the rate lever [B-2236], and certification timing stays with the FAA [B-2241]. Does the phase-out itself make a problem live? No. It is the game's assumption, the same in every row and in the status quo, and the brief reports no supplier distress. Three watch items, none live: (a) the line is now capacity-bound (437 aircraft wanted against 428 delivered in 2050), so the step-downs pace it, not demand; (b) supplier volume is down 37% now and 69% by 2055; (c) LEAP-1B becomes a shrinking minority of CFM's narrowbody book (supplier test).

tests.name: MAX phase-out 2050-60: steps, lines and waiting customers (doctrine plus inference; CEO ask 2; the Board's ask)
tests.threshold: Run the step-downs on the same KPI gate as the up-ladder: no step larger than 5 a month, steps at least 6 months apart (B-2351 applied to step-downs, inference). A step is taken only on stable KPIs at the current rate, and it is never deferred past the capacity path the rules fix. Curtail with a little more demand than airplanes [B-1031]. Accept waiting customers rather than an unstable line [BX-1274]. Nothing rests on regulator leniency.
tests.numbers:
Capacity falls 42.75 aircraft a year, 3.6 a month each year: 35.7 a month (2050), 32.1 (2051), 28.5 (2052), 24.9 (2053), 21.4 (2054), 17.8 (2055), 14.2 (2056), 10.7 (2057), 7.1 (2058), 3.6 (2059), 0 (2060).
- Steps: ten annual step-downs of about 3.5 a month, 12 months apart, each under the cap of 5. The steepest stretch, 2044-46 (-14.7 a month), is behind us.
- Line consolidation (inference; about 15.7 a month per Renton line, Everett North at 10, up to 15 as on the Renton plan): two Renton lines plus Everett North to 2052, and one Renton line from 2053. The last Renton line closes in 2056, and Everett North carries the MAX alone, at 15 a month or less, to the last delivery in 2059. No line closes in the same 6 months as a rate step, and each closure waits for stable KPIs at the receiving line (inference).
- Waiting customers: 51 (2053), 62 (2055), 96 (2060). From 2050 deliveries equal capacity (428 of the 437 wanted), so we end with a little more demand than airplanes, which holds pricing [B-1031]. We tell customers plainly. The flexible ones (49%) take Airbus slots, and a tenth of the rest drop out each year. We do not speed up the line for them [BX-1274], and on the rules no Boeing order can add MAX capacity anyway. On a final hold, the 96 waiting in 2060 have no Boeing airplane to wait for.
- Every step and line move stays inside the FAA-supervised production system; none assumes a waiver [B-2236].

tests.name: Suppliers through the tail, and LEAP-1B OE and spares (doctrine; CEO ask 3)
tests.threshold: Supplier readiness is a hard gate [B-2308]. Keep fragile suppliers funded and hot [BX-1243, B-2330], with buffers [B-2043]. Plan engine supply jointly with CFM [BX-1264, BX-1325].
tests.numbers:
No live supply problem is reported. MAX volume against 2044 (684 a year): -37% (2050), -56% (2053), -69% (2055), -100% (2060).
- Fragile as volume falls (inference): sole-source MAX parts (LEAP-1B, and the fuselage, now in-house [B-2195]), and the suppliers we kept above rate because they needed support [B-2330, BX-1243]. Their fixed cost per shipset rises as volume falls.
- Keep them funded and stable, in doctrine's order: embedded staff [B-0073, B-2097], buffers [B-2043], requalified second sources [B-2285], funding [B-2174, B-2264], and acquisition only as a last resort [B-2195]. Before each supplier's last OE shipset, agree the spares and tooling it keeps for the in-service fleet (inference).
- LEAP-1B OE: 856 engines (2050), 598 (2053), 428 (2055), 0 (2060), plus spares for a fleet that flies for decades. Against Airbus's public signal of 41-45 CFM sets a month for NGSA (to 2050), our -1B tail is about 44-46% of CFM's new narrowbody sets in 2050 and 28-30% in 2055 (inference). CFM says OE comes first and spares never crowd it out, and it claims no -1B durability before the fleet proves it; we claim none either. Plan OE, spares and durability jointly with CFM, rate-gated, to 2060 and beyond, so CFM can support our tail and Airbus's lines [BX-1264, BX-1325].
- None of this adds a second MAX engine source: 1 source and 2 makers in every row.

tests.name: Two-front strain and engineering capacity (doctrine; H4; one major development at a time)
tests.threshold: A Solo fps and the 787 Re-engine overlap at most 2 years. Strain = $3B x overlap / 5, counting the fps from EIS-7 to EIS and the Re-engine from EIS-5 to EIS [B-0341].
tests.numbers:
Recommended plan (Do Nothing): overlap 0, strain $0.
- Re-engine alone (2050-55): $0.
- 10-year fps (2053-60) with the Re-engine (2050-55): overlap 2053-55, 2 years, $1.2B undiscounted (about $0.07-0.08B in PV, inference). H4 allows it.
- 7-year fps (2050-57) with the Re-engine: 5 years, $3.0B. H4 bars it (flag below).
- Caveat (inference): the tracker spreads the 10-year bill over 2050-59, starting at 5% in year 1, so engineering staffs both programmes from 2050; the board counts only the heavy years. The combined row is the most loaded legal row: two developments at the 2-year cap. On top of the fps, the Re-engine adds +0.30 against +0.45 alone. Of the $0.15B lost, I put about $0.07-0.08B on strain and, by inference, the rest on the convex debt penalty (Malave to confirm).
- The Charleston expansion is production capacity, not a development [BX-1317, B-2336].

tests.name: Ramp choice, 7- or 10-year, with engine margin (inference: BX-1331)
tests.threshold: Which ramp can operations deliver predictably with the engines, workforce and suppliers in the brief? Give each ramp's strain, EIS, worst column and engine margin [BX-1298, B-2304].
tests.numbers:
- 10-year: EIS 2060 (2063 at the +3 prior). Strain $0 alone, $1.2B with the Re-engine. Worst column alone -2.47 at Renton and -2.57 at new sites; with the Re-engine -3.21 and -3.31. Stress peak $0.0B.
- 7-year: EIS 2057 (2060 at the prior). Strain $3.0B with the Re-engine, which is barred. Worst column alone -3.37 and -3.50; with the Re-engine -4.24 and -4.37. Stress peaks after 2050: $0.5-0.6B at new sites, $1.6-2.6B with the Re-engine.
- The 10-year beats the 7-year in every column: by $0.90-0.98B alone and $1.02-1.10B with the Re-engine.
- Engine margin under code 7: GTF2 (ready 2036) has 24 years to a 2060 EIS and 21 to 2057. UltraFan NB, if launched on selection now, would be ready in 2057: 3 years of margin to 2060, none to 2057. A Joint Venture formed now would be ready in 2056: 4 years, or 1.
If any fps is launched, the 10-year is the ramp operations can deliver predictably.

tests.name: fps readiness on the one form that passes the buffer: 10-year Solo plus the Re-engine at Renton (doctrine plus inference; CEO ask 5)
tests.threshold: The ramp can be delivered to EIS. Each named engine is ready by EIS, durability first [BX-1298, B-2304]. No production-certification concurrency, and each Renton MAX line comes down only after the fps is certified and has shown rate [BX-1263]. Strain within H4. Solo or partner on IP [BX-1330]. And the CEO's question: does the row pass only on the Re-engine's back?
tests.numbers:
- The Re-engine's back: yes. S3 -2.10 passes the -2.24 limit by $0.14B. Without the Re-engine the row is -2.40 and fails by $0.16B. The Re-engine's +0.30 in S3 is the whole margin, and in S2 it costs -0.74, which gives this row the worst S2 of the 10-year Renton rows (-3.21).
- Ramp: development 2050-59, EIS 2060 (2063 at the +3 prior). On NGSA's ramp shape it reaches 50 a month about 2064 and 100 about 2068. No fps is built at rate before certification [BX-1263].
- Renton: the condition holds on this timetable. The MAX needs no Renton line from 2056, so the fps takes freed lines and no MAX line comes down for it, while Everett North carries the MAX to 2059. Renton is worth +0.10 in every column: the $3.0B capex saving in full (3.0 x 0.0335 at 2060), with no delivery effect. Risk: the Renton lines stand idle 2056-60 (to 2063 at the prior), and their tooling, people and suppliers must be kept warm.
- Engines under code 7: CFM + GTF2, 2 sources at 2060, but none in a scored year. GTF2 has flown on NGSA since 2037, but P&W will give no time-on-wing figure until the fleet has measured it. My durability-first condition wants that record before the code is final (it can change until EIS). Rolls-Royce rules out a solo programme, the Joint Venture is unformed, and CFM is always available.
- Strain: 2053-55, 2 years, $1.2B, which is legal.
- Solo, not via Embraer (IP test).
The row passes on readiness, but readiness does not decide it. It fails the visible-demand test below, and it fails on value: item -1.83 / -2.87 / -1.86 / -1.89 against Do Nothing.

tests.name: 787 Re-engine readiness for a 2050 launch and a 2055 EIS, restated (doctrine; CEO ask 6; the Board's ask)
tests.threshold: An engine path on the record and ready by EIS, durability first [BX-1298]. Engineering capacity free. No production-certification concurrency [BX-1263]. Charleston capacity for the added demand [BX-1317, B-2336].
tests.numbers:
- Engine: the GEnx upgrade has been ready since 2033, 22 years ahead of a 2055 EIS, and CFM/GE calls it ready for 787 customers. GE's widebody engine share moved to 44.8% in 2042. My durability-first condition is met.
- Engineering: one development, strain $0.
- Concurrency: no re-engined 787 is built at rate before certification, and Charleston builds today's 787 until then [BX-1263, B-2228].
- Charleston: on the board the 787 stays at 100 a year (8.3 a month) on every hold row. With a Re-engine entering service in 2055, +1 pp a year takes it to about 108 by 2060 (9.0 a month) and 117 by 2065 (9.75), well inside rates in the teens. Correction: the figure of 117 by 2060 in our 2045 public record assumed a 2045 launch (EIS 2050). It does not hold after the hold we took.
- Watch item: it starts on GE alone. Rolls-Royce (55.2% of widebody engines) has no 787 upgrade on the record [B-0940].
- Slip: the +2-year central prior costs about $0.08B.
Value is +0.45 / -0.59 / +0.45 / +0.45, inside epsilon in every column, so readiness does not decide it; company doctrine launches no Re-engine below epsilon. H3 is in force but not engaged.

tests.name: Invest or partner on IP: fps via Embraer (record: BX-1330, BX-1333, applied by inference)
tests.threshold: fps Solo where Boeing owns the airframe IP. Via Embraer only if the partner adds what Boeing lacks.
tests.numbers: The bill is $100B against $60.32B (+$39.68B), with the same 2060 EIS and no strain or capacity relief on the board. Alone it runs $2.37B behind the 10-year Solo in S1-S3 and $2.28B in S4; with the Re-engine, $2.48B and $2.39B. The S4 narrowing ($0.09B) is the one thing the partner brings: it blocks Embraer's own narrowbody. Stress peaks after 2050: $1.8-3.1B alone, $0.8-5.1B with the Re-engine. The Solo fps and the 787 Re-engine build on our own IP: invest, don't partner.

tests.name: Capacity follows demand: the Rate Increase (one remark: BX-1329; inference)
tests.threshold: Back the Rate Increase only where it adds value against the same plan without it in the expected column, and only where the demand is visible.
tests.numbers: rate_737 hold is the only value; the Rate Increase was a 2030-only order. The grid has no Rate Increase rows. The rules phase out the MAX whatever Boeing orders, so no board lever adds MAX capacity.

tests.name: Capacity follows visible demand: an fps line entering service in 2060 (inference from BX-1329)
tests.threshold: Add capacity where the demand is visible. Set the fps line's ramp against Boeing's visible demand at EIS in the brief.
tests.numbers: In 2060 market demand is 1,106 (replacement 553). COMAC takes 250 off the top, and our preference share is 16%, which leaves 137 new customers a year for us (11.4 a month) plus 96 waiting. At the long-run split a 2060 EIS earns (27%, 23 years behind NGSA), the same 856 new customers give about 231 a year (19 a month), reached around 2071. The fps line ramps on NGSA's shape to 50 a month about four years after EIS and 100 about eight: 2.6 to 5 times the visible demand. Everett North plus one Renton line (about 31 a month) would carry that demand. Airbus has slack (1,489 against 1,106), so no overflow comes to us. The brief gives no demand after 2060, so this is a reading of the brief, not a forecast (inference).

tests.name: Working capital and cash conversion (record: BX-1327, BX-1332, BX-1326, applied by inference)
tests.threshold: For each option, when the bill lands and what it does to cash, as a number. Every scored debt line met, the stress case included.
tests.numbers:
- Do Nothing: no bill. Free cash flow is $13.79B a year ($9.19B in the stress case). Net debt has been $0 since 2029 (2030 in the stress case); stress peak $0.0B.
- Re-engine: $5B over 2050-55, about $1.0B a year (7% of base and 11% of stress free cash flow), booked in 2055. Stress peak $0.0B. Undiscounted penalty $0.6B.
- 10-year fps: $60.32B over 2050-59 ($59.11B after the 2% government share). About $3.0B in 2050 and $8.3B at the year-7 peak (2056): 60% of base and 90% of stress free cash flow. At the tracker's 79%, stress free cash flow stays about $2.7B positive in the peak year (inference). Stress peak $0.0B at either site, with or without the Re-engine. Penalty $19.1B.
- 7-year fps: $65.00B over 2050-56, about $9.1B a year, close to stress free cash flow. Stress peaks after 2050: $0.5-0.6B at new sites, $1.6-2.6B with the Re-engine. Penalty $22.0B.
- Via Embraer: $100B, about $9.8B a year with a $13.7B peak year, about equal to base free cash flow. Stress peaks $0.8-5.1B. Penalty $52.5B.
The CEO's cash timing is confirmed. Recommended plan: pass.

tests.name: Share objectives an fps could buy (rules arithmetic, inference; CEO ask 7)
tests.threshold: Incumbency: preference share of at least 40% in a scored year. The 50/50 split: at least 50%.
tests.numbers: Your reading is confirmed. The scored years end in 2050, when preference is 26% in every row, and the earliest EIS is 2057. Long-run split from a launch now: 30/70 (7-year, 20 years behind NGSA) or 27/73 (10-year, 23 years behind). Starting from 19% (2057) or 16% (2060), Boeing gains 1 pp a year and reaches the split around 2068 or 2071 (inference). Delay Tactics take 5 pp for 5 years from EIS. No fps reaches 40% or 50% in any year. Every row shows 1 engine source in 2050, and still 1 if P&W and Rolls-Royce launch.

tests.name: Trained workforce through the phase-out (the operating seat's judgement, dashboard_game.md §3; inference; CEO ask 4)
tests.threshold: A successor line ready as the MAX phases out, so that the trained workforce and the suppliers keep their work. State the gap in aircraft a year.
tests.numbers:
The board does not price this. Output against 2044, on capacity: -37% (2050), -56% (2053), -69% (2055), -81% (2057), -94% (2059), -100% (2060). On a final hold, this board has no Boeing narrowbody output after 2059, ever. A 10-year launch now puts EIS at 2060 (2063 at the prior): 0 to 3 years of zero output, with the MAX at 43-128 a year in 2057-59. A 7-year launch puts it at 2057 (2060 at the prior). No launch closes the 2055-60 trough.
Plan (doctrine and inference):
(1) Move production people as each step lands: to defence, reversing the 2011-13 move of about 8,000 people into Commercial Airplanes [B-0729], and to Charleston. On the board, though, the 787 stays at 100 a year on a hold, so Charleston absorbs few people on volume.
(2) Keep the experienced narrowbody core on Everett North and the last Renton line to 2059.
(3) With no launch, the narrowbody engineering and production-system team has no airplane. Keep its core on support for the 737 fleet, which runs for decades after the last delivery, and on defence. Fleet support is services work, my BGS record (inference) [BX-1329, BX-1327].
(4) If a launch ever comes, hire at launch, as Boeing hired 10,000 engineers in 2022 [B-1941].
This is advice, not a premium ground: the cheapest fps is $1.83B below Do Nothing and $2.28B below the grid's best.

vetoes.plan: rate_737: increase
vetoes.ground: KPI doctrine veto not invoked. No Rate Increase is on offer (hold is the only value), the brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, and the board has no injects, so my veto has no object. The same KPI gate governs each step-down of the phase-out: a step is taken on the data, and the line steps down early rather than hold a rate it cannot support.

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_7yr together with re787: launch (same round)
vetoes.ground: Hard-rule flag H4, not my veto. The overlap is 5 years (fps 2050-57 against the Re-engine 2050-55), with $3.0B of undiscounted strain, beyond the 2-year cap. The stress-case debt peaks after 2050 at $1.6-2.6B. The rule binds the CEO.

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_10yr (Renton or new sites) together with re787: launch
vetoes.ground: Advice, not a veto and not a red line. It is operations-ready and H4-legal (overlap 2053-55, 2 years, $1.2B). But it passes Malave's buffer only on the Re-engine's +0.30: S3 is -2.10 against the -2.24 limit, and the fps alone is -2.40. It is our most loaded legal row (two developments at the overlap cap), and it fails capacity-follows-demand: 11-19 a month of visible demand against a line built for 50, then 100.

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_7yr (any site)
vetoes.ground: Advice: the 7-year leaves UltraFan NB no margin to a 2057 EIS, runs $0.90-1.10B behind the 10-year ramp in every column, and its stress-case debt peaks after 2050 at $0.5-0.6B at new sites.

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_via_embraer
vetoes.ground: Advice: it fails invest-or-partner on IP. The bill is $100B against $60.32B, with the same EIS and no strain or capacity relief. It runs $2.28-2.48B behind the 10-year Solo in every column, with stress-case debt peaks of $0.8-5.1B after 2050.

vetoes.plan: re787: launch
vetoes.ground: Advice, not a veto. The Re-engine is operations-ready: the GEnx upgrade is 22 years ahead of a 2055 EIS, strain is $0, and Charleston fits. I recommend hold because its value is inside epsilon (+0.45 / -0.59 / +0.45 / +0.45) and company doctrine launches no Re-engine below epsilon, not on any readiness ground. If the CEO launches it, my conditions are: (1) no re-engined 787 built at rate before certification; (2) a conservative public EIS, with the slip range published at launch (about $0.04B of value a year, $0.08B at +2 years); (3) under H5, re-baseline once and never cancel, even if Airbus re-engines the A350 in the same round.

ops.would_change_mind_if: Any of the following would change my orders. (1) A brief that reports a live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. I would hold every development until it clears, and my KPI veto would bind against any rate step (none is on offer) and pace the step-downs. (2) A durability problem on the GEnx upgrade, or a withdrawn engine path: then no Re-engine, on readiness grounds. (3) An A350 Re-engine on the record: no 787 Re-engine (H3). (4) A corrected grid that shows the Re-engine above +$1B in the expected column and no worse than -$1B in any column: I would recommend launching it, since operations is ready. If the CEO breaks this tie for the Re-engine, I have no operations ground against it. (5) An fps row that beats Do Nothing by more than epsilon and passes Malave's buffer on its own merits, with visible demand near the line's rate. Then I would back the 10-year Solo with code 7, at Renton under my wind-down condition, with no date before launch and the slip range published at launch. (6) A partner that brings capital, capacity or IP Boeing lacks, so that via Embraer beats the Solo by more than epsilon in every column. (7) A supplier exit signal in the MAX tail, or -1B durability data that shows a problem. That triggers the supplier doctrine (embed, buffer, requalify, fund, acquire), and if the brief reports it as live, it gates the step-downs.
ops.memo:
My record is thin. The KPI, supplier, strain and workforce results are Boeing's operations doctrine; the delivery, IP, demand and cash tests are my 2022 BGS rules, applied by inference.

First and foremost, on-time predictable delivery. No quality, FAA or supply-chain problem is reported and no rate order is open, so my veto is idle. Capacity falls 3.6 a month each year, from 35.7 now to zero in 2060. We take one step a year, under 5, on the data. Two Renton lines to 2052, one from 2053, Everett North alone from 2056 to the last delivery in 2059. We accept 51 to 96 waiting customers rather than an unstable line.

Second, suppliers. Volume is down 37% now and 69% by 2055. Keep sole-source parts funded and hot. LEAP-1B OE falls from 856 engines to 428, then zero. Lock in OE and spares with CFM.

Third, the 787 Re-engine is operations-ready: the GEnx upgrade is 22 years ahead of EIS, with zero strain. At +$0.45B it is a tie, and doctrine holds it.

Fourth, the fps. The 10-year row with the Re-engine passes the buffer by $0.14B only because the Re-engine adds $0.30B. Demand is not visible: at a 2060 EIS, customers want 11 to 19 airplanes a month from us, against a line built for 50, then 100.

And finally, the workforce. On a final hold, Boeing builds no narrowbody after 2059. The 787 stays at 100 a year, so Charleston absorbs few people. Record it plainly.

other_moves.move: 737 fleet support for the life of the fleet
other_moves.detail: We support every 737 operator long after the last delivery: spares, engineering support, maintenance data and fleet upgrades, through Boeing's services business. This is customer trust in every transaction [BX-1273], and it is where the narrowbody engineering core keeps working. No grid effect.

other_moves.move: Charleston 787 capacity: paced to the demand we can see, with a correction to our 2045 public figure
other_moves.detail: Correction: our 2045 public move said Pope found about 117 787s a year by 2060. That figure assumed a 787 Re-engine launched in 2045 (EIS 2050), which we did not do, so it does not hold. On today's plan the 787 runs at about 100 a year (8.3 a month) and keeps 58.8% of the widebody market. Charleston keeps the capacity the 787 needs, with headroom for hiccups [BX-1317, B-2336, BX-1275]. We add no capacity ahead of demand we cannot see (Pope's capacity-follows-demand test). It is unpriced and funded inside the debt lines. I'd rather correct it now than let it stand [BX-1284].

other_moves.move: Engine supply position: multi-source and durability first (restated, no launch)
other_moves.detail: Our position on engine supply for any Boeing narrowbody is unchanged: a stable supply of parts, engines first, more than one engine source, and durability ahead of everything else [BX-1298]. There is no launch, no date and no engine selection. Code 7 is the request if a case is ever brought. This serves Control's engine enabler at no grid cost. A Joint Venture engine would count as one source. No scored enabler leg can be bought on this board: 1 source on the 737 MAX and two makers in the market.

other_moves.move: Zero-for-zero tariffs in civil aerospace, with the industry
other_moves.detail: We keep working with industry associations for a tariff-free regime for aircraft and parts. It is good for everyone in the industry [B-2290]. No grid effect.

other_moves.move: 737 MAX phase-out 2050-60 on Pope's KPI-gated plan
other_moves.detail: Capacity falls about 3.6 a month each year: 35.7 a month (2050), 24.9 (2053), 17.8 (2055), 3.6 (2059), 0 (2060). Ten annual step-downs of about 3.5 a month, 12 months apart, each under the 5-a-month cap; the up-ladder rule B-2351 applied to step-downs (doctrine, inference). A step is taken only on stable KPIs at the current rate, and we step down early rather than hold a rate the line cannot support. Lines: two Renton lines plus Everett North to 2052, one Renton line from 2053, the last Renton line closed in 2056, and Everett North alone (15 a month or less) to the last delivery in 2059. No line closes in the same six months as a rate step, and each closure waits for stable KPIs at the receiving line. Waiting customers (51 in 2053, 62 in 2055, 96 in 2060) are told plainly. We accept them rather than an unstable line [BX-1274, B-1031]. Nothing rests on regulator leniency; every step stays inside the FAA-supervised production system [B-2236].

other_moves.move: Keep fragile suppliers funded and stable through the tail, with last-shipset agreements
other_moves.detail: MAX volume against 2044 is -37% (2050), -56% (2053), -69% (2055) and -100% (2060), so fixed cost per shipset rises for sole-source parts and for the suppliers we kept above rate [BX-1243, B-2330]. Doctrine's order: embedded staff, buffers, requalified second sources, funding, and acquisition only as a last resort [B-0073, B-2043, B-2285, B-2174, B-2195]. Before each supplier's last OE shipset, we agree the spares and tooling it keeps for the in-service fleet (Pope, inference). We name no supplier problem in public.

other_moves.move: LEAP-1B OE, spares and durability cover to 2060 and beyond, planned jointly with CFM
other_moves.detail: OE falls from 856 engines (2050) to 598 (2053), 428 (2055) and 0 (2060), with spares for a fleet that flies for decades after. The plan is joint and rate-gated, so CFM can support our tail and our competitor's lines [BX-1264, BX-1325]. We make no -1B durability claim before CFM reports the fleet data. This adds no second MAX engine source.

other_moves.move: Workforce through the phase-out, recorded plainly (unpriced)
other_moves.detail: Output against 2044 is -37% (2050), -69% (2055), -94% (2059) and -100% (2060). With this final hold, Boeing builds no narrowbody after 2059. Plan: (1) move production people to defence as each step lands, reversing the 2011-13 move of about 8,000 people into Commercial Airplanes [B-0729]. Charleston takes few on volume, since the 787 stays at about 100 a year. (2) Keep the experienced narrowbody core on Everett North and the last Renton line to 2059. (3) Move the narrowbody engineering and production-system team to 737 fleet support and defence; with no launch it has no new airplane. (4) Record the 2055-60 production gap, and the end of narrowbody output after 2059, without putting a number on them.

other_moves.move: Close the fps and 787 Re-engine files with the full record
other_moves.detail: For the Board's closing record: the 2030, 2035, 2045 and 2050 tests, Malave's split for each round, Pope's readiness results, and the trend in the best fps item (-4.41, -4.77, -3.06, -2.13) and the Re-engine (+2.01 in 2035, +0.74 in 2045, +0.45 in 2050). The record shows the fps improved only because its bill is discounted further, not because the market improved. No fixed-price development was ever offered [BX-1262, BX-1304].

other_moves.move: Return of cash to owners: reserved to the Board
other_moves.detail: The tracker sends surplus cash to the owners as a scoring convention. Any real return of cash is a Board decision and is not part of this package (Board recommendation 7).

decision.public_statement:
The balance sheet is where it belongs, and it has stayed there for a long time. The 737 and 787 lines are running stable. A lot of people built that by doing it the right way every day, and we're not going to give it back.

The 737 MAX is in the last decade of its production life. We're bringing the rate down the way we brought it up: one step at a time, on the data, keeping the line and our suppliers stable. Some customers will wait longer than they'd like. I don't take that lightly, but I'd much rather have a customer waiting than a production system that goes unstable. And when the last 737 leaves the line, we'll keep supporting that fleet for as long as it flies. Every operator flying a 737 can count on that.

On a new single-aisle airplane, I'll be straight with you. We looked at it again this year, and we looked hard. We're ready financially, and the technology is there. The business case isn't. So we are not launching a new single-aisle airplane. I'm not going to launch an airplane that doesn't pay, and I'm not going to launch one to meet a date. I'm also not going to pretend this decision is free. It isn't. It matters to our people, to our customers and to our suppliers, and we'll own it. If that case ever changes, the terms won't: the market, the technology and us all ready, more than one engine source with durability first, headroom in the schedule, and no development at a fixed price. You won't get a date from me before a launch.

Our people are staying with us. As the 737 steps down, skilled people will move into defence, into the 787 and into supporting the fleet in service.

One correction. Last time we put a number on 787 output out to 2060. That number assumed a step we didn't take, so it doesn't hold. Charleston will be sized to the 787 demand we can see, with headroom. I'd rather correct it now than let it stand.

We'll keep working with the whole industry for a tariff-free environment in aerospace. That's good for everybody in this business.

It is so much more important that we do this right than fast. And doing it right includes saying plainly what we've decided and what it costs.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: Do Nothing on every field, for the fourth and final time: fps hold (engine code null, fps_site new_site), rate_737 hold, re787 hold. Every order is the default, so no Board item goes up. It scores -0.24 (S1) / -0.34 (S2) / -0.24 (S3) / -0.27 (S4).

THE TEAM RULE, APPLIED
- Malave's binding veto (buffer test, S3 at or above -2.24 against the grid's Do Nothing row) strikes the 10-year alone (Renton -2.40, new sites -2.50), every 7-year row (-3.15 to -3.46) and every via-Embraer row (-4.58 to -4.87). No verdict changes at -2.29.
- He reads his test as applying to the row as written, so the 10-year with the Re-engine (Renton -2.10, new sites -2.20) carries no veto from him. I accept that ruling, and I do not ask him to stretch his test. That row is struck on my own tests (below), not on his.
- Pope's KPI veto has no object: no quality, FAA or supply-chain problem is live, the board has no injects, and hold is the only rate value. H6 is moot.
- Everything else is mine to decide.

WHY NO fps (MY TESTS)
- Three work streams: the balance sheet is ready (net debt $0 since 2029, stress peak $0.0B on every 10-year row) and the technology is ready (GTF2 since 2036, CFM always available). The market leg fails. The cheapest fps row is $1.83B below Do Nothing in S1, and the airplane alone is $2.13B below. Pope's visible-demand test puts our 2060 demand at 11-19 a month, against a line built for 50 and then 100.
- Doing less, better [BX-1239]: every fps row loses to Do Nothing in every column. Do Nothing also has the highest worst column: -0.34, against -3.21 for the best fps row.
- The Re-engine carrying the airplane: the only fps rows that pass the buffer pass because the Re-engine adds +0.30 in S3, a column that never tests the Re-engine. Pope confirms that this is the whole margin. Neither item passes on its own merits, and I won't let one program carry another through a test. Malave's estimate check settles it: a $2.7B overrun (4.5% of the bill) at Renton, or $0.8B (1.3%) at new sites, uses up the margin, and the grid prices no slip of our own. On my 777X record that is not a margin I would plan against [BX-0550, BX-1318].
- H8 (company hard rule): the cheapest fps row is $2.28B below the grid's best in S1 (+0.21). That is above the $2B cap, and it buys no scored objective, since every row shows 1 engine source in 2050 and Do Nothing already meets every debt line. Malave would flag it as a red-line breach. Company doctrine says the same: launch late only if the fps beats Do Nothing by more than ε.
- Malave's split, which I accept with his corrections: bill $1.98B in PV, discounted penalty $0.62B (the grid already nets it, and I do not subtract it again), gains $0.47B, of which $0.30B is operating gains. To clear +$1B it would need $3.60B of gains, 7.6 times what it has. With no penalty at all it would still trail by $1.51B. Undiscounted scale, shown only for size: 10-year $19.1B, 7-year $22.0B, via Embraer $52.5B.
- My forecast miss, owned: I put a 2050 10-year fps near -1.9, and it came in at -2.13. I missed by about $0.23B on my round figure; Jay puts it at $0.27B. We had the cost right. The gains fell further than a straight five-year shift because the 2060 market is smaller (1,106 against 1,701 in 2055) and the lead deficit is deeper (a 27/73 long-run split).
- Airbus's timeline set none of this [B-2313].

WHY NO 787 RE-ENGINE
- Item value is +0.45 / -0.59 / +0.45 / +0.45, inside ε in every column, so it is a tie. Expected-value breakeven is a 43% chance of a same-round A350 Re-engine. At my 25-35%, its expected value is +0.09 to +0.19.
- Every tie-break points the same way: doing less, better [BX-1239], the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548], Malave's higher worst column (Do Nothing -0.34 against -0.93), and company doctrine, which launches no Re-engine below ε.
- The Board would veto it on its business case (+0.45 against +$1B), so a launch would revert to hold anyway.
- Pope finds it operations-ready (GEnx upgrade ready 22 years ahead, strain $0, Charleston fits). Readiness does not decide it; value does. This hold is final: no later round remains, and the item has fallen from +2.01 (2035) to +0.74 (2045) to +0.45.

THE EXIT, PLAINLY
On this board, this hold means the 737 MAX ends in 2060 with no Boeing narrowbody after it. Delivered share is 22.2% (2050), 12.7% (2055) and 0% (2060), and the last delivery comes in 2059. The 96 customers waiting in 2060 have no Boeing airplane to wait for. The -0.12 political cost of leaving the narrowbody market is already in the grid. The brand, the jobs in Washington and South Carolina, and being the last US airliner maker are not priced. I put no number on them, and I don't use them to carry a plan the numbers reject. I don't like this outcome and I won't dress it up. We held four times because the case was never there: early because the developments and the debt were not finished, and later because the market an airplane would enter kept shrinking faster than its bill was discounted. I would rather Boeing exit honestly than launch a $60B airplane that loses $2B against standing still and leaves the next CEO to take the reset.

WHERE DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD, DROVE A CHOICE
- The no-Re-engine-below-ε rule and H8 are company doctrine.
- The phase-out step rule (no step above 5 a month, at least 6 months apart) is B-2351 applied to step-downs, by inference.
- The supplier funding order and the line-consolidation plan are operations doctrine, through Pope's seat.
- The S2 and S4 weights are my judgement, at Low confidence on Airbus.

WHAT IT COSTS ON THE GRID
In S1, the chosen row is $0.45B below the grid's best (fps hold + 787 Re-engine, +0.21). That gap is logged as the Board's business-case threshold, not as a management premium. Against every fps row the hold gains $1.83B or more. Management premium: $0.

memo_weighing.cfo: Malave is my independent check on program estimates [BX-1316], and his buffer test is the go/no-go. It binds on the 10-year alone, every 7-year and every via-Embraer row. I checked his numbers against the brief, and they agree on every row. I accept his ruling that the test reads the row as written, so the 10-year with the Re-engine carries no veto from him. I took his estimate-ground objection as advice, and it is the strongest point in either memo: the $0.14B margin at Renton is only a $2.7B overrun (4.5%), and the grid prices no slip of our own. I took his reconciliation (political cost $0.073B from 2050 against $0.120B from 2045; -0.17 - 0.073 = -0.243, the grid's -0.24, which governs) and his split with its corrections (penalty $0.62B, gains $0.47B, operating gains $0.30B). I took his reading of the forecast miss: a smaller 2060 market and a deeper lead deficit. His meet-and-beat test breaks the Re-engine tie for Do Nothing on the higher worst column, the same answer I reach on doing less, better. He also confirmed the 43% breakeven, the cash timing, the stress peaks and the 'Fundable when the 777X turns' pass. His seat is thin: his record is one call (Low), so his views beyond the buffer test are advice. This round that advice is arithmetic I can check against the brief, so I gave it full weight. His H8 flag on the combined row is a company hard rule, and I would have struck that row on it in any case.
memo_weighing.ops: Pope's seat runs on operations doctrine with Very low airplane evidence, and she says so. I weigh her results as doctrine and her 2022 BGS rules applied by inference, but they are careful and tied to the brief's numbers. I took her KPI result (nothing live, her veto idle) with her caveat that it confirms no reported problem rather than measuring six KPIs. I took her phase-out plan: ten annual steps of about 3.5 a month, the line-consolidation sequence, and waiting customers accepted. I took her supplier and LEAP-1B plans, including last-shipset spares and tooling agreements. I took her workforce result: it fails, unpriced, and I record it plainly rather than pay a premium H8 would not allow. I took her correction that the 117-a-year 787 figure in our 2045 public record assumed a 2045 Re-engine launch and does not hold. I correct it publicly, and I resize the Charleston move to visible demand. Her answer to my main question was direct: yes, the fps row passes the buffer only on the Re-engine's back. Her visible-demand test (11-19 a month against a line built for 50, then 100) is the operations side of the failed market leg. She finds the Re-engine operations-ready, and value, not readiness, decides it. I agree with that.

decision.expected_scenario: S1: rivals hold. Confidence on Airbus is Low, and I count all four columns as plausible, as the Board does. S2, a same-round A350 Re-engine, is real but less likely than not: about 25-35%. Airbus speaks of A350 steps 'in windows, not dates', and NGSA has been in service since 2037. S3, Delay Tactics, cannot act on an fps-hold row, so S3 equals S1 for the chosen plan. S4, an Embraer launch, is about 15%: it says 'the numbers do not prove the return'. Probability-weighted, Do Nothing is about -0.27.
decision.best_grid_plan_in_expected_scenario: fps: hold + 787 Re-engine, +0.21 in S1 (+0.45 against Do Nothing's -0.24). I do not take it. It is inside ε in every column (+0.45 / -0.59 / +0.45 / +0.45), so it is a tie. Doing less, better [BX-1239], the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548], Malave's higher-worst-column test (-0.34 against -0.93) and company doctrine (no Re-engine below ε) all break the tie for Do Nothing. The Board would also veto it on its business case (+0.45 against +$1B). Chosen plan: Do Nothing (fps hold + 787 hold), -0.24 in S1.
decision.premium_reason:
Management doctrine plus objective premium: $0.
- The 787 Re-engine: the $0.45B gap in S1 between the grid's best plan (fps hold + 787 Re-engine, +0.21) and Do Nothing (-0.24) is logged as the Board's business-case threshold, as the Board asked. It is not a management premium. My own tie-break within ε and Malave's reach the same hold independently. Counted as a doctrine premium instead, it would be $0.45B, inside the $2B cap. On expected value at a 25-35% chance of S2, the gap is about $0.09-0.19B.
- The fps hold costs $0: every fps row is below Do Nothing in every column. The cheapest (10-year at Renton with the Re-engine) is $1.83B below Do Nothing and $2.28B below the grid's best, above the H8 cap, and it buys no scored objective.
- The rate order costs $0: hold is the only value.
- The engine enabler: no premium can buy a scored leg. Every row shows 1 source in 2050, and still 1 if P&W and Rolls-Royce launch.
- What would break the number: a same-round A350 Re-engine (S2) moves Do Nothing to -0.34 and turns the Re-engine's +0.45 into -0.59. No debt line is at risk on a hold.
decision.objective_note:
Control's objectives on the chosen plan, Do Nothing (brief §2 and the metrics table; Malave confirms):
- Repair the balance sheet: met. Net debt reaches the historical level ($0) in 2029.
- Keep it repaired: met. $0.0B at end-2035, 2040, 2045 and 2050.
- Stress case: met. Back to $0 in 2030 and held, peak $0.0B (highest after repair $0.0B, in 2031). Base free cash flow is $13.8B a year, the stress case about $9.2B.
- Defend incumbency: not met. Preference share is 26.0% in 2050, the worst year.
- Hold the 50/50 split: not met (52.6% in 2040, 31.0% in 2045, 26.0% in 2050).
- Engine enabler, sources: not met. CFM alone on the 737 MAX in 2040, 2045 and 2050.
- Engine enabler, makers: not met. Two makers in the market (CFM, P&W). Rolls-Royce is not fitted to NGSA, so three makers cannot be in the market in a scored year.
No fps launched now enters service before 2057, so no plan on this grid can buy a share objective or a scored enabler leg at any premium. The debt objective is met on every row, and I chose the row that meets it without re-levering after 2050. The public multi-source, durability-first requirement and the LEAP-1B supply work serve the enabler at no grid cost.
decision.predictions:
Our score: -0.24 in S1 and S3, -0.34 in S2, -0.27 in S4; about -0.27 probability-weighted. Every debt line is met in every column.

Boeing, observed from the bulletins (capacity path, since deliveries equal capacity from 2050):
- narrowbody deliveries and share: 428 (22.2%) in 2050, 385 (19.3%) 2051, 342 (17.2%) 2052, 299 (16.4%) 2053, 256 (14.5%) 2054, 214 (12.7%) 2055, 171 (10.7%) 2056, 128 (8.9%) 2057, 86 (6.6%) 2058, 43 (3.6%) 2059, 0 in 2060;
- widebody stays at 100 a year and 58.8%;
- we publish no launches.

Airbus: no A350 Re-engine this round is more likely than not. I put the chance of one at about 25-35%, Low confidence. Its capacity stays at 1,489 a year. Delay Tactics have nothing to act on while our fps is unlaunched.

Embraer: it keeps harvesting rather than launching, about 85%.

Engine makers:
- Rolls-Royce's Joint Venture commitment stands, and it runs no solo narrowbody programme.
- P&W stays out of the Joint Venture, so none forms (Medium-Low confidence).
- CFM keeps LEAP-1B on the 737 MAX through the tail and reports -1B durability only when the fleet data is in.
- CFM's narrowbody engine share keeps falling below 58.3% as our LEAP-1B call falls (856 engines in 2050, 428 in 2055, 0 in 2060) and GTF2 grows on NGSA.

board_response.recommendation: 1. Bring one tested case on the grid's own numbers: the submitted row and each Board item at its default, all four columns, expected column named, S3 as Malave's buffer test (limit -2.24), and Malave's reconciliation of -0.24 with -0.29.
board_response.response: Taken up. The submitted row is Do Nothing, the default on every field, so there is no Board item: -0.24 / -0.34 / -0.24 / -0.27 (S1-S4). Expected column: S1, with all four counted as plausible. Buffer test: S3 is -0.24 against a limit of -2.24, a pass with $2.00B to spare. Reference rows I tested and did not take: the Re-engine row (+0.21 / -0.93 / +0.21 / +0.18) and the best fps row, the 10-year at Renton with the Re-engine (-2.07 / -3.21 / -2.10 / -2.16). Malave's reconciliation: the political cost is $0.088B a year for 20 years, $0.120B in PV counted from 2045 and $0.073B from 2050, the decision year. -0.17 - 0.073 = -0.243, which is the grid's -0.24. The grid governs his test because its fps rows are on the same basis. No verdict changes at -2.29.

board_response.recommendation: 2. Hold the 787 Re-engine and treat this hold as final; log the $0.45B as the Board's business-case threshold.
board_response.response: Taken up. re787 is hold, and the hold is final. The $0.45B is logged as the Board's business-case threshold, not a management premium. The hold also stands on my own grounds: a tie inside ε that doing less, better, Malave's higher worst column (-0.34 against -0.93) and doctrine all break for Do Nothing. Pope's findings, restated: the GEnx upgrade has been ready since 2033, 22 years ahead of a 2055 EIS; strain is $0; there is no production-certification concurrency; it starts on GE alone. One correction from Pope: on a hold the 787 stays at about 100 a year (58.8% of the widebody market). The 117-a-year figure in our 2045 public record assumed a 2045 launch, so we correct it publicly, and Charleston is paced to visible demand.

board_response.recommendation: 3. Hold the fps and state the exit plainly; confirm the split; do not let the Re-engine carry the fps through the buffer; record what the hold means.
board_response.response: Taken up. fps is hold, and the rationale states the exit plainly: the 737 MAX ends in 2060 (last delivery 2059) with no Boeing narrowbody after it. The -0.12 political cost is in the grid, and the brand, jobs and last-US-maker costs are not priced and not ours to invent. Malave's split: bill $1.98B, penalty $0.62B, gains $0.47B (operating gains $0.30B). It needs $3.60B of gains to clear +$1B, and it trails by $1.51B even with no penalty. The move from -3.06 to -2.13 is discounting, not a better market. I did not let the Re-engine carry the fps: the combined row passes S3 by $0.14B only on the Re-engine's +0.30, both items fail their own tests, and the row is $2.28B below the grid's best, above the H8 cap.

board_response.recommendation: 4. If the ExCo nonetheless brings an fps, bring the 10-year ramp, weigh Renton under Pope's condition, request code 7, conservative EIS, no date, no fixed price, with Pope's readiness results.
board_response.response: Not applicable: no fps is brought. For the record, had one been brought it would have been the 10-year Solo at Renton under Pope's condition (no MAX line down before the fps is certified and has shown rate; on this timetable the MAX needs no Renton line from 2056), with code 7 (CFM + GTF2 at a 2060 EIS). It would have carried a conservative EIS (Pope's +3-year prior gives 2063), no date before launch and no fixed-price development. Pope finds it operations-ready, but it fails her visible-demand test, and it fails on value.

board_response.recommendation: 5. Report the engine enabler plainly; keep the public multi-source, durability-first requirement and the LEAP-1B OE, spares and durability work with CFM; a Joint Venture engine counts as one source.
board_response.response: Taken up. The enabler is reported as not met: 1 source (CFM) on the 737 MAX in 2050, still 1 if P&W and Rolls-Royce launch, and two makers in the market. No premium is paid. The multi-source, durability-first position stays public, with code 7 as the request if a case is ever brought. LEAP-1B OE, spares and durability cover is planned jointly with CFM, rate-gated, to 2060 and for the fleet after, with no -1B durability claim before the fleet data. A Joint Venture engine counts as one source.

board_response.recommendation: 6. Run the MAX tail, safety first, on Pope's plan: KPI-gated step-downs, fragile suppliers funded, fleet support after the last delivery, people moved to Charleston and defence, the 2055-60 gap recorded plainly, no reliance on regulator leniency.
board_response.response: Taken up as other moves. Ten annual step-downs of about 3.5 a month, 12 months apart, each under the 5-a-month cap and each only on stable KPIs. Two Renton lines plus Everett North to 2052, one Renton line from 2053, the last Renton line closed in 2056, and Everett North alone to the last delivery in 2059. Fragile suppliers stay funded in doctrine's order, with last-shipset spares and tooling agreements. 737 fleet support is public and runs for the life of the fleet. People move to defence first (reversing the 2011-13 move [B-0729]), then Charleston (few on volume) and fleet support. The 2055-60 gap and the end of narrowbody output after 2059 are recorded unpriced. Every step stays inside the FAA-supervised production system.

board_response.recommendation: 7. Keep debt first; any return of cash stays reserved to the Board; keep the public statement measured, promise no new airplane, say plainly the case is not there, no reference to Airbus, no blame on the FAA or suppliers; log every premium; answer each recommendation.
board_response.response: Taken up. Do Nothing meets all three debt lines to 2050 (repaired in 2029; stress case in 2030; peak $0.0B). Any return of cash is reserved to the Board and is not in this package. The public statement says plainly that the business case isn't there and that we are not launching a new single-aisle airplane. It promises no airplane, gives no date, makes no reference to Airbus and blames neither the FAA nor any supplier. It also corrects our 2045 787 figure. Premium: $0 management, with the $0.45B logged as the Board's threshold (H8). All seven recommendations are answered here.

cfo.red_line: None. The orders are the default on every field. H5: nothing is launched, so nothing is cancelled. H4: no development, so no overlap and no strain. H3: no Re-engine is ordered. H8: the management premium is $0. The $0.45B in S1 is logged as the Board's business-case threshold, and even counted as a doctrine premium it would sit inside the $2B cap. H6: hold is the only rate value.

final.public_statement:
The balance sheet is where it belongs, and it has stayed there for a long time. The 737 and 787 lines are running stable. A lot of people built that by doing it the right way every day, and we're not going to give it back.

The 737 MAX is in the last decade of its production life. We're bringing the rate down the way we brought it up: one step at a time, on the data, keeping the line and our suppliers stable. Some customers will wait longer than they'd like. I don't take that lightly, but I'd much rather have a customer waiting than a production system that goes unstable. And when the last 737 leaves the line, we'll keep supporting that fleet for as long as it flies. Every operator flying a 737 can count on that.

On a new single-aisle airplane, I'll be straight with you. We looked at it again this year, and we looked hard. We're ready financially, and the technology is there. The business case isn't. So we are not launching a new single-aisle airplane. I'm not going to launch an airplane that doesn't pay, and I'm not going to launch one to meet a date. I'm also not going to pretend this decision is free. It isn't. It matters to our people, to our customers and to our suppliers, and we'll own it. If that case ever changes, the terms won't: the market, the technology and us all ready, more than one engine source with durability first, headroom in the schedule, and no development at a fixed price. You won't get a date from me before a launch.

Our people are staying with us. As the 737 steps down, skilled people will move into defence, into the 787 and into supporting the fleet in service.

One correction. Last time we put a number on 787 output out to 2060. That number assumed a step we didn't take, so it doesn't hold. Charleston will be sized to the 787 demand we can see, with headroom. I'd rather correct it now than let it stand.

We'll keep working with the whole industry for a tariff-free environment in aerospace. That's good for everybody in this business.

It is so much more important that we do this right than fast. And doing it right includes saying plainly what we've decided and what it costs.
final.rationale:
DECISION: Do Nothing on every field, for the fourth and final time: fps hold (engine code null, fps_site new_site), rate_737 hold, re787 hold. Every order is the default, so no Board item goes up. It scores -0.24 (S1) / -0.34 (S2) / -0.24 (S3) / -0.27 (S4).

THE TEAM RULE, APPLIED
- Malave's binding veto (buffer test, S3 at or above -2.24 against the grid's Do Nothing row) strikes the 10-year alone (Renton -2.40, new sites -2.50), every 7-year row (-3.15 to -3.46) and every via-Embraer row (-4.58 to -4.87). No verdict changes at -2.29.
- He reads his test as applying to the row as written, so the 10-year with the Re-engine (Renton -2.10, new sites -2.20) carries no veto from him. I accept that ruling, and I do not ask him to stretch his test. That row is struck on my own tests (below), not on his.
- Pope's KPI veto has no object: no quality, FAA or supply-chain problem is live, the board has no injects, and hold is the only rate value. H6 is moot.
- Everything else is mine to decide.

WHY NO fps (MY TESTS)
- Three work streams: the balance sheet is ready (net debt $0 since 2029, stress peak $0.0B on every 10-year row) and the technology is ready (GTF2 since 2036, CFM always available). The market leg fails. The cheapest fps row is $1.83B below Do Nothing in S1, and the airplane alone is $2.13B below. Pope's visible-demand test puts our 2060 demand at 11-19 a month, against a line built for 50 and then 100.
- Doing less, better [BX-1239]: every fps row loses to Do Nothing in every column. Do Nothing also has the highest worst column: -0.34, against -3.21 for the best fps row.
- The Re-engine carrying the airplane: the only fps rows that pass the buffer pass because the Re-engine adds +0.30 in S3, a column that never tests the Re-engine. Pope confirms that this is the whole margin. Neither item passes on its own merits, and I won't let one program carry another through a test. Malave's estimate check settles it: a $2.7B overrun (4.5% of the bill) at Renton, or $0.8B (1.3%) at new sites, uses up the margin, and the grid prices no slip of our own. On my 777X record that is not a margin I would plan against [BX-0550, BX-1318].
- H8 (company hard rule): the cheapest fps row is $2.28B below the grid's best in S1 (+0.21). That is above the $2B cap, and it buys no scored objective, since every row shows 1 engine source in 2050 and Do Nothing already meets every debt line. Malave would flag it as a red-line breach. Company doctrine says the same: launch late only if the fps beats Do Nothing by more than ε.
- Malave's split, which I accept with his corrections: bill $1.98B in PV, discounted penalty $0.62B (the grid already nets it, and I do not subtract it again), gains $0.47B, of which $0.30B is operating gains. To clear +$1B it would need $3.60B of gains, 7.6 times what it has. With no penalty at all it would still trail by $1.51B. Undiscounted scale, shown only for size: 10-year $19.1B, 7-year $22.0B, via Embraer $52.5B.
- My forecast miss, owned: I put a 2050 10-year fps near -1.9, and it came in at -2.13. I missed by about $0.23B on my round figure; Jay puts it at $0.27B. We had the cost right. The gains fell further than a straight five-year shift because the 2060 market is smaller (1,106 against 1,701 in 2055) and the lead deficit is deeper (a 27/73 long-run split).
- Airbus's timeline set none of this [B-2313].

WHY NO 787 RE-ENGINE
- Item value is +0.45 / -0.59 / +0.45 / +0.45, inside ε in every column, so it is a tie. Expected-value breakeven is a 43% chance of a same-round A350 Re-engine. At my 25-35%, its expected value is +0.09 to +0.19.
- Every tie-break points the same way: doing less, better [BX-1239], the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548], Malave's higher worst column (Do Nothing -0.34 against -0.93), and company doctrine, which launches no Re-engine below ε.
- The Board would veto it on its business case (+0.45 against +$1B), so a launch would revert to hold anyway.
- Pope finds it operations-ready (GEnx upgrade ready 22 years ahead, strain $0, Charleston fits). Readiness does not decide it; value does. This hold is final: no later round remains, and the item has fallen from +2.01 (2035) to +0.74 (2045) to +0.45.

THE EXIT, PLAINLY
On this board, this hold means the 737 MAX ends in 2060 with no Boeing narrowbody after it. Delivered share is 22.2% (2050), 12.7% (2055) and 0% (2060), and the last delivery comes in 2059. The 96 customers waiting in 2060 have no Boeing airplane to wait for. The -0.12 political cost of leaving the narrowbody market is already in the grid. The brand, the jobs in Washington and South Carolina, and being the last US airliner maker are not priced. I put no number on them, and I don't use them to carry a plan the numbers reject. I don't like this outcome and I won't dress it up. We held four times because the case was never there: early because the developments and the debt were not finished, and later because the market an airplane would enter kept shrinking faster than its bill was discounted. I would rather Boeing exit honestly than launch a $60B airplane that loses $2B against standing still and leaves the next CEO to take the reset.

WHERE DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD, DROVE A CHOICE
- The no-Re-engine-below-ε rule and H8 are company doctrine.
- The phase-out step rule (no step above 5 a month, at least 6 months apart) is B-2351 applied to step-downs, by inference.
- The supplier funding order and the line-consolidation plan are operations doctrine, through Pope's seat.
- The S2 and S4 weights are my judgement, at Low confidence on Airbus.

WHAT IT COSTS ON THE GRID
In S1, the chosen row is $0.45B below the grid's best (fps hold + 787 Re-engine, +0.21). That gap is logged as the Board's business-case threshold, not as a management premium. Against every fps row the hold gains $1.83B or more. Management premium: $0.

memo_weighing.cfo: Malave is my independent check on program estimates [BX-1316], and his buffer test is the go/no-go. It binds on the 10-year alone, every 7-year and every via-Embraer row. I checked his numbers against the brief, and they agree on every row. I accept his ruling that the test reads the row as written, so the 10-year with the Re-engine carries no veto from him. I took his estimate-ground objection as advice, and it is the strongest point in either memo: the $0.14B margin at Renton is only a $2.7B overrun (4.5%), and the grid prices no slip of our own. I took his reconciliation (political cost $0.073B from 2050 against $0.120B from 2045; -0.17 - 0.073 = -0.243, the grid's -0.24, which governs) and his split with its corrections (penalty $0.62B, gains $0.47B, operating gains $0.30B). I took his reading of the forecast miss: a smaller 2060 market and a deeper lead deficit. His meet-and-beat test breaks the Re-engine tie for Do Nothing on the higher worst column, the same answer I reach on doing less, better. He also confirmed the 43% breakeven, the cash timing, the stress peaks and the 'Fundable when the 777X turns' pass. His seat is thin: his record is one call (Low), so his views beyond the buffer test are advice. This round that advice is arithmetic I can check against the brief, so I gave it full weight. His H8 flag on the combined row is a company hard rule, and I would have struck that row on it in any case.
memo_weighing.ops: Pope's seat runs on operations doctrine with Very low airplane evidence, and she says so. I weigh her results as doctrine and her 2022 BGS rules applied by inference, but they are careful and tied to the brief's numbers. I took her KPI result (nothing live, her veto idle) with her caveat that it confirms no reported problem rather than measuring six KPIs. I took her phase-out plan: ten annual steps of about 3.5 a month, the line-consolidation sequence, and waiting customers accepted. I took her supplier and LEAP-1B plans, including last-shipset spares and tooling agreements. I took her workforce result: it fails, unpriced, and I record it plainly rather than pay a premium H8 would not allow. I took her correction that the 117-a-year 787 figure in our 2045 public record assumed a 2045 Re-engine launch and does not hold. I correct it publicly, and I resize the Charleston move to visible demand. Her answer to my main question was direct: yes, the fps row passes the buffer only on the Re-engine's back. Her visible-demand test (11-19 a month against a line built for 50, then 100) is the operations side of the failed market leg. She finds the Re-engine operations-ready, and value, not readiness, decides it. I agree with that.

board_response.response: Taken up. re787 is hold, and the hold is final. The $0.45B is logged as the Board's business-case threshold, not a management premium. Pope's findings, restated: the GEnx upgrade has been ready since 2033, 22 years ahead of a 2055 EIS; strain is $0; there is no production-certification concurrency; it starts on GE alone. One correction from Pope: on a hold the 787 stays at about 100 a year (58.8% of the widebody market). The 117-a-year figure in our 2045 public record assumed a 2045 launch, so we correct it publicly, and Charleston is paced to visible demand.

board_response.recommendation: 3. Hold the fps and state the exit plainly; confirm the split; do not let the Re-engine carry the fps through the buffer; record what the hold means.
board_response.response: Taken up. fps is hold, and the rationale states the exit plainly: the 737 MAX ends in 2060 (last delivery 2059) with no Boeing narrowbody after it. The -0.12 political cost is in the grid, and the brand, jobs and last-US-maker costs are not priced and not ours to invent. Malave's split: bill $1.98B, penalty $0.62B, gains $0.47B (operating gains $0.30B). It needs $3.60B of gains to clear +$1B, and it trails by $1.51B even with no penalty. The move from -3.06 to -2.13 is discounting, not a better market. I did not let the Re-engine carry the fps: the combined row passes S3 by $0.14B only on the Re-engine's +0.30, both items fail their own tests, and the row is $2.28B below the grid's best, above the H8 cap.

board_response.recommendation: 4. If the ExCo nonetheless brings an fps, bring the 10-year ramp, weigh Renton under Pope's condition, request code 7, conservative EIS, no date, no fixed price, with Pope's readiness results.
board_response.response: Not applicable: no fps is brought. For the record, had one been brought it would have been the 10-year Solo at Renton under Pope's condition (no MAX line down before the fps is certified and has shown rate; on this timetable the MAX needs no Renton line from 2056), with code 7 (CFM + GTF2 at a 2060 EIS). It would have carried a conservative EIS (Pope's +3-year prior gives 2063), no date before launch and no fixed-price development. Pope finds it operations-ready, but it fails her visible-demand test, and it fails on value.

board_response.recommendation: 5. Report the engine enabler plainly; keep the public multi-source, durability-first requirement and the LEAP-1B OE, spares and durability work with CFM; a Joint Venture engine counts as one source.
board_response.response: Taken up. The enabler is reported as not met: 1 source (CFM) on the 737 MAX in 2050, still 1 if P&W and Rolls-Royce launch, and two makers in the market. No premium is paid. The multi-source, durability-first position stays public, with code 7 as the request if a case is ever brought. LEAP-1B OE, spares and durability cover is planned jointly with CFM, rate-gated, to 2060 and for the fleet after, with no -1B durability claim before the fleet data. A Joint Venture engine counts as one source.

board_response.recommendation: 6. Run the MAX tail, safety first, on Pope's plan: KPI-gated step-downs, fragile suppliers funded, fleet support after the last delivery, people moved to Charleston and defence, the 2055-60 gap recorded plainly, no reliance on regulator leniency.
board_response.response: Taken up as other moves. Ten annual step-downs of about 3.5 a month, 12 months apart, each under the 5-a-month cap and each only on stable KPIs. Two Renton lines plus Everett North to 2052, one Renton line from 2053, the last Renton line closed in 2056, and Everett North alone to the last delivery in 2059. Fragile suppliers stay funded in doctrine's order, with last-shipset spares and tooling agreements. 737 fleet support is public and runs for the life of the fleet. People move to defence first (reversing the 2011-13 move [B-0729]), then Charleston (few on volume) and fleet support. The 2055-60 gap and the end of narrowbody output after 2059 are recorded unpriced. Every step stays inside the FAA-supervised production system.

board_response.recommendation: 7. Keep debt first; any return of cash stays reserved to the Board; keep the public statement measured, promise no new airplane, say plainly the case is not there, no reference to Airbus, no blame on the FAA or suppliers; log every premium; answer each recommendation.
board_response.response: Taken up. Do Nothing meets all three debt lines to 2050 (repaired in 2029; stress case in 2030; peak $0.0B). Any return of cash is reserved to the Board and is not in this package. The public statement says plainly that the business case isn't there and that we are not launching a new single-aisle airplane. It promises no airplane, gives no date, makes no reference to Airbus and blames neither the FAA nor any supplier. It also corrects our 2045 787 figure. Premium: $0 management, with the $0.45B logged as the Board's threshold (H8). All seven recommendations are answered here.

board_review.note: No Board items: every order is the default.

priorities: Safety and the five pillars first, so no covert move in the last round. No fps is on the public record, so any Delay Tactics move would be naked and draw the $48.32B fine. Against the default row, one move scores -7.81 / -0.14 / -0.14 / -0.16 / -0.14 / -7.80 / -0.13 / -7.80 / -0.13 and both moves score -7.99 to -0.27. Both are negative in every column. That includes the columns where Boeing launches an fps this round, because that fps would enter service in 2057 or 2060, too late for the move to pay. NGSA has been in service since 2037, so no move can change who enters service first [AG-0038, A-0331, AG-0053, A-0474, A-0299, AG-0022].

One programme at a time, funded from our own cash flow, with the last window in view. An A350 Re-engine launched in 2050 (EIS 2055) costs $5B / 5 = $1.0B a year over 2050-54 against the $5.2B line. That leaves $4.2B of headroom, with no overlap with NGSA (whose development ended in 2036) and $0 strain. Against holding it gains +0.57 in S1-S5, S8 and S9. It loses -0.41 in S6 and S7, where a 787 Re-engine entering service in the same year cancels the share gain. That loss is inside the $2B limit, and rule 3 is not triggered. The programme is staged, derivative and self-funded, the kind of programme risk a board at 4 approves, by Qualified Majority. It sits inside the ExCo's $1B band, so launch or hold is the CEO's call. 2050 is the last decision round, so a hold now gives the Re-engine up for good [AX-0022, A-0402, AG-0062, A-0343, A-0401, AX-0104, AG-0049, AG-0011, AG-0056, A-0364, AG-0039].

A disciplined NGSA ramp, and an equally disciplined step-down, on a stable dual-source engine supply. On the brief, NGSA delivers 1,250 aircraft in 2050 against 1,489 of capacity (84%). Deliveries peak at 1,398 in 2052 and fall to 832 by 2060 as replacement demand falls, when the lines would run at about 56% (Board arithmetic). CFM plus P&W GTF2 meets the dual-source enabler in 2040, 2045 and 2050, and the Board wants both makers kept viable through the peak and the step-down. Three narrowbody engine makers is out of reach for any Airbus plan (2 / 2 in every cell, brackets included). The Board trades no PV for it and offers no inducement [A-0303, AX-0015, A-0243, A-0360, AX-0054, A-0159, A-0218].

Liquidity, the rating and fundable returns. On the CFO's static base, net cash at end-2049 is about $21B on the path taken (hold, a 40% payout plus share-plan buybacks). With a Re-engine over 2050-54 it would still rise by about $0.88B a year at that payout (his 2045 figures). Returns stay within the 30-50% payout and an 18-month AGM buyback authority of up to 10% of capital, both reserved to the Board. There will be no equity raise, state support is upside only, and in a shock the dividend goes first [AG-0058, AG-0059, AG-0035, A-0300, A-0402, AG-0062, AG-0054, AG-0034, A-0348, AG-0066].
board_guidance.risk_appetite: Risk-averse (4 of 5) and long-term (4 of 5), unchanged. In the last round the Board accepts one staged, derivative, self-funded programme: an A350 Re-engine at $1.0B a year against the $5.2B line, with $0 strain. Three conditions apply. It must gain in the CEO's named expected column. It must lose no more than $2B in any column; its worst is -0.41, in S6 and S7. And it must pass the operating head's safety and ramp tests with an engine-maturity gate. The Board accepts no covert move, no override (no item can clear $1B) and nothing that strains the rating or the returns. Proof comes before commitment: an engine that is not yet mature is a reason to re-time, never to accelerate.

recommendations.text:
Bring the A350 Re-engine to a decision in this last round, on the ExCo's tests, and record the outcome either way.
- It passes the Board's tests: $1.0B a year over 2050-54 against $5.2B, $0 strain and one launch. It gains +0.57 in seven columns, and its worst is -0.41 in S6 and S7. The Board would approve it by Qualified Majority and would not veto a hold.
- On the CFO's 2045 question: the Board's condition 'Toepfer passes it on cash' meant his peak-cash and liquidity tests, which are the Board's own Liquidity test. The Board does not itself require a $1B margin for a staged, self-funded derivative. Its limit is a gain in the named expected column and no loss above $2B.
- Whether the company's own $1B launch condition (profile §6, written for a 2033-35 launch) still applies in 2050 is for the ExCo to decide, not the Board. If the CFO keeps it as a binding soft veto, the Board will respect it; no override can pass at +0.57.
- The choice inside the $1B band is the CEO's. The Board's horizon favours using a last window it can afford, but it will not press a launch that the ExCo's own tests fail.
- If the CEO holds, he should record the forgone value (+0.57 in seven columns), what is avoided (-0.41 in S6 and S7) and that the Re-engine is then given up for good.

If the Re-engine is launched, gate it on its engine.
- The A350 flies Rolls-Royce Trent XWB engines only. Rolls-Royce has launched no UltraFan widebody: it continues technology maturation inside its existing R&D envelope, with no programme and no dates.
- Wagner should name the engine assumption and say whether any engine can be proven before a 2055 EIS. An UltraFan widebody launched this round would be ready in 2056 at the earliest, since the rules give it 6 years.
- If no engine can be proven in time, EIS re-times later, never earlier. The exposure is recorded honestly at the product-safety review. In public the step is described as a window, gated on engine maturity and proven durability, as our 2045 statement already says.
- Any payment, advance or take-or-pay above EUR 300m to bring a widebody engine to market is a reserved matter and its own Board item. None should be proposed.
- No confidential information is exchanged with any engine maker.

Keep Delay Tactics off in the last round.
- No fps is on the public record, so every move would be naked. One move loses $7.80-7.81B in S1, S6 and S8 against the default and gains nothing in any column.
- Bottleneck and both are vetoed in every round.
- Poaching fails on three counts: no fps is on the public record, it misses the $1B condition, and on the hold row it breaks rule 5.
- No programme, the A350 Re-engine included, is timed or justified to reopen this lever, and it is never named in public.

Plan the NGSA step-down as carefully as the ramp, and report both at the twice-yearly product-safety review.
- On the brief, deliveries are 1,250 (2050), 1,398 (2052, the peak), 1,221 (2055) and 832 (2060), against 1,489 of capacity. Replacement demand falls from 966 (2050) to 553 (2060).
- Pace the extra lines and any capacity additions to demand, not to the calendar. Bring rates down in steps on the data, keeping the line and the suppliers stable.
- Wagner should re-run the supply-crunch test at the 2052 peak, about 116 aircraft a month. On his 43/57 split that is about 50 CFM and 66 P&W sets a month, above the 54-59 P&W sets he cited for 2045-50 (Board arithmetic, inference). He should then set out the step-down path.
- Nothing compresses testing, and a quality or safety escape is acted on at once. The Board will not buy share at a PV cost.
- For the record: the 60/40 goal is met in 2045 (69.0%) and 2050 (74.0%) but fails on 2040 (47.4%), which no order can now change.

Keep the dual-source engine supply whole, and keep the line on three makers neutral.
- CFM plus P&W GTF2 meets the enabler in 2040, 2045 and 2050.
- Extend the rate-gated signals beyond 2050 on the brief's delivery path, upward to the peak and then downward. Size them to our own needs only, with no payment, advance or take-or-pay and nothing reserved against other customers.
- Keep the GTF2 fleet watch, and re-size the contingent CFM framework to the 2052 peak.
- Three makers is out of reach for any Airbus plan (2 / 2 in every cell, brackets included). Wagner should re-confirm that a P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture formed in 2050 would leave NGSA on two sources. How the makers organise is their decision, and the Board trades no PV and offers no inducement for it.
- Disclosure: last round's public supply-signal move published sets-a-month figures (about 41-45 CFM and 54-59 P&W). As the CFO flagged, together they imply our delivery path. Announce signals in general terms only and keep volumes in the private record.
- Nothing on engine selection is coordinated or shared with Boeing.

Keep shareholder returns fundable and reserved to the Board.
- The CFO should bring this year's cash report and his returns proposal: a payout within 30-50% (he proposes 40%), buybacks inside an 18-month AGM authority of up to 10% of capital, and a larger programme only on reported FCF and after a Board re-test.
- If the Re-engine runs, re-test returns against its $1.0B a year. His 2045 condition was a payout of 40% or less.
- No equity raise.
- Launch aid is priced as our own money, and state support stays upside only.
- In a shock, the dividend goes first.

Bring the same scenario-led case, and close the game's record plainly.
- Name the expected scenario and treat all nine columns as plausible.
- Show the worst column for each row: S8 and S9 for hold (+10.52), and S6 and S7 for the Re-engine (+10.41, with the item at -0.41).
- The public line leads with the pillars, describes NGSA as in service and ramping, gives windows rather than dates for any widebody step, and never mentions Delay Tactics.
- Trade advocacy with Boeing and Embraer stays strictly to public trade policy.
- This is the last decision round, so record for the Board the end state of each objective (60/40, the A320 family and the two engine enablers) and of each test the Board applied. The Board can then report on its oversight.

It is 2050, the last decision round. Do we use the last window to launch the A350 Re-engine (EIS 2055), or hold at the company default and give it up for good?
- The Re-engine costs $5B: about $1.0B a year over 2050-54 in a cash view, with no NGSA overlap and $0 strain. On the grid it gains +0.57 in seven columns and loses -0.41 in S6 and S7, so it is inside the $1B band in every column.

OUR POSITION
