tests.threshold: Net cash positive throughout; payout within 30-50%; any buyback inside an 18-month AGM authority of up to 10% of capital; no equity raise; rating anchored on positive net cash (inference)
tests.numbers:
The board reports no FCF, net cash or rating, so these figures are static FY2025 bounds (inference).

Base: FCF $5.2B. The dividend, scaled from EUR 2,527m at 48%, is $1.74B at 30%, $2.32B at 40% and $2.90B at 50%. Share-plan buybacks are about $1.0B, and a EUR 5bn three-year programme is about $1.83B a year.

Net cash path: $2.1B trough at end-2036 (30% floor during NGSA), +$1.21B a year over 2037-44, about $11.8B entering 2045, +$1.88B a year over 2045-49. That gives about $21.2B at end-2049, and I confirm the Board's figure.

Annual change in 2050-54, hold / Re-engine:
- 40% + share plans: +1.88 / +0.88, ending 2054 at $30.6B / $25.6B ($27.5B for the Re-engine at end-2055, its spend done);
- 50% + share plans: +1.30 / +0.30, ending $27.7B / $22.7B;
- 40% + EUR 5bn programme: +1.05 / +0.05, ending $26.4B / $21.4B;
- 50% + EUR 5bn programme: +0.47 / -0.53, ending $23.5B / $18.5B, the worst path tested.
Net cash stays positive on every path.

On the brief's profit path ($18.7-20.8B of operating profit in 2050-52, 5.2-5.8 times 2026's $3.6B), FCF scales up and the fixed $1.0B weighs less, so the static base is conservative. Rating: A+/A1 as of 2026. The record holds no thresholds, and with net cash positive on every path nothing here strains the rating.

Returns proposal, re-tested with the Re-engine: a 40% payout, with 40% or less while the Re-engine runs (my 2045 condition holds: net cash still rises $0.88B a year). Buybacks to cover share plans, inside an 18-month AGM authority of up to 10% of capital. A larger programme only on reported FCF and after a Board re-test. No equity raise. Launch aid is priced as our own money, and state support is upside only. In a shock, the dividend goes first. Returns stay reserved to the Board.

tests.name: Fine exposure: any Delay Tactics move this round (rule 4; ask 7)
tests.threshold: Red line: no move before an fps is on the public record. A naked move draws the $48.32B fine
tests.numbers:
No fps is public, so any move is naked and draws the $48.32B fine, booked at the 2050 order year (about $7.62B in PV at 2026). That is 9.3 years of FCF and 2.3 times end-2049 net cash: on the static base, net cash would fall to about -$26B in 2050.
One move on A, against A: -7.81 / -0.14 / -0.14 / -0.16 / -0.14 / -7.80 / -0.13 / -7.80 / -0.13.
On B, against B: -7.81 to -0.14.
The move is negative in every column, including the fps columns, because an fps launched in 2050 enters service in 2057 or 2060. B plus one move against A peaks at +0.43, which is the Re-engine's +0.57 less the move. It is a red line and struck, and no override applies. NGSA has been in service since 2037, so the team's stricter condition cannot be met.

tests.name: Second move: delay_tactics both (rule 4)
tests.threshold: Red line: never a second move; both counts as two
tests.numbers: Both moves on A, against A: -7.99 in S1, S6 and S8, -0.31 in S4 and -0.27 elsewhere. On B, against B: -8.00 to -0.28. That is $0.13-0.19B worse than one move in every column, because the second $1B buys nothing. The Board vetoes both in every round.

tests.name: Poaching (rule 5)
tests.threshold: Poaching only while NGSA or an A350 Re-engine is in development
tests.numbers: Row A has nothing in development (NGSA has been in service since 2037), so poaching on A breaks rule 5. On B the Re-engine would be in development over 2050-54, which meets rule 5 on paper, but rule 4 still strikes the move. No programme should be timed to reopen this lever.

tests.name: Delay Tactics cash (spend only)
tests.threshold: Spread each $1B move evenly from the order year to fps EIS and add it to that year's spend
tests.numbers: Naked (S1, S6, S8): $1.0B lands in 2050, making 2050 spend $1.0B on A or $2.0B on B. In the fps 7-year column (S4, EIS 2057) it is about $0.14B a year over 2050-56. In the 10-year columns (EIS 2060) it is $0.10B a year over 2050-59. All are under $5.2B; both moves double the add. What fails is the fine (fine-exposure test), not the spend.

tests.name: Cancel (rule 7 and the Re-engine cancel discipline)
tests.threshold: Never cancel NGSA. Cancel an A350 Re-engine only if the 787 Re-engine enters service first and the remaining spend loses at least $1B. Write-off = bill x years elapsed / development years
tests.numbers: There is no cancel option this round: NGSA has been in service since 2037, and no Re-engine is live. A 2050 Re-engine can never be cancelled in this game, because no later round exists. Had it been cancellable, the write-off would be $5B x years elapsed / 5, $1.0B per year elapsed. That is a reported charge, shown even where it is adjusted out of EBIT Adjusted.

tests.name: Capex timing (tie-break within $1B; ask 9)
tests.threshold: Between options within $1B, prefer the later capex start

tests.name: Board items and engine inducement (ask 8)
tests.threshold: Every order above EUR 300m is a Board item; within $1B, prefer fewer
tests.numbers: Row A has 0 Board items. Row B has 1: rea350 launch, $5B (about EUR 4.5bn at $1.10), above EUR 800m, so a Qualified Majority item. No engine inducement is proposed, and any payment, advance or take-or-pay above EUR 300m would be its own item. Each Delay Tactics move would be its own item, and the Board vetoes all three. The fewer-items tie-break favours hold.

tests.name: Disclosure and the public line (ask 10)
tests.threshold: No internal long-term-plan targets and no supply volumes in public; capital-markets statements go to the Board; never mention Delay Tactics
tests.numbers: The frame's public line carries no volumes, no internal plan figures and no widebody dates. One condition: the extended-signals move's published detail must carry no sets-a-month figures. In 2045 it did (41-45 CFM, 54-59 P&W), and together those imply our delivery path. The 2045 figures should be corrected by omission: no public restatement, revision or reference, since any new figure, even a correction, would update the implied path. 'One major development at a time, funded from our own cash flow' holds on either row ($0 or $1.0B against $5.2B). The statement goes to the Board for vetting.

tests.name: Five pillars and integrity (Audit Committee defensibility)
tests.threshold: No order whose integrity or compliance I could not defend to the Audit Committee
tests.numbers: Row A and row B: no flag. Neither has a covert move, an inducement or a confidential exchange, and neither discloses internal plan targets. Bottleneck beyond a first claim on capacity, and both, would be integrity flags; they are struck above.

tests.name: End-of-game record of the CFO's tests, rounds 1-4 (ask 10, for the Board's oversight report)
tests.threshold: Record only what the memos and checks show
tests.numbers:
Round 1 (2030):
- NGSA alone passed peak cash: $5.07B a year over 2030-36, with $0.13B of headroom.
- NGSA plus a 2030 Re-engine failed it: $6.67B a year, a soft veto, plus the rule 6 red line (two launches, 5 years of overlap).
- Robustness passed: NGSA gained +3.59 to +10.86 over hold.
- The Re-engine item (-2.15 in S6 and S7) and the hold-plus-Re-engine row failed.
- Delay Tactics were struck.
- Adopted: NGSA launch, code 7, Alt plan. The Board approved both items.

Round 2 (2035):
- Hold passed peak cash ($5.07B, $0.13B of headroom).
- A 2035 Re-engine failed it: $6.67B a year and about -$1.1B net cash at end-2036, a binding soft veto, accepted.
- Row A was positive in every column (worst S9 +0.48). The base-plan row failed robustness.
- An NGSA cancel ($25.37B write-off) and Delay Tactics were struck.

Round 3 (2045):
- Both rows passed cash ($0; $1.0B) and robustness.
- The Re-engine failed the $1B test (+0.89/+0.90, -0.50), a binding soft veto, accepted.
- Delay Tactics were struck (-11.46).
- Disclosure flag: the sets-a-month figures.

Round 4 (2050): the same pattern. The Re-engine fails the $1B test (+0.57, -0.41), a binding soft veto, and Delay Tactics are struck (-7.81).

Across the game:
- Peak programme cash never exceeded the line: $5.07B at most.
- Static net cash: $13.4B (2025), trough about $2.1B at end-2036, about $21B at end-2049, positive throughout on the floor path. A 48% payout would have breached it in 2036.
- Returns: the EUR 5bn buyback ran 2026-29; the payout sat at the floor through 2036 and at 40% from 2045; buybacks covered share plans; no equity raise.
- Overrides: none. Red lines: none breached by an order. Every veto check concurred.

vetoes.plan: Row B: NGSA hold (A320 Alt plan) + A350 Re-engine launched in 2050 (EIS 2055)
vetoes.ground:
Failed the added-move robustness test, which is the company's $1B launch condition (profile §6). This is a soft veto, and I keep it binding.
- Against hold the item scores +0.57 / +0.57 / +0.57 / +0.57 / +0.57 / -0.41 / -0.41 / +0.57 / +0.57. No column reaches $1B, so no weighting can, and the item is negative in S6 and S7, which the Board counts plausible.
- Grid margin over the best passing option (row A, hold): +0.57 in S1 (the CEO's expected column), +0.57 at best, +0.42 on his weights and +0.35 at equal weights. All are below the $1B override bar, so no override can pass under the team rule.
- Peak cash and liquidity are not the objection: $1.0B a year against $5.2B, with $0 strain, passes. The Board's condition 'Toepfer passes it on cash' is met. The condition 'no soft veto of his left unresolved' is not.
- I keep the $1B condition binding in 2050. It is the company's own launch rule, and the CEO ruled in 2045 that the profile governs. Its dates mark a window, not an expiry. The Board declined to rule it out. The margin has fallen each round. The launch could never be re-timed or cancelled.
- Whether to override is the CEO's call, but at +0.57 none can pass.

vetoes.plan: Any Delay Tactics row (bottleneck, poaching or both), on row A or row B
vetoes.ground:
Company red lines; no override possible.
- Rule 4: no fps is public, so any move is naked and draws the $48.32B fine. One move on A scores -7.81 in S1 and -7.80 in S6 and S8, gains in no column, and would leave net cash about -$26B on the static base.
- Both is a second move.
- Rule 5: poaching on row A has nothing in development.
- A bottleneck move beyond a first claim on capacity, and both, are five-pillars integrity flags that I could not defend to the Audit Committee.

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
Either of two things.

(1) A passing plan shows at least $1B over row A in the CEO's named expected column. None on this grid does: the Re-engine's best is +0.57.

(2) The Board resolves that its own downside test (a gain in the named expected column and no loss above $2B) governs the A350 Re-engine instead of profile §6's $1B condition. The Board has declined to rule and left the point to the ExCo, so this is not met. An ExCo ruling against my soft veto would in effect be an override, and at +0.57 it cannot meet the $1B bar.

Facts that would harden hold rather than change it: Wagner finding no engine provable by 2055, a supply crunch at the 2052 peak, or a cash shock that puts the dividend first. No margin moves me on Delay Tactics, which are red lines.
cfo.memo:
CFO test memo, round 4 (2050).

Fundability. Hold carries no programme cash. The A350 Re-engine takes $5B / 5 = $1.0B a year over 2050-54: 19% of the $5.2B line (EUR 4,753m, at $1.10), with $4.2B of headroom, no NGSA overlap and $0 strain. Cash: pass, no soft veto.

Flexibility. On the static FY2025 base, net cash ends 2049 at about $21B. At a 40% payout plus share-plan buybacks it rises $1.88B a year on hold and $0.88B with the Re-engine. The worst path tested (50% payout, EUR 5bn programme, Re-engine) still ends 2054 near $18.5B. Returns stay fundable. No equity raise.

Value. The item gains +0.57 in seven columns and loses -0.41 in S6 and S7: +0.42 on the CEO's weights. The company's launch condition asks at least $1B over Do Nothing (profile §6). No column reaches it, so no weighting can, and the item turns negative in two plausible columns. Fail: a soft veto, which I keep binding. The condition's dates mark its window, not its expiry. The Board left the point to the ExCo, and a company guardrail is not mine to retire. The margin has fallen each round (+1.54, +0.89, +0.57), and a last-round launch has no re-time or cancel left. No override is possible at +0.57.

Holding forgoes +0.57 for good and avoids -0.41, the $5B and an unpriced slip.

Strikes. Any Delay Tactics move is naked: -7.81 in S1.

Orders: all defaults. No engine code (I defer to Wagner). No Board items.

tests.name: Ask 1: NGSA peak and step-down, 2050-60, safety and quality (report to the Board's twice-yearly product-safety review), both rows
tests.threshold: No order whose execution or public explanation contradicts safety or quality (five pillars, binding, no override). Nothing compresses testing; a quality or safety escape is acted on at once.
tests.numbers:
The brief reports no inject and no safety, quality or supply event. Demand sets our deliveries and there is no waiting backlog. Against flat capacity of 1,489 (124.1 a month):
- 2050: 1,250 (84%, 104.2 a month, 239 aircraft of headroom)
- 2051: 1,354 (91%, 112.8)
- 2052 peak: 1,398 (94%, 116.5, 91 aircraft of headroom)
- 2053: 1,280 (86%); 2054: 1,263 (85%); 2055: 1,221 (82%); 2056: 1,182 (79%)
- 2057: 1,067 (72%); 2058: 964 (65%); 2059: 896 (60%); 2060: 832 (56%, 657 idle slots)
The ramp to the peak is +104 then +44 aircraft (+8.7 and +3.7 a month), all on lines we already run, so no new line and no 1% top-up is needed. The step-down has two steep steps: 2053 (-118, -9.8 a month, straight after the peak) and 2057-58 (-115 and -103, about -9.6 and -8.6 a month). The other years fall 1.4 to 5.7 a month.
Step-down path (inference): (1) meet the peak on existing capacity and add nothing for a two-year spike; (2) take the 2053 step off the extra lines added from 2045 (up to 20 a month), which are surplus once deliveries fall to about the 100-a-month base rate, around 2055-56; (3) from 2057, step the base rate down on the data, about 9, 9, 6 and 5 a month a year to about 69 by 2060, releasing capacity line by line; (4) every rate step passes a production and quality check at the product-safety review, and no step skips a test; (5) keep skilled people by redeploying them to the A350 line and next-generation work, not by losing them; (6) give suppliers the downward signal as early and as rate-gated as the upward one. The Re-engine row adds no narrowbody line work.

tests.name: Ask 1: A320 ramp shield, 2050-60, both rows
tests.threshold: No new programme spend that competes with the open A320 ramp commitment. Passes unless the brief reports a ramp problem (no override).
tests.numbers: The end-2027 commitment (70-75, then 75) is 23 years behind us. The A320 tail ended in 2047, and the brief reports no ramp problem. NGSA deliveries are limited by demand, not capacity, every year to 2060. The Re-engine is widebody work, about $1.0B a year in cash over 2050-54, and on the board it takes no NGSA line capacity.

tests.name: Ask 2: supply-crunch re-test, CFM and P&W engine sets a month at the 2052 peak and through the step-down (doctrine row 12)
tests.threshold: If the brief reports a supply crunch: no new concurrency, and the A350 Re-engine waits (no override). No plan may ask an engine maker for more than the rate-gated signals and ceilings cover.
tests.numbers:
The brief reports no crunch, so row 12 is not triggered. The split is about 43/57: the 2049 bulletin's 41.7% P&W share of Boeing plus Airbus engines puts GTF2 at 57.1% of NGSA (COMAC excluded; inference).
NGSA sets a month, CFM / P&W:
- 2050: 44.8 / 59.4
- 2051: 48.5 / 64.3
- 2052: 50.1 / 66.4
- 2053: 45.9 / 60.8
- 2055: 43.8 / 58.0
- 2057: 38.2 / 50.7
- 2060: 29.8 / 39.5
Ceilings at capacity are 53.4 / 70.7. At the peak, CFM stays under its ceiling. P&W's 66 is above the 54-59 I cited for 2045-50 but inside the ceiling of 71 already signalled.
CFM's total load with LEAP-1B (MAX capacity 428 / 342 / 299 / 214 / 0 in 2050 / 2052 / 2053 / 2055 / 2060) is 80.4 / 78.6 / 70.8 / 61.6 / 29.8 a month. That is below its 106.3 in 2034 and 101.2 in 2044, and it keeps falling.
Watch item, not a fail: P&W must add about 7 sets a month over 2050-52 while its in-service fleet keeps first call on material, and it adds castings and forgings 'in steps'. Its signals cover the peak only if those steps land by 2051-52. If they do not, the rate gate holds our deliveries to the engines available; the build is never accelerated and testing is never compressed. P&W should not build permanent capacity for a two-year peak: its need falls to 61 by 2053 and 51 by 2057.
Widebody engines are a separate supply, so the Re-engine adds no narrowbody engine demand.

tests.name: Doctrine row 11: demand-shock trigger (no A350 Re-engine launch in a shock round)
tests.threshold: In a demand-shock round, no Re-engine launch.
tests.numbers: Not triggered. Narrowbody demand falls from 1,933 (2050) to 1,106 (2060), and replacement from 966 to 553. That is the replacement curve published in rules.md since round 1, not a shock. The brief reports no inject, and the widebody market stays at 170 a year.

tests.name: Ask 3: rate-gated signals beyond 2050 and the contingent CFM framework
tests.threshold: Sized to our own needs only. No payment, advance or take-or-pay; nothing reserved against other customers (five pillars; not a bottleneck move). Volumes stay in the private record.
tests.numbers: Extend the signals on the delivery path, up to the peak and then down: CFM about 45 / 50 / 44 / 38 / 30 and P&W about 59 / 66 / 58 / 51 / 40 sets a month (2050 / 2052 / 2055 / 2057 / 2060), gated on rate, with ceilings at capacity of 53 and 71. Re-size the contingent CFM framework, triggered only by a GTF2 event that leaves NGSA on CFM alone, to the peak: about 117 a month on deliveries, up to 124 at capacity. CFM's total would then be about 145 a month with the MAX, inside the 140-148 band I gave for 2045-50. It falls to about 100 by 2057 and 69 by 2060. Disclosure: my 2045 figures went into the published detail of a public move. This time the public entry carries general terms only and the figures stay in a private entry. Anything above EUR 300m paid to a maker would be its own Board item, and none is proposed.

tests.name: Ask 4: GTF2 fleet watch and the state of the CFM fallback
tests.threshold: A GTF2 durability event calls the contingent CFM framework. The NGSA rate re-times; it is never accelerated to make up a gap.
tests.numbers:
No event is reported. P&W publishes no time-on-wing figure yet ('as the fleet measures it, and not before'), and later-block features enter only 'when proven and instrumented'. GTF2 carries about 57% of NGSA, and its fleet is about 13 years in service by 2050, so shop-visit demand on P&W material rises. That is the second half of the watch item in Ask 2.
The CFM fallback (always available under the rules) is thinnest at the peak. CFM alone would need about 116.5 NGSA + 28.5 LEAP-1B, about 145 sets a month in 2052, against the most CFM has delivered on this board, 106 a month (2034). It eases to 120 (2055) and 113 (2056), and is within 106 from 2057 (about 100), as the MAX ends and our rate steps down.

tests.name: Ask 5: Joint Venture reading, re-confirmed for 2050
tests.threshold: No public line or order that can cost NGSA its second source. A recommendation, not a veto ground; how the makers organise is their decision.
tests.numbers: If P&W commits this round, the Joint Venture forms in 2050. The rules date its engine 6 years later (2056), 'or earlier if a partner folds in a solo programme that is further along'. GTF2 has been ready since 2036, so the plain reading (inference) dates it at once. Fitting was settled at EIS 2037, so NGSA keeps CFM plus P&W's engine: 2 sources, since the Joint Venture counts as one. The only adverse reading is that the fold unfits the in-service GTF2 until 2056. The rules do not support it: a fold writes off spend; it does not unfit a fitted engine. On that reading NGSA would lean on CFM at about 113-145 a month total in 2050-56, more than CFM has ever delivered. Whether Rolls-Royce then counts as a third maker is a ruling for the GM. The brief shows 2 / 2 in every cell, brackets included. Our line stays neutral: no invitation, no discouragement, no inducement, no confidential exchange.

tests.name: Engine supply: NGSA engine code (dual-source enabler)
tests.threshold: CFM in the set plus at least one second maker. A recommendation, not a veto ground.
tests.numbers: Code 7 has been final since EIS 2037, and there is no code order this round (ngsa_engine_code: None). CFM + P&W GTF2 are fitted: 2 sources in 2040, 2045 and 2050, so the dual-source enabler is met. Three makers is out of reach for any Airbus plan (2 / 2 in every grid cell, brackets included), because no live airframe of ours that is not yet in service can trigger a launch_if_selected. No PV is traded for it, and no inducement is proposed.

tests.name: Ask 6: engineering capacity, A350 Re-engine launched 2050 (EIS 2055); rule 6; rule 3
tests.threshold: NGSA / A350 development overlap of 2 years or less ($1.2B strain) unless the grid shows at least $1B more. At most one new launch per round (red line). No A350 Re-engine after a 787 Re-engine (rule 3).
tests.numbers: NGSA development ran 2030-36, and the Re-engine would develop over 2050-54. Overlap is 0 years and strain $0 ($3B x 0/5). It is the only launch, so rule 6 passes. Rule 3 is not triggered: no 787 Re-engine is on the record. The development teams have been free for 14 years. Watch item, not a fail: the Re-engine's development years run through the NGSA peak (2052), when production engineering is at full load. From 2053 the step-down releases people, so talent binds less each year.

tests.name: Ask 6: A350F and Spirit absorption, A350 Re-engine 2050
tests.threshold: No A350 Re-engine while the A350F and the Spirit A350 work packages are being absorbed (round 2 at the earliest).
tests.numbers: The A350F has been in its industrial phase since 2025, and the Spirit A350 packages were acquired in 2025 and are on our record as fully integrated: 25 years of absorption.

tests.name: Ask 6: production readiness, the A350 line
tests.threshold: A derivative launches only on a production system that is ready for it (soft veto if failed).
tests.numbers: It is a derivative on a running line: the A350 builds 70 a year on the board (41.2% of 170, about 6 a month), as the A330neo did on the A330 line. No new line and no new wing. The line passes; the engine does not (next test).

tests.name: Ask 6: production readiness, the Re-engine's engine (durability proven before EIS 2055)
tests.threshold: A Re-engine launches only with an engine that can have its durability proven before EIS. If the engine is late, EIS re-times later, never earlier, within a window that can honestly go to the Board. An engine commitment counts only once it is public. Soft veto if failed.
tests.numbers:
Engine assumption: the A350 flies Rolls-Royce Trent XWB only, and the A330neo precedent is a Rolls-Royce re-engine.
- No maker has an A350 engine programme on the record. Rolls-Royce: 'No widebody programme and no dates'; UltraFan maturation sits inside its R&D envelope.
- If Rolls-Royce launches UltraFan WB this round (orders are sealed, so we cannot know), it is ready in 2056 at the earliest. That is a year after the priced 2055 EIS and before any time on wing.
- If it holds, no new widebody engine reaches the record in this game.
- No Trent XWB derivative is on the record. Rolls-Royce's improvement work feeds the in-service Trent, which is A350 Do Nothing, not a Re-engine.
- The GEnx upgrade has no standing: on this record it is a 787 engine ('ready for our 787 customers'), and dashboard_game.md §5 says profile §11.2's GEnx fallback numbers do not carry over.
So no engine can be proven by 2055, and I cannot give a bounded re-time window either: 2056 or later if Rolls-Royce launches today, open-ended if it does not.
What changed since 2045, when I passed with a re-time condition and held no veto: then a later round could still re-test, re-time or cancel, and Rolls-Royce could still launch after seeing ours. Now there is no later order, and profile §11.2's own rule (if the widebody engine is not public, defer the launch) has no round left to defer to.
Honest slip exposure (direction only): in S6 and S7 a 787 Re-engine launched in 2050 enters service in 2055, first if ours slips, so our share gain never starts and the A350 margin is 6.47%, not 10.76%. That is worse than the grid's -0.41. Booking the bill later is the one offset (about $0.54B in PV at 2055, $0.50B at 2056).
Grid margin over the best passing option (row A): +0.57 in S1-S5, S8 and S9, and -0.41 in S6 and S7 (+0.42 on the CEO's weights, +0.35 at equal weights). It is below $1B in every column, so no override is available.

tests.name: Ask 6: A350 Re-engine on the no-override tests (safety, quality, ramp shield, supply crunch)
tests.threshold: Explicit pass or fail. The Board accepts no override of these tests.
tests.numbers: Safety: pass. A launch with an engine-maturity gate at the product-safety review puts nothing into service before its durability is proven. The engine gap is a readiness failure (previous test), not a safety breach in the order itself. But the Board should read it plainly: I judge that no engine can be proven before the priced 2055 EIS. Quality: pass, on a running line with no event reported. Ramp shield: pass; it takes no narrowbody capacity. Supply crunch: pass. None is reported, and widebody engines are a separate supply. No payment, advance or take-or-pay to bring a widebody engine to market is proposed (above EUR 300m it would be its own Board item), and there is no confidential exchange with any maker.

tests.name: Delay Tactics, any row (rules 4 and 5, five pillars)
tests.threshold: Only after an fps is on the public record and before its EIS. At most one move ('both' is two). Bottleneck only as a first claim on scarce capacity for our own ramp. Poaching only while a programme of ours is in development. Red line; no override.
tests.numbers:
No fps is public, so any move is naked and draws the $48.32B fine (rule 4).
- One move on A, against A: -7.81 / -0.14 / -0.14 / -0.16 / -0.14 / -7.80 / -0.13 / -7.80 / -0.13.
- Both moves on A: -7.99 in S1, S6 and S8; -0.31 in S4; -0.27 elsewhere.
- On B, against B: one move -7.81 to -0.14; both moves -8.00 to -0.28.
Every row is negative in every column, the fps columns included (an fps launched now enters service in 2057 or 2060).

Engine enablers:

ops.would_change_mind_if:
Toward the Re-engine:
(1) A widebody engine for the A350 is on the public record with a ready date that can be proven before EIS, or within a bounded window I can take to the Board. This cannot happen before orders seal this round.
(2) The GM rules that the board's Re-engine flies an engine already proven. The board prices it independently of any engine maker, and UltraFan WB 'counts only once a re-engined ... A350 is in service'.
On either, I withdraw the engine fail and pass the launch with an engine-maturity gate at the product-safety review and a window, not a date, in public. The choice inside the $1B band would then be Guillaume's.

Toward a harder fail on the ramp:
(3) A reported supply crunch (LEAP, GTF2, castings and forgings, titanium) or a quality escape at the 2052 peak.
(4) A GTF2 durability event. NGSA would then lean on CFM at about 145 sets a month at the peak, above anything CFM has delivered.
(5) A signal from P&W that it cannot step to about 66 sets a month by 2052.
(6) Any payment, advance or take-or-pay to a maker without its own Board item, or anything that compresses testing.

Nothing on this board moves me on Delay Tactics while no fps is public.
ops.memo:
Operating test, 2050. My tests come from my role; nothing on record is in my own words, so confidence is Very low.

NGSA peak and step-down: pass on safety, quality, the ramp shield and supply crunch. Deliveries peak at 1,398 in 2052, 94% of our 1,489, and fall to 832 by 2060. The steep steps are 2053 (-118) and 2057-58 (-115, -103). Stand the extra lines down first, then step the base rate down on the data, keeping people and suppliers stable. Nothing compresses testing.

Engines: no crunch. At the peak we need about 50 CFM and 66 P&W sets a month, inside the signalled ceilings of 53 and 71. P&W's 66 is my watch item: seven more sets in two years, while its fleet keeps first call on material. CFM's total load falls from 80 to 30 sets as the MAX ends, so the CFM fallback is thinnest at the peak (about 145 a month) and sound from 2057. Signals run up and down, our needs only, no volumes in public.

A350 Re-engine: passes capacity (no overlap, $0 strain), absorption, the line, safety, quality, the ramp shield and supply crunch. It fails on its engine. The A350 flies Trent XWB only; no maker has an A350 engine programme. UltraFan WB launched today is ready in 2056; if Rolls-Royce holds, never in this game. No later round can re-time it. That is a production-readiness soft veto, binding: best margin +0.57, below $1B. Recommend hold. Code 7 stays: two sources.

other_moves.move: NGSA peak and step-down report to the Board's twice-yearly product-safety review
other_moves.detail:
Wagner reports safety, quality and supply at the peak and through the step-down. Deliveries against flat capacity of 1,489:
- 1,250 (2050, 84%), 1,354 (2051), 1,398 (2052 peak, 94%, 91 aircraft of headroom);
- 1,280 (2053), 1,263 (2054), 1,221 (2055), 1,182 (2056);
- 1,067 (2057), 964 (2058), 896 (2059), 832 (2060, 56%).
The step-down path (Wagner, inference):
1. Meet the peak on existing lines and add nothing for a two-year spike.
2. Take the 2053 step (-118) off the extra lines added from 2045.
3. From 2057, step the base rate down on the data, line by line.
4. Every rate step passes a production and quality check at this review, and no step skips a test.
5. Keep skilled people by redeploying them to the A350 line and next-generation work.
6. Give suppliers the downward signal as early and as rate-gated as the upward one.
Nothing compresses testing. A quality or safety escape is acted on at once [AX-0015, AX-0056, AX-0010, A-0303, A-0485].

other_moves.move: GTF2 fleet watch and P&W peak watch at the product-safety review
other_moves.detail:
GTF2 carries about 57% of NGSA, and its fleet is about 13 years in service by 2050. Wagner reports P&W time on wing as P&W makes it public.
- Watch item: P&W must step to about 66 sets a month by 2052 while its in-service fleet keeps first call on material. If its castings and forgings steps do not land by 2051-52, the rate gate holds our deliveries to the engines available. The build is never accelerated and testing is never compressed.
- A GTF2 durability event calls the contingent CFM framework. The CFM fallback is thinnest at the peak (about 145 sets a month in total with LEAP-1B) and is sound from 2057 [AX-0054, A-0218].

other_moves.move: Long-range, rate-gated supply signals extended beyond 2050 (NGSA engine sets only)
other_moves.detail: We extend our long-range, rate-gated signals to our engine and parts suppliers for the years ahead, upward and then downward as replacement demand eases. They are sized to our own needs only. There is no payment, advance or take-or-pay, and nothing is reserved against other customers. Announced in general terms only [A-0159, A-0243, A-0360, AX-0005, AX-0004].

other_moves.move: Supply signals and contingent CFM framework: private record of volumes
other_moves.detail:
Private record only. None of these figures goes into any public entry.
- Signals on the delivery path, CFM / P&W sets a month (Wagner): about 45 / 59 (2050), 50 / 66 (2052), 44 / 58 (2055), 38 / 51 (2057), 30 / 40 (2060). Gated on rate, with ceilings at capacity of about 53 and 71.
- The contingent CFM framework is triggered only by a GTF2 event that leaves NGSA on CFM alone. It is re-sized to the 2052 peak: about 117 a month on deliveries, up to 124 at capacity. It covers our own needs only and claims no capacity Boeing uses.
- The sets-a-month figures published in 2045 are corrected by omission, as Toepfer advises. There is no public restatement, revision or reference, because any new figure would update the implied delivery path [AX-0005, AX-0004].

other_moves.move: NGSA engine line: code 7 final, two sources, neutral on how the makers organise
other_moves.detail:
NGSA flies CFM and P&W GTF2, so the dual source is whole. How the engine makers organise themselves is their decision: we neither invite nor discourage the Rolls-Royce / P&W Joint Venture.
- On Wagner's reading, fitting was settled at EIS 2037. If P&W commits, NGSA keeps CFM plus P&W's engine, which is two sources, since the Joint Venture counts as one.
- Whether Rolls-Royce would then count as a third maker is a ruling for the game master.
- No payment, advance or take-or-pay to induce any engine launch. Anything above EUR 300m would be its own Board item, and none is proposed. No confidential information is exchanged with any maker, and nothing on engines is coordinated with Boeing [A-0243, A-0360, AX-0054].

other_moves.move: A350 Re-engine: hold, given up for good, recorded for the Board
other_moves.detail:
Recorded for the Board at its request.
- What holding forgoes: +0.57 in S1-S5, S8 and S9 (+0.42 on my weights, +0.35 at equal weights).
- What it avoids: -0.41 in S6 and S7, the $5B ($1.0B a year over 2050-54), and an unpriced engine-slip exposure. No widebody engine on the record can be proven by 2055: UltraFan WB, if launched this round, would be ready in 2056 at the earliest, and if Rolls-Royce holds, no new widebody engine reaches the record in this game. The plan's floor stays at +10.52 rather than +10.41.
- Why: two binding soft vetoes, neither of which can be overridden at +0.57. They are Toepfer's company $1B launch condition (profile §6) and Wagner's production-readiness fail on the engine.
- 2050 is the last decision round, so the Re-engine is given up for good. The A350 stays at Do Nothing, with continuous improvement and competition on price, as the A330 did before the A330neo [A-0003, A-0090, A-0091, A-0253].

other_moves.move: CFO's 2050 cash and returns report to the Audit Committee; returns proposal to the Board
Secure our own materials and work packages
other_moves.detail: Titanium through Aubert & Duval, additive manufacturing, the raw-materials watchlist, and the integrated Spirit work packages. All of it serves our own production, up to the highest rates and through the step-down [AX-0060, AX-0061, AX-0062, AX-0063].

other_moves.move: Recruiting, training and redeployment through the step-down
other_moves.detail: Our own hiring, apprenticeships and training, in Europe and across our global footprint. As narrowbody rates step down, skilled people are redeployed to the A350 line and next-generation work rather than lost. It targets no rival's staff [A-0485, A-0366].

other_moves.move: Zero-for-zero trade advocacy in an industry coalition
other_moves.detail: With industry associations on both sides of the Atlantic, Boeing and Embraer included as allies on trade. It stays strictly to public trade policy, with no exchange of pricing, capacity, programme or engine-selection information [AX-0088, AX-0046].

other_moves.move: End-of-game record for the Board's oversight report
other_moves.detail:
OBJECTIVES (scored by the GM; no PV was traded for any of them)
- Defend 60/40: not met. 2040 was 47.4%, a capacity outcome of the 2039-40 transition (827 and 852 deliveries). 2045 was 69.0% and 2050 74.0%.
- Protect the A320 family: met (worst counted year 60.0%).
- Enabler, dual sources: met in 2040, 2045 and 2050 (CFM + P&W GTF2, code 7).
- Enabler, three makers: not met. Rolls-Royce was not ready by EIS and was dropped, and the Joint Venture never formed. After EIS no Airbus order could add a maker.

BOARD TESTS, END STATE
- Liquidity: peak programme cash never exceeded the $5.2B line. The maximum was $5.07B a year over 2030-36.
- One clean sheet: one launch in the game (NGSA, 2030, EIS 2037, inside the technology clock), with no concurrent Re-engine.
- Downside: NGSA lost in no column (+3.59 to +10.86 in 2030), and every hold row after it was positive in every column.
- Returns fundable: the EUR 5bn buyback ran 2026-29, the payout sat at the floor through 2036 and at 40% from 2045, and there was no equity raise. Static net cash troughed at about $2.1B (end-2036) and is about $21B at end-2049.
- Integrity: no Delay Tactics move in any round, no inducement and no confidential exchange.
- Overrides: none used.
- Board items: the 2030 NGSA launch (code 7) and the Alt plan, both approved. There were no items in 2035, 2045 or 2050.
- Safety, quality and supply: no event in the game.
- Disclosure: the one flag was the 2045 sets-a-month figures, corrected by omission in 2050.

A350 RE-ENGINE ACROSS THE GAME
- 2030: failed cash and rule 6.
- 2035: failed cash, a binding soft veto.
- 2045: failed the $1B condition (+0.89).
- 2050: failed the $1B condition (+0.57) and engine readiness.
- Given up for good.

decision.public_statement: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft has been in service since 2037. In the years ahead its production passes its highest rates and then steps down gradually as replacement demand eases. We will manage that step-down as we managed the ramp-up: in a disciplined and controlled way, in steps and on the data, paced by our customers' demand, keeping our people, our lines and our suppliers stable, and never at the expense of safety or quality. The aircraft flies with two engine sources, CFM and Pratt & Whitney. A stable, diversified supply of parts, engines first, remains a condition of our production. We are extending our long-range, rate-gated signals to our suppliers for the years ahead, sized to our own needs. How the engine makers organise themselves is their decision. On widebodies, the A350 family continues to serve our customers, and we keep improving it step by step. Any further step would be taken only once its engine is mature and its durability is proven, and we speak of it in windows, not dates. We take on one major development at a time and fund it from our own cash flow, preserving our financial flexibility and a strong balance sheet. With our partners across the industry, on both sides of the Atlantic, we keep working for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero trade regime in civil aerospace. And we keep recruiting, training and developing, in Europe and across our global footprint, the people who design and build Airbus aircraft.
decision.rationale:
DECISION, 2050 (last round): every field at its default. ngsa hold, no engine code, rea350 hold, delay_tactics none, a320_plan alt. No Board items.

THE TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP
1. Strike red-line and pillar breaches. Every Delay Tactics row is struck.
- Rule 4: no fps is public, so any move is naked and draws the $48.32B fine. One move scores -7.81 in S1 and is negative in every column.
- Rule 5: poaching on the hold row has nothing in development.
- Bottleneck and both breach the five pillars.
- The Board vetoes all three.
- The team's stricter condition (the move must change who enters service first) cannot be met, since NGSA has been in service since 2037. I do not set it aside [AX-0073, AX-0081, A-0299, A-0474].

2. Survivors. Row A (hold) passes both colleagues' tests. Row B (Re-engine) fails both, on independent grounds:
- Toepfer keeps the company's $1B launch condition (profile §6) as a binding soft veto. Its best column is +0.57.
- Wagner holds a binding production-readiness soft veto on the engine. The A350 flies Trent XWB only, and no maker has an A350 engine programme on the record. UltraFan WB launched now would be ready in 2056 at the earliest, a year after the priced 2055 EIS, and never in this game if Rolls-Royce holds.
- Both pass B on cash ($1.0B a year against $5.2B, $0 strain), and Wagner passes it on safety, quality, the ramp shield and supply crunch.

3. Highest-grid survivor in my expected column (S1). Row A at +10.86, which is also the company default. Row B (+11.43) is $0.57B above it, inside the $1B band in every column.

4. Override. Not available. B's margin over the best passing option is +0.57 at best, +0.42 on my weights, and -0.41 in S6 and S7. All are below the $1B bar.
- The Board would also veto a launch carried over either soft veto.
- The override budget closes the game unused.

5. Tie-breaks inside the band all point to hold:
- no early EIS: the priced 2055 date is ahead of any engine on the record;
- later capex start: in the last round that means none;
- fewer Board items: none.

THE $1B CONDITION
The Board left it to the ExCo. In 2045 I ruled that the profile governs, and I did not press Thomas to retire it in the last round. He gave his reasons on the record:
- its dates mark a window, not an expiry;
- the margin has fallen each round (+1.54, +0.89, +0.57);
- the item now lowers the plan's floor (+10.41 against +10.52);
- the launch could never be re-timed or cancelled.
Even had he withdrawn it, Lars's engine fail stands on my own Low appetite for technology and EIS risk: re-time, never accelerate [AX-0006, AX-0020]. And there is no round left to re-time into.

THE BOARD'S HORIZON ARGUMENT
I take seriously the point that a last window it can afford should not lapse unused. In 2045 I said I would use the band the other way only on clean passes from both colleagues and an engine that can be proven by EIS. I have neither. The Board said it would not press a launch the ExCo's own tests fail.

WHAT HOLDING FORGOES AND AVOIDS (recorded as asked)
- It forgoes +0.57 in seven columns (+0.42 on my weights, +0.35 at equal weights).
- It avoids -0.41 in S6 and S7, the $5B, and an unpriced engine slip. In S6 and S7 a slip would let a 787 Re-engine enter service first, which is worse than the grid's -0.41.
- The A350 Re-engine is given up for good. The A350 stays at Do Nothing with continuous improvement [A-0090, A-0091, A-0253].

THE ROUND'S OPERATING TASK: the NGSA peak and the step-down
- Wagner passes safety, quality, the ramp shield and supply crunch, with P&W's step to about 66 sets a month by 2052 as a watch item.
- I adopt his step-down path: extra lines first, then the base rate in steps on the data, with people redeployed and suppliers signalled down as early as they were signalled up [AX-0010, AX-0015, A-0303].
- Doctrine rows 11 and 12 are not triggered: the demand fall is the published replacement curve, and no crunch is reported.

DISCLOSURE
- Signals are announced in general terms. Volumes stay in a private entry.
- I accept Thomas's advice to correct the 2045 sets-a-month figures by omission, not by restatement. This refines my frame's word 'correct'.
- No internal plan targets, no widebody dates, and no mention of Delay Tactics [AX-0004, AX-0005].

BOARD-GATE LINES
None: every order is at its default, so no item goes to the Board.

For the record, the rejected item would have read as follows. rea350 launch:
- five pillars: pass;
- Toepfer: cash pass, $1B condition fail (binding);
- Wagner: safety, quality, ramp shield and supply crunch pass, engine production readiness fail (binding);
- grid ΔPV: +0.57 / +0.57 / +0.57 / +0.57 / +0.57 / -0.41 / -0.41 / +0.57 / +0.57.
Not brought.

CONFIDENCE
My decision style and thresholds rest on inference (Low). The colleagues' tests are role-derived: Toepfer Low, Wagner Very low.

memo_weighing.cfo:
Toepfer, accepted in full (role-derived tests, Low confidence).

PASSED
- Peak cash on both rows: $0 on A; $1.0B a year over 2050-54 on B, with $4.2B of headroom and $0 strain.
- Robustness on both rows: A's worst is +10.52 (S8 and S9), B's is +10.41 (S6 and S7).
- The Board's downside test: the item's worst is -0.41, inside $2B.
- Rule 6: one launch, 0 years of overlap.
- Liquidity and returns: net cash positive on every path, 40% payout or less, no equity raise.
- Capex-timing and Board-item tie-breaks: both favour hold.
- Disclosure: passes on condition that public entries carry no volumes. I met the condition and adopted his correction by omission.
- Five pillars.

FAILED
- The added-move $1B launch condition on B (+0.57 at best). A binding soft veto, which I accept. He kept it on his own reading with four reasons. I did not press him; the Board said it would respect it; and at +0.57 no override is possible under the team rule.
- Delay Tactics: fine exposure, the second move and rule 5. These are red lines, struck, with no override.

He recorded fairly what cuts the other way: cash is not the objection, and the expected value is positive. His recommended orders match mine.
memo_weighing.ops:
Wagner, accepted in full (role-derived tests, Very low confidence).

PASSED
- The NGSA peak and step-down on safety, quality, the ramp shield and supply crunch. I adopt his step-down path.
- Supply crunch: 50 CFM and 66 P&W sets a month at the peak, inside the ceilings of 53 and 71. P&W's step is a watch item, not a fail.
- The demand-shock trigger: not triggered.
- Signals and the CFM framework: our own needs, no inducement.
- The GTF2 watch.
- The Joint Venture reading: NGSA keeps two sources.
- The dual-source enabler: met.
- For the Re-engine: engineering capacity (0 years of overlap, $0 strain; talent at the 2052 peak a watch item), A350F and Spirit absorption, the A350 line, and the no-override tests (safety, quality, ramp shield, supply crunch).
- Five pillars.

FAILED
- Production readiness on the Re-engine's engine. No engine can be proven by 2055, and no bounded re-time window can go to the Board with no later round. A binding soft veto, which I accept. It matches my own Low technology and EIS risk appetite (re-time, never accelerate), and at +0.57 no override is possible. It is not a safety fail, as he states plainly.
- Delay Tactics on every row: red lines, struck.

His change-of-mind conditions (a public widebody engine before the seal, or a GM ruling that the Re-engine flies a proven engine) are not met. I did not seek them, since Toepfer's veto would stand regardless. His recommended orders match mine.

final.public_statement: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft has been in service since 2037. In the years ahead its production passes its highest rates and then steps down gradually as replacement demand eases. We will manage that step-down as we managed the ramp-up: in a disciplined and controlled way, in steps and on the data, paced by our customers' demand, keeping our people, our lines and our suppliers stable, and never at the expense of safety or quality. The aircraft flies with two engine sources, CFM and Pratt & Whitney. A stable, diversified supply of parts, engines first, remains a condition of our production. We are extending our long-range, rate-gated signals to our suppliers for the years ahead, sized to our own needs. How the engine makers organise themselves is their decision. On widebodies, the A350 family continues to serve our customers, and we keep improving it step by step. Any further step would be taken only once its engine is mature and its durability is proven, and we speak of it in windows, not dates. We take on one major development at a time and fund it from our own cash flow, preserving our financial flexibility and a strong balance sheet. With our partners across the industry, on both sides of the Atlantic, we keep working for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero trade regime in civil aerospace. And we keep recruiting, training and developing, in Europe and across our global footprint, the people who design and build Airbus aircraft.

DECISION, 2050 (last round): every field at its default. ngsa hold, no engine code, rea350 hold, delay_tactics none, a320_plan alt. No Board items.

THE TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP
1. Strike red-line and pillar breaches. Every Delay Tactics row is struck.
- Rule 4: no fps is public, so any move is naked and draws the $48.32B fine. One move scores -7.81 in S1 and is negative in every column.
- Rule 5: poaching on the hold row has nothing in development.
- Bottleneck and both breach the five pillars.

- The team's stricter condition (the move must change who enters service first) cannot be met, since NGSA has been in service since 2037. I do not set it aside [AX-0073, AX-0081, A-0299, A-0474].

2. Survivors. Row A (hold) passes both colleagues' tests. Row B (Re-engine) fails both, on independent grounds:
- Toepfer keeps the company's $1B launch condition (profile §6) as a binding soft veto. Its best column is +0.57.
- Wagner holds a binding production-readiness soft veto on the engine. The A350 flies Trent XWB only, and no maker has an A350 engine programme on the record. UltraFan WB launched now would be ready in 2056 at the earliest, a year after the priced 2055 EIS, and never in this game if Rolls-Royce holds.
- Both pass B on cash ($1.0B a year against $5.2B, $0 strain), and Wagner passes it on safety, quality, the ramp shield and supply crunch.

3. Highest-grid survivor in my expected column (S1). Row A at +10.86, which is also the company default. Row B (+11.43) is $0.57B above it, inside the $1B band in every column.

4. Override. Not available. B's margin over the best passing option is +0.57 at best, +0.42 on my weights, and -0.41 in S6 and S7. All are below the $1B bar.
- The Board would also veto a launch carried over either soft veto.
- The override budget closes the game unused.

5. Tie-breaks inside the band all point to hold:
- no early EIS: the priced 2055 date is ahead of any engine on the record;
- later capex start: in the last round that means none;
- fewer Board items: none.

THE $1B CONDITION
The Board left it to the ExCo. In 2045 I ruled that the profile governs, and I did not press Thomas to retire it in the last round. He gave his reasons on the record:
- its dates mark a window, not an expiry;
- the margin has fallen each round (+1.54, +0.89, +0.57);
- the item now lowers the plan's floor (+10.41 against +10.52);
- the launch could never be re-timed or cancelled.
Even had he withdrawn it, Lars's engine fail stands on my own Low appetite for technology and EIS risk: re-time, never accelerate [AX-0006, AX-0020]. And there is no round left to re-time into.

THE BOARD'S HORIZON ARGUMENT
I take seriously the point that a last window it can afford should not lapse unused. In 2045 I said I would use the band the other way only on clean passes from both colleagues and an engine that can be proven by EIS. I have neither. The Board said it would not press a launch the ExCo's own tests fail.

WHAT HOLDING FORGOES AND AVOIDS (recorded as asked)
- It forgoes +0.57 in seven columns (+0.42 on my weights, +0.35 at equal weights).
- It avoids -0.41 in S6 and S7, the $5B, and an unpriced engine slip. In S6 and S7 a slip would let a 787 Re-engine enter service first, which is worse than the grid's -0.41.
- The A350 Re-engine is given up for good. The A350 stays at Do Nothing with continuous improvement [A-0090, A-0091, A-0253].

THE ROUND'S OPERATING TASK: the NGSA peak and the step-down
- Wagner passes safety, quality, the ramp shield and supply crunch, with P&W's step to about 66 sets a month by 2052 as a watch item.
- I adopt his step-down path: extra lines first, then the base rate in steps on the data, with people redeployed and suppliers signalled down as early as they were signalled up [AX-0010, AX-0015, A-0303].
- Doctrine rows 11 and 12 are not triggered: the demand fall is the published replacement curve, and no crunch is reported.

DISCLOSURE
- Signals are announced in general terms. Volumes stay in a private entry.
- I accept Thomas's advice to correct the 2045 sets-a-month figures by omission, not by restatement. This refines my frame's word 'correct'.
- No internal plan targets, no widebody dates, and no mention of Delay Tactics [AX-0004, AX-0005].

CONFIDENCE

frame.question:
What game are we playing in 2050, and how do we win? [CX-0467]

This is the last round, and it is still the installed-base game [CX-0422]. On this board it is the LEAP fleet's game, and the window has nearly shut. The board counts the narrowbody market to 2056 and the widebody market to 2061. Anything we launch today is ready in 2056 at the earliest:
- a Ducted counts for one year;
- a CFM engine on Embraer's jet counts from 2057;
- an Open Fan is ready in 2060.

So the question is plain. Does anything on this grid earn its bill in a column the record supports? My read is no. Hold is the best plan in all three columns (-9.47 / -9.47 / -9.55). If that survives your tests, we close the game the way we have run it: safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order [CX-0658]. That means LEAP time on wing, OE engines on time, spares that never crowd them out, and RISE kept whole as technology with Safran. We are not going for share [CX-0493].

We don't have a birthright on that next order [CX-0564], so I read S2 and S3 as hard as S1. This round they cost us little on the board:
- S2 costs $0. An fps launched now enters service in 2060.
- S3 costs $0.08B. Embraer's jet enters in 2054 on the rival engine.

The one live risk to the share objective is a Joint Venture. No column prices it, and no lever on this grid answers it.

One new point. On my reading of the grid, an Open Fan's wait penalty bites from its launch year. A 2050 launch would then lose money and also take the 2050 share well below 50% (inference). We can't have both objectives. We keep the one we hold.

cfo.memo:
Larry, the money in dollars. Your grid checks to the cent. Hold is the best plan in every column: -9.47, -9.47, -9.55, at least $5.58B ahead of the next row. The Ducted grosses $0.22B on a $6B bill, one counted year, and loses $5.78B everywhere. Volumes first passes on hard rule 3, but a trigger permits a defence; it doesn't pay for one. Embraer's +0.20 in S3 is its jet flying CFM from 2054, not the share move, which counts from 2057. It can't carry the Ducted. The best Open Fan plan needs $15.10B, above the allowance, and its penalty bites from 2050, taking that year to about 31%. Strain is confirmed at $2.00B. So hold passes every binding test: $0 premium, $0.65B of $4.0B for the game, no new R&D, payout and rating whole.

What the case leaves out is a Joint Venture: about -$2.0B counting at once, -$1.7B from 2051. The 2050 share goes to 49.9-50.1%, on the line, and nothing on this board lifts it. If the GM counts a third maker on NGSA, it roughly doubles. On the uncommitted side's words I'd say one in five, but my record on rivals is thin, and we guide low.

Book -10.0: weighted -9.48 less one in four. Last round we said -11.0; the rivals held, so we raise one step, not to -9.47. Floor -11.6. But the good news is the LEAP load falls to 1,355 by 2056, easing supply. Your terms pass; I'll re-check the exact text.

Ducted: -5.78 / -5.78 / -5.78 (-15.25 / -15.25 / -15.33 less -9.47 / -9.47 / -9.55). Ducted + Partner Embraer: -5.78 / -5.78 / -5.58. Open Fan: -17.17 / -17.17 / -17.11. Check file: /tmp/wargame-cfm/dash-2050-emb/work/r4_ali_tests.py.

vetoes.ground: Not a veto now: Culp plans no date and the round-3 register. At the veto check, binding ground 2 applies to any of the following: a Ducted ready date (2056 is an untested board year); any Open Fan or RISE entry date (2060 included); any RISE ground-test or flight-test date; a CFM engine on Embraer's jet before 2057, or a line implying CFM at that jet's entry; any line implying that a new CFM engine acts on the 2050 share or answers a Joint Venture; any LEAP-1B time-on-wing result, or a date for one; any LEAP-1A cycles figure beyond 'certified, in every new -1A engine, going in at shop visits'. Inference note: my veto right over dates in public is an inference from my 2024 'turn on and turn off' and 'real testing' words as VP of Engineering, read in my current role. Under the team rule it binds unless Culp answers it with evidence.

ops.would_change_mind_if:
Only test and field data, never analysis.
(1) LEAP-1B fleet data in cycles, harsh and neutral, against the 8,000 / 17,000 targets. That closes the item open since round 1. It changes the statement, not the orders.
(2) A durability or safety finding from test or the field on the LEAP family on NGSA or the MAX, or on GEnx. It goes to the cross-functional team first. It would change the LEAP moves (inspection, shop-visit priority, spares against OE) and would put a flag on any launch until Culp answers it on evidence.
(3) Measured output at the 9 suppliers and 15 sites behind 80% of past shortages, at today's falling rate and carrying shop-visit spares beside OE. That would let me read the $2B strain as enough rather than a floor. It does not change hold.
(4) On the Partner Embraer veto, either of two things. One: a CFM installation on Embraer's jet, turned on and turned off in test by the jet's entry into service. Two: a correction from Ghai or the GM showing that the S3 +0.20 rests on no year before 2057. The second corrects my reading of the board, not a test result, and I would drop the veto on it.
(5) A Ducted core turned on and turned off in hot-and-harsh test. That would make 2056 a tested date. It cannot make the date earlier, so it buys back no counted years.
(6) A RISE ground and flight test that measures 'more than 20%', with open-fan blade and compact-core durability in dust. That confirms the physics but does not move the calendar: NGSA has been in service since 2037.
(7) An airframer launch on the record with CFM in its code, where the grid pays. The column is Culp's call; I would test only its dates.
ops.memo:
I report against what I said.

Dates. A 2050 launch gives a Ducted in 2056, launch plus six; an Open Fan in 2060; Embraer counting from 2057. These are the board's years. No test backs 2056: nothing ducted has been turned on and turned off. Hold rests on no ready year. It passes.

Against the airframes. NGSA entered service in 2037: the Ducted is nineteen years behind it, the Open Fan twenty-three. Embraer's S3 jet, 2054: Ducted two years late, Open Fan six. The S2 fps, 2060, is outside the window. The Ducted counts one year. One year of slip takes its $0.22B to zero, and my demonstration dates have slipped.

A correction. Partner Embraer is worth +0.20 in S3 on either engine, even beside an Open Fan ready only in 2060. Its share counts from 2057, so that value can only be CFM engines on Embraer's jet from 2054. No engine of ours is ready then. In round 3 I passed it without tracing that. It fails my date test: binding on any Partner Embraer launch. Hold does not touch it.

Physics. A ducted engine has less than half the open-fan gain. Never the next generation. RISE is designed for more than 20%, untested in flight.

Durability. LEAP-1A hardware is certified and in every new engine. The LEAP-1B fleet outcome is not in my record. No flag is open.

Supply. 1,926 engines this year, a quarter below our 2034 peak. Supplier output: not measured.

Orders: hold everything.

other_moves.move: RISE kept whole as technology with Safran
other_moves.detail: RISE stays fully funded as a joint CFM technology programme. There is no product launch and no 'program dividend' [CX-0174, CX-0214], and it is never cancelled for cost [CX-0398]. Testing continues with our partners, and RISE technology keeps flowing into LEAP upgrades [CX-0162]. No entry date, and no ground-test or flight-test date [CX-0205, CX-0009]. This fits joint practice: Safran is a full partner in RISE. Nothing is said on the term or renewal of the CFM partnership.

other_moves.move: LEAP durability and delivery first
other_moves.detail: LEAP-1A durability hardware is certified. It is in every new -1A engine and goes into the fleet at shop visits [CX-0225, CX-0209]. We report LEAP time on wing in cycles once the fleet has proven it, and we claim nothing before then. That is Ali's wording; the -1B fleet outcome is not in his record [CX-0210, CX-0009]. OE engines come first, and spares never crowd them out [CX-0529]. This is joint practice with Safran. Facts only, no promise dates [CX-0436].

other_moves.move: Support NGSA with the LEAP family on Airbus's extended rate-gated signals, jointly with Safran
other_moves.detail: CFM is fitted on NGSA on the record. We answer Airbus's long-range, rate-gated supply signals, now extended, on standard terms. No launch-era pricing, no concession, no free upgrade. We quote no volume or rate of Airbus's and do not repeat its set counts or ceilings in public (Ghai's advice). Narrowbody price and capacity are a joint decision with Safran [CX-0184, CX-0166, CX-0160]. The LEAP load on the board falls from 1,926 engines (2050) to 1,355 (2056). So capacity follows the signals and is not built ahead of them: lean before capital [CX-0540, CX-0653]. OE comes first and spares never crowd it out [CX-0529]. Platform talks stay private [CX-0586].

other_moves.move: Step the LEAP-1B line down with the 737 MAX on Boeing's data, jointly with Safran
other_moves.detail: We follow Boeing's step-down on its data, without getting ahead of the airframer [CX-0307, CX-0452]. CFM narrowbody capacity is joint with Safran [CX-0184]. Enhanced inspection of safety-critical parts in new-make shops and MRO does not step down with the rate [CX-0010], and any quality finding goes to a cross-functional team first [CX-0012]. The installed -1B fleet keeps its support through the shops, with retrofits at shop visits [CX-0649]. Neither my record nor Ali's covers keeping the experienced people, so we make no claim on it. No rates, no dates, no board effect.

other_moves.move: Engine talks with Boeing and Embraer, jointly with Safran
other_moves.detail: We refuse no one and lock no one out (H1) [CX-0587, CX-0185]. A LEAP derivative is on offer for the fps (Boeing has said it will request code 7 at launch) and for Embraer's next jet, on standard terms. Narrowbody price and capacity are joint with Safran [CX-0184]. Boeing wants more than one engine source, durability first, so we bring time-on-wing facts we can back with test or field data, and no price. A new CFM engine comes only when an airframer and the returns are both there. Talks stay private. No comment on trade disputes between governments.

other_moves.move: Answer the market with win rates, not reactions
other_moves.detail: No public comment on any rival or any Joint Venture, and no price cut in response [CX-0580, CX-0609, CX-0625]. We compete on LEAP durability, time on wing, delivery and standard terms, jointly with Safran. That's the scoreboard [CX-0218]. Ghai's Joint Venture sizing stays on the internal watch list: -$1.7B to -$2.0B, a 2050 share of 49.9-50.1%, and -$3.9B to -$4.9B if the GM counts a third maker on NGSA. No board effect.

other_moves.move: Measure supplier output (lean before capital)
other_moves.detail: Ali reports that output at the 9 suppliers and 15 sites behind 80% of past shortages is still not measured [CX-0613]. We measure it at supplier level, at today's falling rate, against OE plus shop-visit spares. We fix flow before we add capital [CX-0540, CX-0633]. No capital commitment and no board effect.

other_moves.move: Hot-and-harsh core testing inside the RISE envelope
other_moves.detail: Compact-core HPT durability testing in dust continues inside the existing joint RISE budget, and its results feed LEAP upgrades [CX-0222, CX-0216]. It builds the turn-on, turn-off test basis Ali says we lack [CX-0009]. No Ducted launch, no date and no new bill.

decision.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That's how we run this business, and it's how we made this call.

Here's what we know. CFM, with our partners at Safran, is on Airbus's new single-aisle, and we'll earn our place on it every day, on time on wing. We'll support that ramp on the signals Airbus gives us, jointly with Safran, and spares won't crowd out new engines. As the 737 MAX line steps down, we'll step down with it on Boeing's data, jointly with Safran. Inspection on safety-critical parts doesn't step down with the rate. LEAP-1A durability hardware is certified. It's in every new -1A engine and going into the fleet through the shops. We'll report LEAP time on wing in cycles once the fleet has proven it. The GEnx upgrade is ready for our 787 customers.

Here's what we don't know: when the next new narrowbodies will be launched, by whom, and on which engines. That's really not for us to say. It's the airframers' call. We don't have a birthright on that next order. We intend to earn it. A LEAP derivative is on offer to every airframer, and a new engine comes when an airframer and the returns are both there.

RISE stays all in as technology, together with Safran. When that architecture enters service is really not for us to say. We'll tell you about dates when the testing tells us.

We get paid in dollars, not in percentages. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: hold on ducted, open_fan, partner_embraer and lobby_emissions; genx can only be hold. Every field is at its default, so no item goes to the Board. Premium $0. No override.

1. WHAT GAME, HOW DO WE WIN [CX-0467, CX-0422]
It is the installed-base game, and on this board the window has nearly shut:
- The board counts the NB market to 2056 and the WB market to 2061.
- Anything launched today is ready in 2056 at the earliest. A Ducted counts one NB year (2056). Partner Embraer's share move counts from 2057. An Open Fan is ready in 2060.
- Slots: NGSA has had CFM fitted since 2037 alongside the rival engine, and every column carries that split. The fps and Embraer's jet are open, with no launch on the record. A LEAP derivative is on offer to both, and CFM is always available on a new airframe.
We win by running the LEAP fleet: time on wing, OE engines on time, spares that never crowd them out. RISE stays whole as joint technology. We are not going for share [CX-0493].

2. THE GRID AGAINST HOLD (S1 / S2 / S3, $B; check file /tmp/wargame-cfm/dash-2050-emb/work/r4_culp_decide.py, brief numbers only)
- Hold: -9.47 / -9.47 / -9.55. Best plan in every column. Weighted -9.48 at .65/.20/.15 and -9.50 at equal weights.
- Ducted: -5.78 / -5.78 / -5.78. It grosses $0.22B on a $6B bill ($4B R&D plus the $2B strain next to the running GEnx).
- Ducted + Partner Embraer: -5.78 / -5.78 / -5.58.
- Open Fan: -17.17 / -17.17 / -17.11, which is $7.1-7.2B beyond its $10B bill: the wait penalty, biting from 2050.
- Best Open Fan plan (Open Fan + Partner Embraer + Lobby): -15.10 / -15.10 / -14.86.
- Ducted + Open Fan combinations: -18.65 to -20.95.
Strain confirmed: the Ducted is worth +2.00 more next to an Open Fan than alone. So the GEnx counts as a running project, and any single launch carries the $2B.
S2 equals S1: a 10-year fps launched in 2050 enters service in 2060, after the last counted NB year (2056). S3's -0.08 is Embraer's jet entering in 2054 on the rival engine. Ghai and Ali both confirm these readings.

3. MY TESTS
- No birthright [CX-0564]: I read S2 and S3 as hard as S1. S2 costs $0 against S1 and S3 costs $0.08B, and hold is best in both.
- Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301, CX-0355]: nothing is. The Ducted's S1 cost is its whole $5.78B gap; the best Open Fan plan loses at least $14.86B.
- Low case first [CX-0248, CX-0536]: S1 is the expected column on the record. Boeing: 'the business case isn't there yet' and 'you'll get a date from me when we launch'. Embraer: 'the numbers do not prove the return' and 'no decision to announce'. Booked at -10.0, not S1's -9.47.
- H2, the airframer sets the date [CX-0205, CX-0469]: an Open Fan ready in 2060 against NGSA's 2037 entry waits in every column. The RISE exception fails both parts: there is a penalty in every column, and the best plan needs $15.10B, above the $15B cap.
- H3, Ducted only as a defence: the trigger is on the record (GTF2 fitted next to CFM on NGSA; the Joint Venture commitment standing). I invoke it for the record only. It permits a defence; it does not pay for one. No column shows the Ducted buying back a slot. Ali adds that one year of slip takes its $0.22B to zero.
- Suppliers: hold adds no project and no strain. Ali reads the $2B as a floor, and supplier output is still unmeasured.
- Next generation, my 20% line [CX-0217, CX-0208]: no Ducted is in the orders, so the line is not engaged. The statement never calls a Ducted the next generation. RISE is the next engine, at a 'more than 20%' design point that is untested in flight (Ali).
- Tie-break: not needed. Hold leads every row by at least $5.58B, more than the $1B ε.
- Premium cap (H9): $0 this round. The game closes at $0.65B of $4.0B. The RISE allowance is unused.

4. TEAM RULE: I propose and decide
- Ghai's binding tests (pays for itself, volumes first, terms) all pass on hold. His binding vetoes cover every launch and are not engaged.
- Ali's binding date test passes: hold rests on no ready year. He now carries a binding veto on any Partner Embraer launch: its S3 +0.20 rests on CFM engines on Embraer's jet from 2054, before any new CFM engine is ready. I accept his tracing, and Ghai's reading of the +0.20 matches it. Hold does not engage it.
- Neither colleague's test fails on the plan I chose, so overrides is empty.

5. SAFRAN GATE (H7; CFM parity rule)
- ducted: hold, so consent is not engaged. Consent would have been assumed on the H3 trigger, but the order fails on money.
- open_fan: hold, so it is not engaged. A RISE product launch with no airframer path is outside joint practice, and there is no stated reason Safran would agree.
- partner_embraer: hold, so it is not engaged. It would follow consent on a passing CFM engine, and none passes.
- lobby_emissions: hold, so it is not engaged. It serves RISE and falls with the Open Fan.
- genx: GE alone, no gate.
Every NGSA, MAX, fps or Embraer supply or engine-talk move says price and capacity are joint with Safran [CX-0184, CX-0166, CX-0160]. Nothing is said on the partnership's term or renewal.

6. ALI'S READY YEARS AGAINST THE FIRST NEW-NB ENTRY (board years, not test results)
- Ducted 2056: 19 years after NGSA's 2037 entry, 2 years after the S3 Embraer jet (2054), 4 years ahead of the S2 fps (2060).
- Open Fan 2060: 23 years after NGSA and 6 years after the S3 jet.
- Partner Embraer counts from 2057.
- GEnx has been ready since 2033 and counting since 2042.
Flags and fleet data:
- No safety or durability flag is open on the LEAP family on NGSA or the MAX, or on GEnx, so I have nothing to answer cross-functionally this round [CX-0012].
- The LEAP-1B fleet outcome is not in Ali's record, so we claim nothing either way.
- Supplier output at the 9 suppliers and 15 sites is unmeasured.

7. RED LINES HELD
- H1: a LEAP derivative is on offer to every airframer.
- H2: no Open Fan wait.
- H3: no Ducted.
- H5: RISE is not cancelled and pays no programme dividend.
- H6: no date in the statement (Ali's watch list checked: no Ducted, Open Fan or RISE date, no CFM on Embraer's jet, no -1B result, no -1A figure beyond 'certified, in every new -1A engine, going in at shop visits').
- H7: Safran gate as above.
- H8: no rival or Joint Venture named, no blame.
- H9: $0 premium.
- My 20% and durability lines: not traded.

8. DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD, DROVE
- Partner Embraer and Lobby: doctrine §6, with my 'additive' rule applied.
- The Joint Venture response: doctrine §5 and §7, no public reaction and no price cut [CX-0609].
- Supply: Ali's memo, checked against doctrine (§2 strain as a floor; lean before capital).
- The LEAP-1B step-down move rests on Ali's CX-0010 and my deference to the airframer on rates [CX-0452]. Neither record covers the workforce, so we claim nothing on it.

9. BIASES, CHECKED
- Guide low and raise [CX-0270, CX-0654]: booking -10.0, up one step from round 3's -11.0 because the rivals held, but not to -9.47 while a Joint Venture can form.
- Installed-base lens ('the price of admission' [CX-0557]): it could rationalise a Ducted to be 'on' the fps. The fps is off the board, and CFM is always available on a new airframe.
- Deference to airframers: here the board's calendar closes the door, not deference.

10. WHAT HOLD GIVES UP
Nothing on the grid. Off the grid, a P&W-RR Joint Venture formed this round could cost about $2.0B and put the 2050 share at 49.9-50.1% (Ghai). No lever on this board acts on 2050. We answer it with time on wing, delivery and standard terms, jointly with Safran.

memo_weighing.cfo:
Ghai's memo is weighed fully, and his tests carry the decision. His profit calls land; his volume dates slip [CX-0910, CX-0987], and here he dates no volumes.
- He checks my grid to the cent: hold -9.47 / -9.47 / -9.55, the Ducted -5.78 everywhere, the best Open Fan plan -15.10 / -15.10 / -14.86.
- He confirms the $2.00B strain (the GEnx counts as a running project), that S2 equals S1, and that S3's -0.08 comes from Embraer's jet on the rival engine.
- His binding tests all pass on hold. His binding vetoes (every launch; any price talk without Safran) are not engaged.
- His Partner Embraer reading (the +0.20 is the jet flying CFM from 2054, not the share move) matches Ali's tracing. I take it.
- Joint Venture sizing: -$2.0B if it counts at once, -$1.7B from 2051; 2050 share 49.9-50.1%. The tail, if the GM counts a third maker, is -$3.9B to -$4.9B. It is an estimate calibrated on the grid, not a column, so I keep it as the watch number.
- On the odds: he reads the record at one in five but books at my one in four because his record on rivals is thin. I adopt his booking of -10.0 (-9.98).
- I take his terms advice: no Airbus set counts in our statement, and 'jointly with Safran' on every capacity line, including the MAX step-down.
- Capex frame (about $2.5B a year) is advice. Hold uses $0, so the 70% payout and the A-range rating stay whole [CX-0645, CX-0252].
memo_weighing.ops:
Ali's memo is weighed on two levels. His own record is thin: engineering only, ending in March 2024. On supply I am reading my own description of his job [CX-0633], so I weigh that part against company doctrine.
- Dates (his binding ground): pass. The board's years are 2056, 2060 and 2057, and hold rests on none of them. He says plainly that 2056 is the board's year, not a test result, so no Ducted date appears anywhere.
- His correction on Partner Embraer: its S3 +0.20 rests on CFM engines on Embraer's jet from 2054, before any new CFM engine is ready. That fails his date test and binds on any Partner Embraer launch. He owns the round-3 miss, which is the right way to do it. Ghai's reading supports his tracing, so I accept it. Hold does not engage it.
- H2: his readiness reading matches the grid (23 years after NGSA's entry). He does not contest my penalty-timing arithmetic and calls it board arithmetic, not his ground. Fair.
- Durability: he states the LEAP-1A facts on test (certified December 2024, in every new -1A engine, going in at shop visits), says plainly that the -1B outcome is not in his record, and has no flag open. I keep his wording in public.
- Supply: his reading rests on assembled totals only. The 2050 Airbus load is about 44.6 sets a month inside Airbus's stated path, and the load is falling. Supplier-level output and spares volumes are unmeasured. That checks against doctrine ($2B strain as a floor; lean before capital), so supplier measurement stays an action.
- LEAP-1B step-down: he gives enhanced inspection that does not step down with the rate [CX-0010] and no workforce evidence. I use the first and claim nothing on the second.
His watch list for the statement is checked: no Ducted, Open Fan, RISE or Embraer date, no -1B result, no line implying a new engine acts on 2050.

decision.premium_reason:

- Doctrine premium: $0. Hold is the best grid plan in every column.
- Objective premium: $0. An Open Fan launched in 2050 is ready in 2060, so 'ready by 2050' cannot be bought, and no PV is given up for it. The share objective is met on hold.
- RISE allowance: $0, unused for the game. It is closed by the airframer path, not by cost: NGSA has been in service since 2037, so an Open Fan waits in every column. For the record, the best Open Fan plan is -15.10 against hold in S1, above the $15B cap.
- Round total: $0 of $2.0B. Final game total: $0.65B of $4.0B (round 2's doctrine premium).
decision.objective_note:
Dominate narrowbody engines (CFM NB share of at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050): met on the board.
- 74.5% in 2040, 62.8% in 2045 and 57.4% in 2050, the worst year.
- At risk only from a P&W-RR Joint Venture, which no column prices. Ghai's estimate puts 2050 at about 49.9-50.1% if it forms this round and counts at once, and about 39-43% if the GM counts a third maker on NGSA (inference).

Introduce the Open Fan (launched and ready by 2050): unmet, for good. A 2050 launch is ready in 2060, and NGSA's 2037 entry closed the airframer path. No PV is given up for it (objective premium $0). RISE stays all in as joint technology with Safran.
decision.predictions:
