- In S2 an fps launched now enters service in 2060, and our engine would be ready in 2057, on a market counted only to 2056. The $8B buys nothing, and it would put $8.0B against the $4B bound.
I withhold my co-signature. Acceptable alternative: `hold`.

vetoes.plan: `ultrafan_wb: launch`, in any plan
vetoes.ground:
The hurdle and the downside both fail.
- Beside the standing commitment it is -4.43 weighted, with -9.00 in S3, worse than its own $4B bill, including $5B of strain.
- Beside a withdraw it is -3.93.
- No Re-engine is on the record. Even in S4 and S5 it loses (-3.68, -3.32), because it is ready in 2056 against a 2055 Re-engine EIS.
- The gap is far above the $1B sub-cap.
I withhold my co-signature. Acceptable alternative: `hold`.

vetoes.plan: `t1000_upgrade: launch` while the Joint Venture commitment stands
vetoes.ground:
The unselected downside exceeds the item's own bill: -6.73 in S3 against a -$2B bill, including $5B of strain, and -2.22 weighted. No premium can cure that. It also breaks 'never both'; I flag that for the CEO to strike, and it is not my ground.
I withhold my co-signature. Acceptable alternative: `hold`.

vetoes.plan: `t1000_upgrade: launch` beside a withdraw, without a declared premium
`jv_with_pw: withdraw` (advice: a withdraw is not a launch or commit, so it is not my veto)
vetoes.ground:
I do not support it.
- The item is 0, 0, -1.22, 0, 0, 0: -0.12 weighted, below 0 on any weight for S3, and it gains nothing anywhere.
- It fails the 2050 test we set: the formation column is +1.22, and the off-grid worst case is the $4B bill.
I would back a withdraw only if Watson rules, with reasons, that a 2050 formation compresses maturity or cannot have support in place in 2050, when our share starts. The Board vetoes it otherwise.

vetoes.plan: Balance-sheet vetoes (equity raise, leverage above about 1.5x, levering up for buybacks)
vetoes.ground: None applies. The plan needs no equity and no borrowing. The S3 share is funded from free cash flow even if booked in one year (£2.94bn), and nothing is levered for buybacks.

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
I would back a withdraw, and my 2035 signature on a 2050 formation would go, if Watson rules with reasons either of two things:
- a 2050 formation cannot put the folded engine on NGSA without compressed maturity;
- support (P&W's GTF2 network, partner shops, spares and field service inside the $4B) cannot be in place in 2050, when our share starts on the grid.
The S3 column would then no longer carry +1.22 on any reading I could sign.

I would withhold my support on the terms in two cases:
- if a formation would put P&W's fleet obligations from before formation, or any concession it has given, on our account, because the worst case could then exceed the $4B bill;
- if the CEO attaches a payment, concession or launch-style pricing to bring P&W or Airbus in.
Any change of terms needs joint CEO-CFO sign-off.

On the other levers:
- I would re-test `launch_if_selected` or a Solo only against an airframer naming RR on an airframe whose EIS our engine can meet, with enough counted market left to pay back $8B. On this board none remains after 2056.
- I would re-test UltraFan WB only against an A350 Re-engine, or a 787 Re-engine naming UltraFan, on the record with a row that beats hold.
- I would re-test the upgrade only with its shortfall declared as a premium beside a withdraw that had passed on Watson's ground.

Delivered numbers and announced customers move me. Projections do not.
cfo.memo:
Safety, then the balance sheet. All four at hold passes both. It is the best plan in every column, so the premium is $0.

The 2050 review. I set the test last round and apply it as written. Keeping the commitment against a withdraw is 0, 0, +1.22, 0, 0, 0, or +0.12 on Board weights. P&W's "opening no terms" is no signal. I'd guide S3 lower, to 0.05, and the answer doesn't move. It is above zero, but thin: $5.22B of engine value for $4B, on a market counted to 2056. On a crude cash basis that's roughly 17-24%, at or just above our hurdle. In 2045 it was about 120%.

Worst case: Airbus's "counts as one" case, our $4B for no share, is -4.00. That's the bill and no worse, provided the GTF2 write-off and P&W's pre-formation fleet obligations stay with P&W. Standard terms, not a concession.

My 2035 co-signature covers a 2050 formation, on Rob's ruling that nothing is compressed and support is in place in 2050 itself. If he can't confirm that, my signature goes and I'd back a withdraw.

I won't sign a Solo (-7.20), launch_if_selected (-0.80), UltraFan WB (-4.43) or the upgrade beside the commitment (worst -6.73). Withdraw plus upgrade gives up $1.85B for nothing on our 2050 measures.

S3's £2.94bn comes from free cash flow: no equity, no borrowing. My record on launch economics is thin. Hold the commitment as free unless P&W comes. That's our best view at the minute.

tests.name: Ready by EIS
tests.numbers:
Plan tested: all four fields at hold, with the 2035 commitment standing.

NGSA (Airbus): launched 2030, EIS 2037, in service. Code 7 is final, and CFM and P&W GTF2 are fitted. We can reach it only through the Joint Venture.

S3 (P&W commits this round): the Joint Venture forms in 2050 with GTF2 folded in.
- GTF2 was launched in 2030 and has been ready since 2036 (bulletin), on P&W's six-year programme. It has been in service on NGSA since 2037, so by 2050 it has thirteen years of fleet time.
- The ready year the board prices is the formation year, 2050, because the folded engine is already ready. rules.md: the engine is ready 'earlier if a partner folds in a solo programme that is further along'. Without the fold it would be formation + 6, which is 2056, the last year of the counted narrowbody market.
- The engine was ready one year before NGSA's 2037 EIS. A 2050 formation changes who holds the share, not the engine's definition or its ready year.
- Grid: 26.1% of narrowbody engines in 2050, for $4.0B of our money, with $0 strain.
- Ruling: nothing is compressed, and the fold starts no new clock.
- Condition: UltraFan content goes in only as later insertions, each on its own test programme. The core definition stays the proven GTF2, and the case counts on none of the insertions. P&W says the same: 'Any later-block feature enters the fleet only when it is proven and instrumented.'

fps (Boeing): not launched, and no date. Against an fps launched this round, UltraFan NB launched in 2050 is ready in 2057.
- 10-year or via Embraer (S2): EIS 2060, three years of margin. Pass. The engine would arrive after the counted market ends in 2056. That is McCabe's price (-8.00 in S2), not a maturity ground.
- 7-year: EIS 2057, zero margin. Pass, with a note. No column shows this case.
- `launch_if_selected` passes by construction.
- An unconditional Solo would be ready in 2057 for no airframe on the record. Fail (advice); not on the lean.

Embraer (S6): it flies P&W or CFM, not us. Not applicable.

Widebody:
- UltraFan WB launched in 2050 would be ready in 2056, against a 787 or A350 Re-engine EIS of 2055 (S4, S5). One year late: fail (advice). No Re-engine is on the record, and the grid prices it at -3.68 in S4 and -3.32 in S5.
- The Trent 1000 upgrade would count from 2053 (2050 + 3), after 2035. No readiness issue. Widebody share in 2050 does not move.

tests.name: No early date
tests.numbers:
The CEO's draft statement gives no date and nothing on NGSA's fitting: '...No solo narrowbody programme. Maturity sets the date, and we compress nothing. Support through our partners will be in place before we take any share of the fleet...'. The support line is my no-date form from last round. Pass.

The draft public other moves give no dates either: the commitment restated on standard terms, and UltraFan maturation inside base R&D. I recheck the final text at step 4.

Notes, not veto grounds:
(1) Say nothing on when our share of NGSA would start. If S3 forms, the bulletin publishes the ready date; do not restate it.
(2) Do not revive 'formation plus six' (2056). It contradicts the fold. Being late, not early, it is not a veto ground.
(3) Do not answer Airbus's question in public ('fitting was settled at EIS', 'the Joint Venture counts as one'). It is Airbus's call and the GM's ruling. A remark on NGSA's fleet could read as a date.

tests.name: Support before EIS
tests.threshold: RR has no narrowbody MRO scale. A support plan through partner shops must exist before any narrowbody EIS; for a fold, before our share starts (inference). A standing commitment that can form this round counts as a commit for this test.
tests.numbers:
Lead time: zero years. The board counts our share in 2050 (26.1% in S3), the formation year.

The plan must therefore be in place at formation. It can be, only because support already exists: P&W's network has supported GTF2 on NGSA for thirteen years. The plan, named in round 3, carried forward unchanged:
(1) P&W's GTF2 network on NGSA is the base from day one, written into the Joint Venture agreement at formation.
(2) Partner shops on the Singapore Joint Venture model, named at formation, take work only once each is qualified. They add to the base; they do not carry the day-one load.
(3) A spares pool, repair technology and field service, inside our $4B share.
(4) Castings and forgings from high-performing suppliers, off the Trent lines.
(5) A fleet-transition team with Airbus and the NGSA operators, so the flying fleet sees no break in support when the engine moves into the Joint Venture. There is no new EIS, because the engine is already in service.
(6) Our V2500 operator relationships, from the regional and A320ceo fleet.
Before our share starts we review GTF2's fleet time on wing and size the spares pool to it. P&W will report that record 'as the fleet measures it, and not before'. I report the plan through the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee.

Pass, on two conditions:
- the plan goes into the rationale and a private move again;
- the terms do not leave us carrying narrowbody support alone from day one.
If either fails, that is a Civil veto ground at step 4.
If the GM rules that RR does not count as a third maker, we take no share and have nothing to support. That is McCabe's off-grid case (-4.00, the bill), not a support failure.

tests.name: Engineering load
tests.threshold: $5B of strain whenever a narrowbody project (UltraFan NB or the Joint Venture) and a widebody project (UltraFan WB or the Trent 1000 upgrade) are both on record, whatever their dates. Only cancelling one before it is ready removes it. Red lines: no UltraFan WB beside an UltraFan NB Solo unless both are selected, and no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development (inference).
tests.numbers:
All-hold: $0 strain in every column. In S3 our own narrowbody money is $4.0B, with $0 strain.

Confirmed: any widebody item beside the standing commitment costs $5B in S3.
- Upgrade row (S3): $4.0B / $5B. Its item against hold is -1.73, -1.73, -6.73, -1.73, -1.62, -1.73, which is -2.22 weighted. The worst column is beyond its $2B bill.
- UltraFan WB row (S3): $4.0B / $5B. Its item is -4.00, -4.00, -9.00, -3.68, -3.32, -4.00, which is -4.43 weighted. The worst column is beyond its $4B bill.
- Overlap (inference): the upgrade's 2050-53 work, or UltraFan WB's 2050-56, would sit on the same engineers as the Joint Venture's formation, integration and support set-up from 2050. The board charges the strain whatever the dates.
- Once formed, the Joint Venture engine is ready at formation and cannot be cancelled before it is ready, so the strain could not be removed.

Beside a withdraw: the upgrade carries $0 strain and is -1.73 flat (-1.62 in S5), or -1.72 weighted, against the withdraw row. UltraFan WB beside a withdraw is -3.93.

On all-hold no red line is touched. The upgrade or UltraFan WB beside the commitment would break 'never both' and Control's mission: a red-line flag, not my veto.

tests.name: Capacity and suppliers
tests.threshold: State RR's engines a year from the brief's year table. The board has no capacity limit, so the result is not applicable unless the brief reports one. A narrowbody ramp is flagged as needing partner MRO and high-performing supplier capacity, as advice (inference).
tests.numbers:
Hold year table: 188 widebody engines a year from 2042 to 2060 (197 to 2041), with 0 narrowbody. The brief reports no constraint.

S3: 26.1% of narrowbody engines in 2050. On 2050 demand of 1,933 aircraft at two engines each, that is about 1,009 engines a year credited to us, or about 1,031 on 2049's 1,976 observed deliveries. Both are inference, because the board counts aircraft actually delivered. That is about 5.4 times the Trent rate, for six counted years (2050-56).

Supply (inference): the volume rides on an engine already in production. Airbus's rate-gated signals run to 2050 (about 54-59 P&W sets a month on the delivery path). P&W is adding castings and forgings capacity in steps, with the fleet keeping first call on material. We add no new line.

Advice:
- P&W's network leads overhaul. We add partner-shop capacity on the Singapore model and high-performing supplier capacity.
- Trent XWB, Trent 7000 and Trent 1000 time on wing keep first call on engineers, shops and castings.
- My shop-visit baseline is my midterm figure of 1,100-1,200 a year, not the 1,400-1,500 Helen gave.

tests.name: Widebody dominance
tests.threshold: RR widebody engine share of at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050 on the brief's projection. Time on wing is the lever (inference).
tests.numbers:
Observed: 58.0% in 2040; 55.2% in 2045 after the GEnx upgrade took 2.8 points from 2042.
2050 on all-hold: 55.2% in every column (58.0% in S5), 5.2 points above the line. The worst year is 55.2%.
The upgrade would count from 2053, so 2050 share stays at 55.2%; the franchise test is not triggered. UltraFan WB shows 55.2% in 2050 on every column of the grid.

I close last round's A350 flag (S5).
- No Re-engine is on the record.
- UltraFan WB launched now would be ready in 2056, against a 2055 EIS. It loses even in S5 (-3.32).
- The board counts widebody to 2061.
- Airbus: any further step 'only once its engine is mature and its durability is proven', in 'windows, not dates', and 'one major development at a time'. No window is open on this board.
After 2061 the franchise is off-grid. It rests on Trent XWB time on wing and UltraFan maturation inside base R&D. That is qualitative.

Risk the board does not show (note): Charleston adds 787 capacity, about 117 a year by 2060. The 787 is where we are one of two makers, and the board does not move engine shares with the airframe split. Trent 1000 time on wing in base R&D is the answer to that.

The durability case for the upgrade, as I read it: the grid's upgrade is a share programme (+5 points from 2053). It is not the durability fix. That fix (the Trent 1000 package, retrofit in base durability spend) is already funded [RG-0068]. The grid misses no durability case that justifies a $2B programme, whether beside the commitment (-6.73 worst) or beside a withdraw (-1.72).

tests.name: Technology pull-through
tests.threshold: An idle or cancelled UltraFan still feeds the Trent fleet. Noted qualitatively; grid values are never adjusted (inference).
tests.numbers: UltraFan maturation inside base R&D feeds Trent time on wing and durability; no new programme, no bill. In S3 a two-way flow of geared-architecture durability learning between GTF2, UltraFan and the Trent is possible (inference), and UltraFan content enters the Joint Venture engine only as later tested insertions. No grid adjustment.

vetoes.plan: Row A, 'UltraFan NB: hold' with the 2035 commitment standing (the CEO's lean and my recommendation)
vetoes.ground:
Not invoked. At step 4 I check the Civil veto on its grounds only. Under the team rule it binds if any of these holds:
(a) The final statement or a public other move gives an EIS or ready date, an NGSA date, or when our engine or share joins NGSA's fleet. Nothing may be earlier than the bulletin's folded-GTF2 ready year (2036) or formation + 6 (2056).
(b) The statement, an other move or the rationale counts on UltraFan content entering service inside the Joint Venture engine before it is tested, which would reopen the test programme. Or it counts on any engine before its ready year.
(c) The rationale and the private moves carry no partner-shop support plan in place before our share starts, for a commitment that can form this round. Or the terms leave us carrying narrowbody support alone from day one.
These grounds rest on attributed transcript turns [RX-0296, RX-0284, RX-0283].

vetoes.plan: Rows B and D: any withdraw of the Joint Venture commitment
vetoes.ground:
No Civil ground. I rule that a 2050 formation does not compress maturity:
- GTF2 was launched in 2030 and has been ready since 2036, with thirteen years on NGSA.
- The ready year is the formation year.
- UltraFan content goes in only as later insertions.
I also rule that support can be in place before our share starts, because P&W's network is the base from day one.
So the condition on which the Board would accept a withdraw on its own is not met. Whether to withdraw is the CEO's and the CFO's call, on the partner test: the withdraw item is 0, 0, -1.22, 0, 0, 0, or -0.12 weighted.

vetoes.plan: Row C (Trent 1000 upgrade beside the standing commitment) and row E (UltraFan WB)
vetoes.ground:
These are red-line and strain concerns, not Civil vetoes.
- Each breaks 'never both' in S3, at $5B of strain: the upgrade is -6.73 and UltraFan WB -9.00, both worse than their own bills. The CEO strikes the breach.
- UltraFan WB also fails Ready by EIS, as advice: it would be ready in 2056, against a 2055 Re-engine EIS, and no Re-engine is on the record.
- The upgrade is my time-on-wing tool, but on this grid it counts only from 2053 and buys no 2050 share. Durability stays in base R&D.
- Row D (withdraw + upgrade) carries no strain and no red line, but it gives up $1.85B against A. That is not my ground; if it is taken, it is a declared premium for McCabe to co-sign.

vetoes.plan: Rows F and G: UltraFan NB `launch_if_selected` and the unconditional Solo
vetoes.ground:
Not invoked, and conditional.
- G fails Ready by EIS, as advice: it would be ready in 2057 for no airframe on the record.
- F passes readiness by construction: ready in 2057, against an fps EIS of 2060 (three years of margin) or 2057 (zero margin).
- Either would be an all-RR narrowbody with no P&W network behind it. If either is submitted without a partner-shop support plan in place before EIS, ground (c) binds at step 4.
- That the engine arrives after the counted market ends in 2056, and the $8B against Control's $4B bound, are Tufan's and Helen's call.

ops.would_change_mind_if:
I would invoke the Civil veto, or change my advice, in seven cases.

Cases where the veto binds at step 4:
(1) The Joint Venture terms put UltraFan content into the core definition before it is tested, reopening the folded engine's test programme. That is compressed maturity. The veto binds unless the content moves to a later insertion.
(2) The rationale leaves out the support plan. Or the terms leave us carrying narrowbody support alone from day one. Or the fold breaks support to the NGSA fleet already flying.
(3) The statement or a public other move gives any date: an EIS, a ready date, an NGSA date, or when our engine or share joins NGSA's fleet.

Cases where my advice changes:
(4) Public fleet evidence shows GTF2 failing on durability or time on wing on NGSA. The folded engine would no longer be a mature base, and I would re-rule on maturity before our share starts. P&W has published no such record; it reports 'as the fleet measures it'.
(5) The CEO and CFO withdraw on the partner test, so no narrowbody programme is on record. I would then back the Trent 1000 upgrade only as a declared premium, at least $1.72B, with Helen's co-signature. I would not press for it: it counts from 2053 and buys no 2050 share.
(6) A 787 or A350 Re-engine on the record names UltraFan, with an EIS that a 2056 ready year can meet. I would re-test UltraFan WB, with the $5B strain if the Joint Venture has formed.
(7) An fps is launched naming RR. `launch_if_selected` passes readiness (ready 2057, against EIS 2060 or 2057), and I would test its support plan. The money and the bound are Tufan's and Helen's call.
ops.memo:
Tufan, Helen: one Rolls-Royce, one programme on record: the commitment we made.

My ruling on a 2050 formation (S3): nothing is compressed. GTF2 was launched in 2030, ready in 2036, and has flown on NGSA since 2037: thirteen years of fleet time. The fold brings a proven engine and starts no new clock. Without it, formation plus six would be 2056, the year the counted market ends. UltraFan content goes in only as later insertions, each on its own test programme, and the case counts on none of it.

Support. The board counts our share in 2050 itself: no lead time. That works only because support already exists: P&W's GTF2 network is the base from day one. On top: partner shops on the Singapore model, taking work as each qualifies; spares and field service inside our $4B; castings and forgings off the Trent lines; a fleet-transition team with Airbus and the operators, so the flying fleet sees no break. Carry the plan in the rationale, or I veto at step 4. I report through the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee.

I find no Civil ground for a withdraw.

Load: $0 strain on all-hold. Any widebody item beside the commitment costs $5B in S3.

Widebody: 55.2% in 2050, every column; 58.0% in S5. A350 flag closed: UltraFan WB would be ready in 2056 against a 2055 Re-engine EIS, and none is on the record. Durability stays in base R&D.

All four at hold, no veto. We're pacing that programme properly.

other_moves.move: Standing Joint Venture commitment with Pratt & Whitney, kept after the review and restated on standard terms
other_moves.detail: The 2035 `jv_with_pw: commit` stands after review. It is for an airframe that has chosen both makers. The terms credit the technology Rolls-Royce brings; that asks for value and is not a concession. No payment to P&W or to any airframer, no launch-style pricing, no free upgrades. The terms are unchanged, so no new joint CEO-CFO sign-off is needed. No dates. Nothing on any airframer's fleet, on NGSA's fitting, on how Airbus counts its engine sources, or on when our share would start.

other_moves.move: Continue UltraFan technology maturation inside the existing R&D envelope
other_moves.detail: Demonstrator and geared-architecture work continues inside base R&D and feeds Trent time on wing and durability. No new programme, no new bill, no dates.

other_moves.move: Narrowbody support plan, written into the Joint Venture agreement at formation and in place before our share starts (Watson)
other_moves.detail:
If P&W commits this round, the plan is in place at formation, because our share counts from the formation year itself:
(1) P&W's GTF2 network on NGSA, which has supported the fleet since it entered service, is the base from day one and is written into the agreement.
(2) Partner shops on the Singapore Joint Venture model are named at formation. Each takes work only once it is qualified. They add to the base and do not carry the day-one load.
(3) A spares pool, repair technology and field service, funded inside our $4B share.
(4) Narrowbody castings and forgings go to high-performing suppliers, off the Trent lines.
(5) A fleet-transition team with Airbus and the NGSA operators, so the flying fleet sees no break in support when the engine moves into the Joint Venture.
(6) Our V2500 operator relationships.
Before our share starts we review GTF2's fleet time on wing and size the spares pool to it. We will not accept terms that leave us carrying narrowbody support alone from day one. Trent XWB, Trent 7000 and Trent 1000 time on wing keep first call on engineers, shops and castings. Watson reports the plan through the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee. Milestones stay private.

other_moves.move: UltraFan insertion rule for the Joint Venture engine
other_moves.detail: The core definition is the folded GTF2, a proven engine; the fold starts no new clock. UltraFan content goes in only as later insertions, each on its own test programme. Nothing that would reopen the folded engine's test programme goes in, and nothing changes the core definition before it is proven. The business case counts on none of it. This is Watson's condition.

other_moves.move: Joint Venture terms: pre-formation fleet obligations stay with P&W (McCabe's condition)
other_moves.detail: Standard terms, not a concession. P&W's fleet obligations from before formation, and any concessions it has given to GTF2 operators, stay on P&W's account. GTF2's write-off at the fold falls on P&W. Spares and field service for our share sit inside our $4B. This keeps the reasonable worst case of a formation at our own bill (-4.00) and no worse. Any change of terms comes back for joint CEO-CFO sign-off.

other_moves.move: Widebody: Do Nothing on programmes; time on wing inside base R&D
other_moves.detail: Widebody share is 55.2% in 2050 in every column (58.0% in S5), above the 50% line. No 787 or A350 Re-engine is on the record. The Trent 1000 durability package is already funded in base durability spend. Trent XWB, Trent 7000 and Trent 1000 time on wing and durability stay in base R&D, which is not a programme and carries no strain. Watson's A350 franchise flag from 2045 is closed. Charleston 787 capacity is noted as a Trent 1000 time-on-wing priority, not a programme.

other_moves.move: Pricing discipline on every engine campaign
other_moves.detail: No concessions to buy a narrowbody selection or to induce P&W or Airbus. Every new contract goes through the Investment Committee, with win-win terms and value paid for. Any aggressive term needs joint CEO-CFO sign-off, and none is proposed.

other_moves.move: Capital order unchanged
other_moves.detail: Balance sheet first, then the dividend (30-40%), then investment and extra distributions. No equity, no new borrowing, no levering up for buybacks. If the Joint Venture forms, our $4B share (about GBP 2.94bn at 1.36 $/GBP) is funded from free cash flow and redeployed from base UltraFan maturation inside a broadly flat R&D envelope. Booked at formation it falls in one year; McCabe flags that as advice on the envelope, not a ground.

other_moves.move: Game close on the record
other_moves.detail: Last round; no review follows. The commitment stands unformed at game end unless P&W commits, at no cost. Enter-narrowbody cannot be met in full (2045 was 0.0%); only its 2050 half is open, through S3. Widebody dominance and both of Control's mission measures are met in every column on this plan.

decision.public_statement: So. We reviewed our commitment to a Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney, and it stands. When we commit something, we honor it. Standard terms, terms that credit the technology we bring. No payment, no concession. No solo narrowbody programme. Maturity sets the date, and we compress nothing. Support through our partners will be in place before we take any share of the fleet. Widebody is our core, and we will protect it. We are not after market share. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.
decision.rationale:
Decision: all four at hold. This was my proposal, both memos recommend it, and it is the Board's lean. Nothing differs from the default, so there is no Board item and nothing needs McCabe's co-signature.

1. Start from the proposal
Row 'UltraFan NB: hold': -0.56, -0.56, +0.66, -0.56, -0.22, -0.56 (S1-S6). Weighted -0.42, worst -0.56. The brief names it the best plan against every column, so no plan beats it anywhere and the premium is $0.

Weights: S1 0.55, S2 0.10, S3 0.10, S4 0.10, S5 0.05, S6 0.10. This is the Board's illustrative set, the one the ExCo used in 2045.
- No airframer has named UltraFan.
- P&W 'opening no terms' is no signal, so S3 is at most about 0.10. McCabe would guide it to 0.05; the item is then +0.06 and the answer does not move.
- Boeing's code-7 line weakens S2.
- The bulletin rules out no column. The decision does not turn on the weights.

2. The 2050 review, read openly
We set the test in 2045: keep the commitment if the formation column is at least 0 against a withdraw and its off-grid worst case is within the $4B bill.
- Keep against withdraw: 0, 0, +1.22, 0, 0, 0, or +0.12 weighted. Above 0. A withdraw ('hold + withdraw JV commitment': -0.56, -0.56, -0.56, -0.56, -0.22, -0.56) gains nothing in any column.
- Frankly, it is thin. That is $5.22B of engine value for a $4B bill on a market counted to 2056, down from +6.57 in 2045. McCabe's crude cash check is about 17.5-23.6% on every shape she tried, at or just above the mid-to-high-teens hurdle.

Even then the 2050 doctrine chooses Launch only above +2 yp in S1, and this grid gives only +1.0 yp at a zero own share. So it would take a different grid as well: about 3x the operating profit, or a market that holds after 2060. To pass the advice lines too (2x leverage, investment grade), our own share would have to fall to about $0.95B. No round follows 2050, so in this game the answer is Do Nothing. The company's horizon is longer than the game's: we keep the balance sheet healthy and the Team Korea talks going, with funding defined at approval. As soon as we have more visibility, then we can make any change.
cfo.memo:
Felipe here. Expected column S1, as Gomes Neto named it; risk column S3, the worst plausible, since none is labelled. Tests and thresholds inherited from Garcia, unchanged; the 5-point limit is the team rule.

Leg 1, partners: pass. Team Korea 30% ($3.0B), suppliers 10%, Brazilian research 5%: $4.5B, all in the brief. Our 55%, $5.50B, is booked at entry into service in 2054.

Leg 2, cost of capital: fail. Launch against Do Nothing in S1 is -0.22 $B, -2.0 yield points, debt penalty netted once ($0.59B rise, $0.03B in present value). My rebuild: $0.11B operating profit, less $0.30B bill, less $0.03B. S2 -0.20, S3 -0.23: below zero everywhere.

Leg 3, bad case: pass. S3 is -2.1 points, inside 5. It does not cure leg 2.

I veto a 2050 launch, and the team rule makes it binding.

The tie band does not help. Even at a zero own share S1 is only +1.0 point, short of the 2-point band.

Advice, inherited from Garcia: net debt to $6.2B, 56% of enterprise value, about 7.5x against "below 2x"; in my reading investment grade does not survive. The cash call is $1.375B a year in 2050-53, 69% of the $2B floor each year. No round after 2050: a one-way door.

The better row is discounting, not product. Valued at its own entry into service, operating profit fell from $3.8B to $3.0B to $2.0B against $6.1B of cost. A trend, not a one-off, right?

No objective left to buy: premium zero. Do Nothing.

tests.name: Market window against fps and NGSA (veto leg a; CEO ask 1)
tests.threshold: From the bulletin, find any launched fps or NGSA and its EIS. Window = the first new-generation EIS minus ours. Pass if none is launched, or if the window covers our ~6-year ramp. Flag (advice) if it is shorter than the ramp. Fail (soft veto, leg a) if a new-generation type is in service or due at or before our EIS. Shut (H3, no launch) if fps and NGSA are each in service at our EIS or due within 2 years after it. Basis: my E2 record applied to a narrowbody by inference, plus company record (no head-to-head entry while Boeing and Airbus hold the segment).
tests.numbers: Bulletin: NGSA launched 2030 and in service since 2037. fps was not launched in 2030, 2035 or 2045. Our EIS is 2054 (2050 + 4). Window = 2037 - 2054 = -17 years, so the narrowbody would enter service seventeen years behind a new-generation type in S1, S2 and S3. The CEO's count is confirmed: the window is narrow in every column and shut in none. An fps sealed this round enters service in 2057 (S3, 7-yr, 3 years after ours) or 2060 (S2, 10-yr, 6 years after). H3 needs 2056 or earlier, so it is not engaged in any column. H6: fps via Embraer is not live. How much value depends on the rivals: no column has neither type in service, because NGSA is a fact and not a sealed order. The second type moves the row by -0.01 $B (S3: -0.23 against -0.22) and +0.02 $B (S2: -0.20). Leg (a) fails on the public record (record, by inference; company record).

tests.name: Share path through the ramp, by column: who sets deliveries (CEO ask 2)
tests.threshold: Read our share at EIS and at full rate from the brief, and say whether the line, the share or overflow sets deliveries. I use the rules' demand curve, linear between its points, both on total demand and with COMAC's 250 a year taken off the top (in brackets) (inference).
tests.numbers: The line is confirmed: 16 (2054, my reading), 32 (2055, brief), 48, 64, 80, then 96 (2059), 96 (2060, brief), and 96 a year to 2073 (20 market years). Wanted at 6.3% of demand: 110 (94) in 2054, 107 (91) in 2055, 100 (84) in 2056, 92 (76) in 2057, 85 (69) in 2058, 77 (61) in 2059 and 70 (54) in 2060. S1: the line sets deliveries in 2054-58 (to 2057 on the COMAC-off basis), and the share sets them from 2059. In 2060 the brief's 96 is 8.7% of about 1,103 delivered. That is about 26 jets (42 on the COMAC-off basis) above the 6.3% want, filled by overflow. My inference from the rules: the MAX phases out to none by 2060 and there is no fps in S1, so Boeing customers whom neither Boeing nor Airbus serves take our free slots. S3: 3.6% from 2057 wants 53, 48, 44 and 40 against a line of 64, 80, 96 and 96, so the share binds from fps EIS. S2: 6.3% to 2059 as in S1, then 3.6% in 2060 (40 wanted). Why S2 reads $0.02B better than S1: the share cannot explain it, since S2's share is equal or lower every year. It is overflow (inference). A 10-yr fps enters service in 2060, just as the MAX reaches zero, so Boeing's preference revives from 2060 while its line ramps slowly (rate 50 about four years after EIS), and more unserved customers reach our line, mostly after 2060. Operating profit in PV: my line-to-2060 rebuild gives $0.094B. The grid implies $0.108B (S1), $0.128B (S2) and $0.098B (S3), so the tail after 2060 is +$0.014B, +$0.034B and +$0.004B. I count the tail the grid implies and no more. Bound: at 96 a year sold to 2073 the row is -0.12, still below zero. Share-bound with no overflow, to 2060: $0.086B (S1), $0.081B (S2), $0.065B (S3). Work: work/r4_meijer_test_calc.py.

tests.name: Product edge over the A320neo and 737 MAX (CEO ask 6)
tests.threshold: State the edge in the brief's numbers and whether it is compelling (company record: no head-to-head entry without a compelling advantage). By inference, my E2 case does not carry over to a 150-180 seater. Advice only, not a veto leg.
tests.numbers: Rules: the narrowbody is 'slightly better for airlines than the 737 MAX and A320neo and worse than a new-generation airplane'. By 2054 the types it beats are gone or going. Airbus's A320neo LEAP-1A and GTF tail ends by 2047 (bulletin), and the MAX falls from 2044 to none by 2060 (rules). So its real rival is NGSA, with 17 years in service at our EIS, and our airplane is worse than NGSA. Its share falls from 12% to 7% with one type in service, then to 6.3% after the US cut. $50M at 12% gives $6.0M a jet, $0.576B a year at 96. That edge is slight, not compelling. My E2 case (trip cost, complementing the big jets) does not carry over to a 150-180 seater fighting them head-on, and the first E-Jet 'struggled to get to the right cost level'. I name my E2 anchoring here. Advice only.

tests.name: Customers and campaigns
tests.threshold: Back a launch only where Embraer's share is positive at EIS and at full rate in the expected case, and Hold's E2 business is not reduced (inference from record).
tests.numbers: Expected column S1, share of the market's deliveries: about 0.9% in 2054 (16 of about 1,747, my reading), 1.9% in 2055 (32, brief) and 8.7% in 2060 (96, brief). It is positive. The brief says the E-Jets and business jets are the same in every plan, so Hold's E2 business is not reduced. Caveat: from 2059 the share fills only 77 of 96 (70 in 2060), and overflow does the rest. Buyers (inference): E-Jet operators moving up, multi-OEM buyers, lessors and low-cost carriers, won with local sales and support. I note my campaign optimism; only the brief's share is in these numbers.

tests.name: Price discipline (CEO ask 6, margin)
tests.threshold: Report the price effect from the brief and whether it reaches Embraer's own margin, as a number (inference). Advice only.
tests.numbers: Rules: from 2053, one year before our EIS, the price of every new single-aisle Boeing and Airbus deliver falls in a straight line over 7 years: 0.29% in 2053, 0.57% in 2054, 1.43% in 2057 and 2.0% from 2059. On Boeing it is up to 2.6% in years with no new Boeing narrowbody in service: every year in S1, to 2056 in S3 and to 2059 in S2. The cut falls on their margins, not ours: the brief fixes ours at $50M and 12%. Advice (inference against company record): 12% is 4.6 times the 2.6% Commercial Aviation earned in 2025. Each 1 pp of our margin is worth about $0.009B in PV on this row. Zero in S1 would need about 36.5% at $50M, and the override bar about 98%. The brief shows 12%, so no credit. Pricing to win against NGSA would push the margin down, not up.

tests.name: Supply chain and ramp (veto leg b; CEO ask 4)
tests.threshold: Take the brief's ramp as given and never plan a faster one. Fail (soft veto) if the brief reports a supply-chain problem that would hold the line. Flag a lesser risk as advice. Mostly company record.
tests.numbers: The brief reports no supply-chain problem, so leg (b) passes on supply. The ramp is taken as given: 16 in 2054 to 96 a year from 2059, six years. Advice, not a veto ground. (1) Company record: the E-Jet line is climbing toward about 120 commercial jets a year, 'if the investments justify the return', with bottlenecks that move from one supplier to another. Adding 96 gives about 216 a year by 2059, 1.8 times that target. (2) Bulletin: Airbus delivered 1,267 narrowbodies in 2049. It has extended rate-gated NGSA engine-set signals to 2050, adds lines from 2045 and is securing its own titanium, additive and Spirit work packages. P&W adds castings and forgings in steps, and the fleet keeps first call on material. So a second line competes for a supply base already being loaded (inference). (3) Record: our supply-chain hit has been 'a lot less than on the competitors', partly because core work stays in-house.

tests.name: Engines and system supply (veto leg b; CEO ask 3)
tests.threshold: Pass if the brief shows an engine on offer by EIS with no live delivery or durability problem. Fail (soft veto) if no engine is on offer, or if a live engine problem would hold the line. Record plus company record.
tests.numbers: Rules: the narrowbody flies P&W, the E2's maker. CFM's Embraer partnership is not live. Bulletin: GTF2 has been ready since 2036, 18 years before our 2054 EIS, and has been in service on NGSA since 2037. P&W offers Embraer GTF2 or the GTF family at the GTF Advantage standard, at our choice, on standard terms. Both are installations, not developments. The brief reports no engine problem, so nothing holds the line or the four-year development. Advice, not a veto ground. (1) Full rate needs 192 engines a year (8 sets a month) before spares, about 14-15% on top of P&W's 54-59 NGSA sets a month. The A320neo GTF tail ended by 2047, which frees some of that flow (inference). (2) P&W: 'the fleet flying today keeps first call on material', and it reports GTF2 time on wing only 'as the fleet measures it'. (3) Engines were 'part of the supply chain challenges' in our guidance (record). Korea has no airliner engine (research, unverified).

tests.name: Clean-sheet schedule, certification and the one-way door (CEO ask 5)
tests.threshold: Advice only: set the board's 4-year development and 6-year ramp against our own record. A slip is a veto ground only if the brief reports one (inference).
tests.numbers: The brief reports no development or certification problem, so there is no veto ground. Company record: the E2, a re-wing and re-engine of an existing family, took about 4 years 10 months from launch (June 2013) to first delivery (April 2018), with a clean entry into service. The board gives a clean-sheet 150-180 seater, a step Embraer has never taken, four years (2050-2054), then a six-year ramp to 2059. One-way door: 2050 is the last decision year, so no round could cancel or answer a slip. The board prices no slip. Embraer integrates and certifies, and the partner cannot fill that gap (research, unverified).

tests.name: Partner fit (Team Korea)
tests.threshold: Report the partner's share of the bill from the brief. Flag a plan that relies on the partner for integration or certification (inference).
tests.numbers: Brief: Team Korea carries 30% ($3.0B), risk-sharing suppliers 10% ($1.0B) and Brazilian state research money 5% ($0.5B), so partners carry $4.5B in all. Embraer carries 55% ($5.50B), booked at EIS 2054: PV $0.296B at a discount factor of 0.0538. Embraer leads the airframe (inference from the 2011 lead-airframer stance), and the brief does not rely on the partner for integration or certification. On my rebuild, anchored to the grid, zero in S1 needs our own share near 19.6%: partners near 80%, about $3.5B more than the $4.5B shown. S2 needs 23.1% and S3 17.8%. No credit. The funding verdict is Santana's.

tests.name: Customer politics and the high-volume market (CEO ask 6)
tests.threshold: Advice only: report the tariff effect from the brief and discount US campaigns by a number (company record plus inference).
tests.numbers: Brief: the US climate cuts our share of new customers by 10% (7% to 6.3%, 4% to 3.6%), and the cut is in the grid. In S1 the line binds to 2058, so with no overflow the cut costs about $0.003B to 2060, and overflow refills part of that. So the discount on US campaigns is 10% of share, worth $0.00-0.01B on this grid. Is it a product for the big market? By share of deliveries it looks like one (8.7% in 2060), but from 2059 it lives on overflow: 6.3% of demand falling from 1,933 (2050) to 1,701 (2055) and 1,106 (2060) fills 70 of 96 jets in 2060. In S3, 3.6% fills about 40-55%. Not priced: BNDES credit, the golden share, any US response to a Brazil-Korea airliner. Over 40% US content cuts both ways (company record).

tests.name: Override of my soft veto (team rule; CEO ask 7)
tests.threshold: An override needs a plan more than 5 yp (+$0.55B) better than Hold in the expected column, recorded by the CEO as a Board item.
tests.numbers: Expected column S1: Launch is -0.22 $B (98.0%, -2.0 yp) against Hold at +0.00. The bar is +0.55 $B, so the launch falls $0.77B (7.0 yp) short. At a zero own share the row is about +0.108 $B (+1.0 yp), operating profit alone, still $0.44B short. Only a margin near 98% at $50M would reach the bar, and the brief shows 12%. No valid override exists on this brief, and none is possible on these terms. Confirmed.

tests.name: Hard-rule check (H1 partner, H3 shut window, H6 fps via Embraer)
tests.threshold: Flag an order the rules or the profile's hard rules forbid. This is not my veto. H2 and the funding legs are Santana's; I state the grid only.
tests.numbers: H1: Team Korea's 30% is in the brief. H3: at EIS 2054 only NGSA is in service (since 2037). fps would be due in 2057 (S3) or 2060 (S2), not within 2 years, so H3 is not engaged. H6: fps via Embraer is not live. If Boeing orders it this round, its order stands and our launch is refused. For H2, the grid only: -0.22 (S1), -0.20 (S2), -0.23 (S3). My rebuild: bill PV $0.296B; debt-penalty rise $0.590B (net debt $0.7B to $6.2B, 56% of EV), $0.032B in PV, counted once; -0.23 with the line to 2060 only. A launch would read below zero in every column (hard-rule flag below, not binding as mine).

vetoes.plan: Launch the new narrowbody with Korea in 2050 (EIS 2054)
vetoes.ground: Narrow window, leg (a). The bulletin shows NGSA launched in 2030 and in service since 2037, seventeen years before our 2054 EIS. In S1, S2 and S3 the narrowbody would enter service behind a new-generation type. Its share of new customers is cut to 6.3% (7% less the US 10%) before its first delivery, and to 3.6% once fps follows (2057 in S3, 2060 in S2). The window is narrow, not shut. H3 is not engaged, because fps is due more than 2 years after our EIS, and H6 is not live. Leg (b) passes: P&W is fitted, GTF2 has been ready since 2036 on standard terms as an installation, and the brief reports no engine or supply-chain problem. Under the team rule this is a soft veto. It binds unless Gomes Neto records an override, as a Board item, for a plan more than 5 yp (+$0.55B) better than Hold in the expected column. In S1 the launch is -0.22 $B (-2.0 yp), $0.77B short of that bar. Even a zero own share gives about +0.11 $B (+1.0 yp), so no valid override exists on this brief. For the Board, plainly: in S1 the line sets deliveries to 2058, and from 2059 the 96 a year leans on overflow (8.7% of the market's deliveries in 2060, against 6.3% of falling demand). The bill ($0.30B in PV) and the penalty ($0.03B) against about $0.11B of operating profit are what sink the row.

vetoes.plan: Hard-rule flag on any 2050 Launch: H2 grid condition (not my veto)
vetoes.ground: H2's game test needs the grid, debt penalty included, at or above zero in the expected column. The Launch row reads -0.22 $B (S1), -0.20 $B (S2) and -0.23 $B (S3), below zero in every column, so the condition is unmet whichever column is named. The funding verdict and its binding veto belong to Santana. I flag only the numbers. H6 note: if Boeing orders fps via Embraer this round, our launch is refused and reverts to Hold.

vetoes.plan: Readiness advice on any launch (not binding)
vetoes.ground: Advice only, not a veto ground, because the brief reports none of these as a problem. (1) Supply base: about 216 commercial jets a year by 2059 (1.8 times the E-Jet target of about 120), on suppliers that also feed Airbus's 1,267 narrowbodies a year and its extra lines. (2) Engines: 192 P&W engines a year at full rate, about 14-15% on top of the 54-59 NGSA sets a month, with the in-service fleet keeping first call on material. (3) Schedule: a clean sheet certified in four years against the E2's roughly five, in the last decision year, so a one-way door with no cancel round. (4) US tariffs: worth $0.00-0.01B on this grid. (5) Product: slightly better than types that leave production by 2047 (A320neo) and 2060 (MAX), and worse than NGSA, its real rival.

ops.would_change_mind_if: On the window, leg (a): nothing can change it. NGSA in service since 2037 is a bulletin fact, no column has it out of service, and 2050 is the last round. Toward a launch, two things would have to be in a brief, and neither is in this one. First, ΔPV at or above zero in S1 with the debt penalty included: our own share near 19.6% (partners near 80%, about $3.5B more than the $4.5B shown), or a margin near 36.5% at $50M. Second, to clear my veto by override, more than +0.55 $B in S1. That is out of reach even at a zero own share (+0.11 $B) and would need a margin near 98%. Toward a harder line, either of two things. First, a reported P&W delivery or durability problem, or a supplier constraint that would hold the line (leg b). Second, a bulletin showing an fps in service or due by 2056, which would shut the window under H3.
ops.memo:
That's a triple layer question. So let me start with the window.

First, the window. NGSA has been in service since 2037. Our entry into service would be 2054, seventeen years behind it, in S1, S2 and S3. That is leg (a) of my soft veto, and it stands. It is narrow, not shut. An fps sealed this round comes in 2057 or 2060, more than two years after us, so H3 is not engaged, and fps via Embraer is not live. An override needs a plan five yield points better than Hold. This one is 2.0 below. Even with partners paying the whole bill, the airplane earns about $0.11B against a $0.55B bar. No override exists.

Second, the line. P&W is fitted, and GTF2 has been ready since 2036, on standard terms, as an installation. The brief reports no engine or supply problem, so leg (b) passes. Advice only: about 216 commercial jets a year by 2059 on a supply base Airbus is loading, 192 P&W engines a year, and a clean sheet in four years through a one-way door.

Third, the customers. At 6.3% they want about 107 jets in 2055 against a 32 line, so the line sets deliveries to 2058. Then demand falls to 1,106 by 2060, 6.3% is about 70, and the line of 96 relies on overflow, not preference.

The money is Felipe's test. The row is below zero in every column.

Hold. Window and customers rest on my E2 record, by inference; supply and schedule on company record.

other_moves.move: Deliver the plan and keep building cash to support a potential next move
other_moves.detail: We keep delivering the E2 family, the business jets, defence and services to plan, in the harvest season. Productivity comes before new capacity. Commercial output rises toward about 120 jets a year only where the return justifies it, and we keep supply-chain headroom [EX-0053, EX-0080, EX-0077, EX-0078, EX-0087]. Net debt stays at $0.7B, and the cash is there to support a potential next move. The board does not price this move.

other_moves.move: Keep technology readiness funded for the next product cycle
other_moves.detail: Studies continue for a new cycle of products, naming no segment and no date. We keep talking to all the engine makers and select none, because engine selection comes before any business case [EX-0112, EX-0141, EX-0133, EX-0044]. Meijer's 2050 readiness advice is logged for any later case. First, about 216 commercial jets a year at full rate, on a supply base Airbus is loading. Second, 192 P&W engines a year, about 14-15% on top of the NGSA engine sets, with the in-service fleet keeping first call on material. Third, a four-year clean-sheet certification, against the E2's 4 years 10 months. None of these is a veto ground on this brief.

other_moves.move: Keep the Team Korea / KAI talks alive past 2050 on a funding solution defined before any approval
other_moves.detail: I follow the talks personally every two weeks [EX-0028]. The aim is a funding solution defined at the time of any business-case approval [EX-0046, EX-0034]. On this brief's terms, a launch reaches zero in S1 only with our own share near 19.6%: partners near 80%, about $3.5B more than the $4.5B the brief shows. Even then, net debt would be 24% of enterprise value at entry into service. No money counts until a brief shows it. No segment, no date, no commitment. Embraer keeps control and no military technology moves, so no state consent is needed for these talks (golden share; inference).

other_moves.move: Carry the 2030-2050 decision record forward for any next move
other_moves.detail: We keep the four Launch rows against Do Nothing: -1.02 $B (2030), -0.58 (2035 rebuild), -0.28 (2045) and -0.22 (2050) in the expected column. The row improved only because a constant $6.09B of cost (our $5.50B share plus the $0.59B rise in the debt penalty) was booked later. Its present value fell from $1.57B to $0.55B to $0.33B. Operating profit in present value fell from $0.99B to $0.27B to $0.11B. Valued at each entry into service, it fell from $3.84B to $3.00B to $2.00B. Any next case starts from that trend: it needs partners near 80% of the bill, or about 3x the operating profit, before it can pay its cost of capital.

other_moves.move: Trade: argue for zero tariffs in aerospace, on data
other_moves.detail: More than 40% of our aircraft is US content [EX-0124]. Tariffs mean fewer aircraft sold in the US, fewer US parts bought, fewer US jobs and a limited ability to invest in the future [EX-0101, EX-0102]. We ask both governments to talk and take no side, and we discuss no politics [EX-0100, EX-0098, EX-0106]. The 10% share cut is already in the grid and is worth about $0.01B on this row. It is no reason for this decision either way.

decision.public_statement:
Safety first and quality always: that is the foundation of our culture. We believe we are still in our harvest season, right? We keep delivering our plan with the products we have: the E2 family, our executive jets, defence and services. And we keep a healthy balance sheet to support a potential next move.

On a new airplane I will give you the same answer I always give. We are investing in new technologies so that we are prepared to make that decision when the time comes. A launch needs a strong product with a strong value proposition and a robust, I mean, funding strategy, because we don't want to put in risk the financial health of the company. We have done the work again this year, with our partners, and the numbers do not prove the return. The investment has to prove its return. So today we have no decision to announce, and we will not discuss a segment or a date. We continue to talk to our partners, including in Korea, and to all the engine makers. Any large investment will be made with partners, with the funding defined at the time of approval. This does not depend only on us. I will not say conservative, but I would say, realistic.

On the decisions of other manufacturers: those are their decisions. We have our own strategy, and I can only speak for Embraer.

On trade, Embraer is about engineering. We focus on data and things that are under our control. More than 40% of our aircraft is US content, so tariffs mean fewer US parts bought and fewer US jobs. We continue to work with both governments for zero tariffs in aerospace, and we are cautiously optimistic.

We compete hard in every campaign, but we don't sell our aircraft below cost. As we proudly say in Embraer, We Live for the Challenge.
decision.rationale:
Decision: Hold (Do Nothing, no new narrowbody), for the fourth round running. Hold is the default and not a Board item. It is the brief's best plan in all three columns: +0.00 $B (100.0%).

THE GRID. Launch the new narrowbody with Korea against Do Nothing, debt penalty included and counted once:
- S1 (Rivals hold): -0.22 $B (98.0%, -2.0 yp).
- S2 (Boeing launches fps 10-yr): -0.20 $B (98.2%, -1.8 yp).
- S3 (Boeing launches fps 7-yr): -0.23 $B (97.9%, -2.1 yp).
My expected column is S1. The bulletin shows no fps launched in three rounds, and I do not speculate on Boeing's sealed order. The risk column is S3, the worst plausible one, because the brief labels no risk case. The row is below zero in every column, so the decision does not turn on which column I name.

MY FOUR QUESTIONS, ON THE BRIEF'S NUMBERS.
(1) Strong product, strong value proposition? No.
- Entry into service would be 2054, 17 years after NGSA.
- By the rules the jet is slightly better than the A320neo and 737 MAX and worse than a new-generation airplane. By 2054 the A320neo tail has ended (by 2047) and the MAX is phasing out to none by 2060, so its real rival is NGSA.
- After the US cut it wins 6.3% of new customers, and 3.6% once fps follows.
- Demand falls from 1,933 a year in 2050 to 1,701 in 2055 and 1,106 in 2060.
- The line sets deliveries to 2058. From 2059 the 96 a year (8.7% of the market's deliveries in 2060) leans on overflow, about 26 jets above the 6.3% want.
- Operating profit in present value is only about $0.11B. That is a product for overflow, not for the big market [EX-0085].
(2) Robust funding, without risk to financial health? No.
- Team Korea's 30% ($3.0B) is in the brief, and partners carry $4.5B in all. H1 and leg 1 pass.
- Our 55%, $5.50B, is booked at entry into service in 2054. Net debt goes from $0.7B to $6.2B, 56% of enterprise value. The debt penalty rises by $0.59B, $0.03B in present value, already netted in the grid and never subtracted twice.
- Santana's leg 2 fails: -0.22 $B in S1, below zero in every column. His leg 3 passes: S3 at -2.1 yp is inside the 5-point limit. Under the team rule his veto binds, with no override [EX-0140, EX-0046].
(3) Technology available? Yes, on the brief.
- P&W, the E2's maker, is fitted, and GTF2 has been ready since 2036, offered on standard terms as an installation. The brief reports no engine or supply problem, so Meijer's leg (b) passes.
- His leg (a) fails: NGSA has been in service since 2037, before our 2054 entry into service, in every column. That is his soft veto.

Safety first and quality always: that is the foundation of our culture. We believe we are still in our harvest season, right? We keep delivering our plan with the products we have: the E2 family, our executive jets, defence and services. And we keep a healthy balance sheet to support a potential next move.

We have done the work again this year, with our partners, and the numbers do not prove the return. The investment has to prove its return. So today we have no decision to announce, and we will not discuss a segment or a date. We continue to talk to our partners, including in Korea, and to all the engine makers. On the decisions of other manufacturers: those are their decisions. We have our own strategy, and I can only speak for Embraer.

- Leg 1 passes: Team Korea 30% ($3.0B), suppliers 10%, Brazilian research money 5%, so partners carry $4.5B.
- Leg 2 fails: S1 -0.22 $B (-2.0 yp); S2 -0.20 and S3 -0.23 are below zero too.
- Leg 3 passes: S3 -2.1 yp, inside 5.
His rebuild matches mine: $0.094B of operating profit with the line to 2060, less $0.296B of bill, less $0.032B of penalty, gives -0.234 against the grid's -0.22. The grid implies a tail after 2060 of only $0.014B in S1. I adopt his finding that the line-to-2060 reading is the one this grid bears out, and that the pure-discount reading understated the loss by $0.05B. I accept the debt penalty counted once ($0.59B rise, $0.032B in PV).
I weighed his advice lines as confirming the result, not deciding it:
- net debt 56% of enterprise value, about 7.5x against the inherited 'below 2x';
- investment grade not surviving;
- a cash call of $1.375B a year in 2050-53, 3.4x the capex run rate and 69% of the ~$2B floor;
- four years of suspended cash conversion.
The leverage line rests on his EV/EBITDA conversion, an inference, so it stays advice. I adopt his gap-closing shares (19.6% in S1, 23.1% in S2, 17.8% in S3, 53.5% for the Board's -2 yp) with no credit given. I also adopt his finding that even a zero own share (+1.0 yp) clears neither the 2-yp band nor the override bar. Premium zero, confirmed.
memo_weighing.ops:
Taken in full. His soft veto stands, and I record no override, because none is possible.
- Leg (a) fails: NGSA has been in service since 2037, 17 years before a 2054 entry into service, in S1, S2 and S3. The window is narrow, not shut. H3 is not engaged, since fps would come in 2057 or 2060. H6 is not live.
- Leg (b) passes: P&W is fitted, GTF2 has been ready since 2036 on standard terms as an installation, and the brief reports no engine or supply-chain problem.
- The override bar is +$0.55B in S1. The launch is $0.77B short, and a zero own share reaches only +$0.11B.
I take his account of who sets deliveries: the line to 2058, the share from 2059, and overflow for about 26 of the 96 jets in 2060 (8.7% of about 1,103 delivered, against 6.3% of falling demand). He says S2's $0.02B edge comes from overflow after 2060. I note that as his inference; it does not change the answer. He judges the product edge slight, not compelling, with NGSA as the real rival, and the big market served only through overflow. I adopt that, and it answers my first question. His readiness flags are logged as advice for any later case: 216 jets a year, 192 P&W engines a year, a four-year clean sheet against the E2's 4 years 10 months, and a one-way door. His margin note, 12% in the brief against 2.6% for Commercial Aviation in 2025, points to real-world risk on the downside. It is not priced and not a ground here. He named his E2 anchoring, and I weighed his product and window reading with that in mind.

But no premium can be logged against a failed H2 or a failed CFO leg 2, and no objective is left to buy: a 2054 entry into service cannot meet 'in service by 2040'. Premium logged: $0.00B (0 yp).
final.objective_note:
Briefing goal: a profitable place in the large single-aisle market, without risking the balance sheet.
- 'New narrowbody in service by 2040' is not met. It has been out of reach since the 2035 Hold, the last round whose launch (entry into service 2039) could meet it. A 2050 launch, entering service in 2054, cannot meet it.
- 'ΔPV at or above zero, debt penalty included' is met under Hold, which ends the game at +0.00 $B (100.0%). A Launch would break it (-0.22 $B in S1).
On this brief, a place in the market is not available profitably. The Board does not buy one at about -2 yp against a failed funding test, and neither do I.
